the-chat-to-deployment-flow.title: The chat-to-deployment flow
the-chat-to-deployment-flow.content:
## Overview

Emergent transforms natural-language descriptions into deployed applications through a five-phase workflow. You describe what you want in chat, AI agents write and test the code, you preview the result in real time, iterate until it's right, and then deploy to production—all without leaving the platform.

This page walks through the complete arc from your first prompt to a live URL.

---

## The five phases

<Steps>

<Step title="Prompt: Describe your app">

Start a conversation in the Emergent chat interface (web or [mobile](/building-from-the-emergent-mobile-app)). Write what you want to build in plain language:

- **Simple apps**: "A to-do list with tags and due dates"
- **Data-driven tools**: "A CRM that tracks customer interactions and sends email reminders"
- **Consumer products**: "A recipe sharing app where users can save favorites and comment"

The AI agents parse your intent, ask clarifying questions if needed, and generate a technical plan. You don't need to specify frameworks, libraries, or architecture—the platform selects the stack automatically.

<Tip title="Start broad, then refine">
You'll have many chances to iterate. Begin with the core idea; worry about styling and edge cases later.
</Tip>

</Step>

<Step title="Build: Agents write, test and wire everything">

Once you confirm the plan (or the agents infer enough confidence), code generation begins:

- **Backend services** (API routes, database schemas, authentication) are scaffolded and connected.
- **Frontend UI** (React components, navigation, forms) is generated with responsive design patterns.
- **Integrations** (email, payment APIs, third-party SDKs) are wired in when requested.
- **Tests** run automatically to catch regressions before you see the preview.

The build typically completes in seconds to a few minutes, depending on app complexity. You'll see live progress in the chat and a status indicator in the [workspace](/a-tour-of-the-workspace).

</Step>

<Step title="Preview: Interact with the running app">

As soon as the build succeeds, Emergent spins up a **preview environment**—a fully functional instance of your app at a temporary URL. You can:

- Click through every screen and flow.
- Create test accounts, submit forms, trigger workflows.
- Open the preview on desktop, tablet, or phone to verify responsive behavior.

The preview environment includes live databases, auth, and any third-party integrations you've configured (using sandbox/test keys when appropriate). It's isolated from production, so you can experiment freely.

<Info>
Preview environments persist until you explicitly delete them or deploy a new version. You can share the preview URL with teammates or stakeholders for feedback.
</Info>

Learn more about the [separation between preview and deployed instances](/preview-vs-deployed-separate).

</Step>

<Step title="Iterate: Refine in natural language">

Spot a bug? Want a different layout? Return to the chat and describe the change:

- "Make the search bar sticky at the top"
- "Add a dark mode toggle in settings"
- "Fix the email validation—it's rejecting valid addresses"

The AI agents apply the edits incrementally, re-run tests, and refresh the preview. You can iterate as many times as needed. Each change is version-controlled, so you can roll back if something breaks.

<Tip title="Use screenshots and screen recordings">
Paste images or link to videos in chat to show exactly what needs fixing. The agents understand visual context.
</Tip>

</Step>

<Step title="Deploy: Push to production">

When you're satisfied with the preview, click **Deploy** in the workspace. Emergent:

1. Provisions production infrastructure (databases, storage, CDN).
2. Applies environment-specific configuration (production API keys, domain settings).
3. Runs a final test suite and security scan.
4. Deploys the app to a live, autoscaling environment.

Your app is assigned a default `*.emergent.run` URL immediately. You can [map a custom domain](/custom-domain) anytime after deployment.

<Warning title="Preview and production are separate">
Data, user accounts, and integrations in preview **do not** carry over to production. Plan your production setup (real API keys, payment processors, etc.) before the first deploy.
</Warning>

</Step>

</Steps>

---

## What happens under the hood

While you chat, Emergent's agent orchestrator:

- **Parses requirements** into discrete tasks (UI mockup, data model, API design).
- **Delegates to specialist agents** (frontend, backend, testing, deployment).
- **Runs incremental tests** after every code change to catch regressions.
- **Manages state** so context persists across conversations (you can return days later and pick up where you left off).

All code, configs, and database schemas are generated from scratch or modified in place. Nothing is templated—each app is unique.

---

## Key concepts to know

| Concept | What it means |
|---------|---------------|
| **Workspace** | The central hub where you manage builds, previews, and deployments. See [a tour of the workspace](/a-tour-of-the-workspace). |
| **Preview environment** | A temporary, fully functional instance for testing. Isolated from production. |
| **Deployed instance** | Your production app, live at a public URL with real users and data. |
| **Universal LLM Key** | A single API key that routes to multiple LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, etc.). Required for apps that use AI features. See [the Universal LLM Key](/the-universal-llm-key). |
| **Emergent Auth** | Built-in user authentication (email/password, OAuth, magic links). No third-party auth service needed. See [Emergent Auth](/emergent-auth-built-in). |

Browse the full [glossary of Emergent terms](/glossary-of-emergent-terms) for more definitions.

---

## Mobile apps

Emergent can generate native iOS and Android apps from the same chat-based workflow. The process mirrors web:

1. Prompt for a mobile experience (or convert an existing web app with [web ↔ mobile conversion](/web-mobile-conversion-canonical)).
2. Preview in the mobile simulator or on a physical device via TestFlight / APK.
3. Iterate until ready.
4. Deploy to the App Store and Play Store (Emergent handles [build generation](/build-generation-for-a-pre-existing-play-store-app) and submission prep).

<Note>
Mobile builds take longer than web (3–10 minutes for the first compile) due to native code compilation and app store requirements.
</Note>

---

## Common first-time questions

<AccordionGroup>

<Accordion title="Do I need to write any code?">
No. Emergent generates and maintains all code. You can inspect it in the workspace editor, but editing by hand is optional—most users stay in chat.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Can I connect my own database or API?">
Yes. Emergent provides a managed [MongoDB database](/database-mongodb) by default, but you can connect external PostgreSQL, MySQL, Firebase, or any REST/GraphQL API via environment variables.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="How much does preview cost?">
Preview environments are free and unlimited during your trial. After that, they count toward your plan's build minutes and storage, but there's no separate preview fee.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="What if I don't like the design?">
Iterate in chat. Describe the changes ("use a card layout instead of a list," "match the colors from example.com") and the agents will rebuild. You can also attach design mockups or reference screenshots.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Can I roll back a deployment?">
Yes. Every deployment is versioned. You can revert to any previous version from the workspace **Deployments** panel with one click.
</Accordion>

</AccordionGroup>

---

## Next steps

<CardGroup cols={2}>

<Card title="Tour the workspace" icon="compass" href="/a-tour-of-the-workspace">
Get familiar with the interface, panels, and controls before your first build.
</Card>

<Card title="Start building from mobile" icon="mobile" href="/building-from-the-emergent-mobile-app">
Use the Emergent iOS or Android app to prompt and preview on the go.
</Card>

<Card title="Set up Emergent Auth" icon="lock" href="/emergent-auth-built-in">
Add user sign-up, login, and session management to your app in one prompt.
</Card>

<Card title="Connect a custom domain" icon="globe" href="/custom-domain">
Replace the default `*.emergent.run` URL with your own domain after deployment.
</Card>

</CardGroup>
the-chat-to-deployment-flow.description: The big-picture arc of building on Emergent: prompt -> build -> preview -> iterate -> deploy. A map of the whole journey before diving in.

package-name-bundle-id-app-id.title: Package name, Bundle ID & App ID
package-name-bundle-id-app-id.content:
## What are package names, bundle IDs and app IDs?

Every mobile app needs a unique identifier that distinguishes it from all other apps on the platform. These identifiers are platform-specific:

- **Android package name** — a reverse-domain-style string like `com.yourcompany.appname` that uniquely identifies your app on Google Play and Android devices.
- **iOS bundle ID** — a similar reverse-domain string (e.g. `com.yourcompany.appname`) that identifies your app in the App Store and across Apple's ecosystem.
- **App ID** — in Apple's developer portal, the bundle ID is registered as an "App ID" that controls entitlements, certificates and provisioning profiles.

Emergent automatically generates these identifiers for you during your first build or publish. You don't need to register them yourself — the platform handles provisioning and signing behind the scenes.

<Note title="Generated at first build">
The package name and bundle ID are created when you request your first mobile build or submit to an app store. Until that moment, they don't exist in the project.
</Note>

## Package name & bundle ID cannot change after first build

Once Emergent has published your first build (or submitted to an app store), the package name and bundle ID are **permanently locked** for that project. You cannot rename or change them later.

<Warning title="Plan your identifier before first publish">
Choose your app's name and branding carefully before triggering the first build. Changing the package name or bundle ID later requires creating an entirely new app listing in the stores — your existing installs, reviews and rankings will not transfer.
</Warning>

### Align integrations with the same identifier

Any third-party integration you configure — Apple Music APIs, Firebase services, OAuth providers, push notification certificates — must be registered using the **exact same** bundle ID or package name that Emergent generated.

If you register an Apple Music integration under `com.example.myapp` but your iOS bundle ID is `com.example.myapp2`, the integration will fail at runtime. Always verify that external dashboards (Apple Developer, Google Cloud Console, etc.) use the identifier Emergent assigned.

<Tip>
You can find your app's package name and bundle ID in the workspace under **Settings → Mobile** after the first build has completed.
</Tip>

## Native mobile apps do not require a domain

Unlike web apps, native iOS and Android applications do not need a custom domain to function. The app stores distribute your APK or IPA directly to users' devices; there is no URL to visit.

<Info title="No domain purchase required">
You can build, publish and distribute a mobile app on Emergent without buying or configuring a domain. If you later decide to add a companion website or [convert your app to web](/web-mobile-conversion-canonical), you can attach a [custom domain](/custom-domain) at that time.
</Info>

Universal links (iOS) and App Links (Android) *can* use a domain to deep-link into your app, but the app itself runs independently of any web address.

scheduled-tasks-background-jobs-in-your-.title: Scheduled tasks & background jobs in your app
scheduled-tasks-background-jobs-in-your-.content:
<Callout type="warning" title="In-process schedulers will fail under scale-to-zero">
If your app uses an in-process scheduler—APScheduler, Celery beat, Python's `threading.Timer`, or similar—those tasks **will not run** when your container scales to zero. On lower tiers that scale to zero after inactivity, scheduled jobs can silently die, causing missed runs and data inconsistency.
</Callout>

## Why in-process schedulers break

Emergent's platform automatically scales your container to zero replicas when no HTTP requests arrive for a period. This saves resources and keeps costs predictable. When the next request arrives, a fresh container spins up.

**The problem:** schedulers like APScheduler and Celery beat run inside your application process. When the container stops, the scheduler stops. When a new container starts later, it has no memory of what was scheduled—missed intervals are lost, and one-time jobs scheduled for a past timestamp will never fire.

Common symptoms:

- Daily data exports never run
- Periodic cleanup tasks accumulate stale records
- Notification reminders are skipped
- Background aggregations drift out of sync

## Recommended patterns

Choose one of the following approaches based on your tier and workload:

<Tabs>
<Tab title="External cron (recommended for most apps)">
**Use an external service to trigger an HTTP endpoint** on your app at the desired interval. This works on every tier, including those that scale to zero.

<Steps>
<Step title="Create a task endpoint">
Add a route that performs the scheduled work:

```python
@app.post("/tasks/daily-cleanup")
def daily_cleanup(request):
    # Validate secret header to prevent abuse
    if request.headers.get("X-Cron-Secret") != os.getenv("CRON_SECRET"):
        return {"error": "Unauthorized"}, 401
    
    # Perform the task
    db.stale_records.delete_many({"created_at": {"$lt": cutoff_date}})
    return {"status": "ok"}
```
</Step>

<Step title="Protect the endpoint">
Set a secret environment variable (`CRON_SECRET`) and check it in the handler to prevent public abuse.
</Step>

<Step title="Configure an external trigger">
Use a service like:

- [GitHub Actions scheduled workflows](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule) (free, YAML cron syntax)
- [EasyCron](https://www.easycron.com/) or [cron-job.org](https://cron-job.org) (free tiers available)
- Cloud provider cron (AWS EventBridge, GCP Cloud Scheduler, Azure Logic Apps)

Point the trigger at `https://your-app.emergent.run/tasks/daily-cleanup` with the secret header.
</Step>
</Steps>

**Pros:**  
• Works on all tiers  
• Reliable timing even when app is idle  
• Simple to test and debug

**Cons:**  
• Requires external dependency  
• Adds a small coordination overhead
</Tab>

<Tab title="Always-on tier">
If you upgrade to a tier that **does not scale to zero**, in-process schedulers will work reliably because at least one container is always running.

Check your plan's scaling behavior in the [workspace settings](/a-tour-of-the-workspace#deployment-tiers). Tiers labeled "always-on" or "minimum 1 replica" maintain scheduler state.

**Pros:**  
• Familiar libraries (APScheduler, Celery beat)  
• No external coordination needed

**Cons:**  
• Higher cost (containers run 24/7)  
• Still at risk if your single replica crashes and restarts
</Tab>

<Tab title="Decoupled async workers">
For complex task graphs or high-volume queues, use a **dedicated message broker and worker process**:

- **Broker:** Redis (via [Upstash](https://upstash.com/) or self-hosted) or a managed queue (AWS SQS, GCP Pub/Sub)
- **Worker framework:** Celery with Redis backend, or RQ (Python)
- **Scheduler:** External cron pushes messages to the broker; workers consume them

This pattern decouples scheduling from execution and scales workers independently of your web tier.

**Pros:**  
• Resilient to web-tier restarts  
• Scales task processing independently  
• Supports retries, task prioritization, and parallel execution

**Cons:**  
• More infrastructure to manage  
• Additional cost for broker and worker containers
</Tab>
</Tabs>

## Migration checklist

If you currently rely on an in-process scheduler:

<Steps>
<Step title="Audit scheduled tasks">
List every cron, interval, or delayed job currently running in-process.
</Step>

<Step title="Choose a pattern">
External cron for simple periodic tasks; always-on tier or decoupled workers for complex workloads.
</Step>

<Step title="Refactor to HTTP endpoints">
Move task logic into routes protected by a secret header.
</Step>

<Step title="Configure external triggers">
Set up GitHub Actions workflows, cloud cron jobs, or a third-party service.
</Step>

<Step title="Remove in-process scheduler">
Delete APScheduler, Celery beat, or threading logic from your app startup to avoid confusion.
</Step>

<Step title="Test end-to-end">
Trigger the endpoint manually, then wait for the scheduled run to confirm the external service is working.
</Step>
</Steps>

## Example: migrating APScheduler to external cron

**Before (in-process, fails on scale-to-zero):**

```python
from apscheduler.schedulers.background import BackgroundScheduler

scheduler = BackgroundScheduler()
scheduler.add_job(cleanup_stale_records, 'cron', hour=2)
scheduler.start()
```

**After (external cron triggers HTTP endpoint):**

```python
@app.post("/tasks/cleanup")
def cleanup_task(request):
    if request.headers.get("X-Cron-Secret") != os.getenv("CRON_SECRET"):
        return {"error": "Unauthorized"}, 401
    
    cleanup_stale_records()
    return {"status": "completed"}
```

**GitHub Actions workflow** (`.github/workflows/daily-cleanup.yml`):

```yaml
name: Daily cleanup
on:
  schedule:
    - cron: '0 2 * * *'  # 02:00 UTC daily
jobs:
  trigger:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Call cleanup endpoint
        run: |
          curl -X POST https://your-app.emergent.run/tasks/cleanup \
            -H "X-Cron-Secret: ${{ secrets.CRON_SECRET }}"
```

<Tip>
Store `CRON_SECRET` in your repository's GitHub secrets and mirror it as an environment variable in your Emergent [workspace settings](/a-tour-of-the-workspace#environment-variables).
</Tip>

## Related topics

<CardGroup cols={2}>
<Card title="Deployment tiers" icon="layer-group" href="/a-tour-of-the-workspace">
Compare scaling behavior and replica policies across plans
</Card>
<Card title="Database (MongoDB)" icon="database" href="/database-mongodb">
Persist task state, job history, and execution logs
</Card>
</CardGroup>

your-first-build-walkthrough.title: Your first build (walkthrough)
your-first-build-walkthrough.content:
## Before you begin

This walkthrough assumes you have signed into Emergent and are looking at a blank project or the home screen. If you're not familiar with the workspace, take a quick look at [A tour of the workspace](/a-tour-of-the-workspace).

<Note title="What you'll build">
This guide walks you through building a small, scoped app—a book tracker—so you can see the entire flow from prompt to live app in under 20 minutes.
</Note>

## Step 1: Pick a simple idea

Start small. Your first build should be something you can describe in a few sentences and that doesn't require complex integrations.

**Good first projects:**
- A personal book tracker (title, author, rating, read/unread status)
- A habit tracker with daily checkboxes
- A quick notes app with tags
- A simple expense logger

**Avoid for your first build:**
- Marketplaces with payments and user matching
- Apps requiring third-party APIs you've never used
- Complex workflows with multi-step approvals

<Tip>
The simpler your first idea, the faster you'll see results and understand how the platform thinks.
</Tip>

## Step 2: Write your first prompt

A strong first prompt includes four elements:

1. **Purpose** — what the app does in one sentence
2. **Core features** — 3–5 bullet points of what users can do
3. **Design hint** — visual style or mood (e.g. "clean and minimal," "warm and colorful")
4. **UX hint** — how it should feel to use (e.g. "fast data entry," "one-tap actions")

**Example prompt:**

```
Build a book tracker app where I can:
- Add books with title, author, cover image URL, and rating
- Mark books as read or unread
- Filter by read status
- Search by title or author

Design: Clean and minimal, good use of whitespace.
UX: Fast to add a new book—prefer a floating action button and inline form.
```

<Info>
You don't need to specify tech stack, database schema, or file structure—the agent will handle those details. Focus on *what* the app should do and *how* it should feel.
</Info>

For more on effective prompting, see [What and How](/what-and-how).

## Step 3: Answer the agent's clarifying questions

After you submit your prompt, the agent will ask a few setup questions. Common ones include:

<AccordionGroup>
<Accordion title="Universal LLM Key vs. your own API key">
The **Universal Key** is included with your Emergent account and covers most builds. If you have your own OpenAI or Anthropic key and want to use it (for cost control or higher rate limits), you can provide it here.

For most first builds, choose the Universal Key. Learn more in [The Universal LLM Key](/the-universal-llm-key).
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Authentication preferences">
The agent will ask if your app needs user accounts and login. For a personal book tracker, you might skip auth. For a shared or multi-user app, choose [Emergent Auth](/emergent-auth-built-in) (built-in, zero setup) or bring your own (Clerk, Auth0, etc.).

You can always add auth later.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Design preferences">
If you didn't specify design details in your prompt, the agent may ask about color scheme, layout style, or component library. You can answer briefly ("modern, dark mode preferred") or say "your choice" and let the agent decide.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Start building now or discuss the plan first?">
The agent will offer to either start building immediately or walk you through the plan first.

- **Start building now**: Faster; good when your idea is clear.
- **Explain the plan first**: Safer for complex projects; you can refine before credits are spent.

For your first build, **"explain the plan first"** is recommended—you'll see what the agent intends to build and can adjust before work begins.
</Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

<Warning title="Credit spend starts when building begins">
Clarifying questions and plan discussions do not consume build credits. Credits are deducted once the agent starts generating code, running tests, and deploying. If you ask the agent to explain first, you can review and cancel before any credits are used.
</Warning>

## Step 4: Watch it build

Once you confirm, the agent begins building. You'll see a real-time stream of steps in the chat:

- **Planning** — breaking your spec into components and routes
- **Scaffolding** — creating project structure, installing dependencies
- **Implementation** — writing React components, API routes, database schema
- **Testing** — running automated checks for errors
- **Deployment** — pushing to a live preview URL

Each step includes a short explanation of what's happening and why. You can expand individual steps for code diffs and logs.

<Steps>
<Step title="Build starts">
The agent confirms the plan and begins scaffolding the project. You'll see progress indicators for each phase.
</Step>

<Step title="Real-time updates">
As the agent writes code, it streams explanations and file changes. You can scroll through the chat to see what's being built.
</Step>

<Step title="Testing and fixes">
If the agent detects errors (missing imports, type mismatches, etc.), it will fix them automatically and re-run tests. You'll see these iterations in the chat.
</Step>

<Step title="Deployment">
Once tests pass, the agent deploys your app to a live preview URL. The link appears in chat—click it to open your app in a new tab.
</Step>
</Steps>

<Info title="Typical build duration">
Most first builds take **5–15 minutes**, depending on complexity and current platform load. Simple CRUD apps (like a book tracker) are usually closer to 5 minutes.
</Info>

## How long builds take & working while you wait

Build time depends on the scope of your prompt and the number of features:

| App complexity | Typical duration |
|----------------|------------------|
| Single-model CRUD (e.g. book tracker) | 5–10 minutes |
| Multi-model app with relationships | 10–20 minutes |
| App with external API integrations | 15–25 minutes |
| Complex workflow or custom auth | 20–40 minutes |

**What you can do while waiting:**

- **Keep the tab open** — you'll see progress updates and can jump in if the agent asks a question.
- **Work in another tab** — builds run in the background; you'll get a browser notification when deployment is ready.
- **Review the build log** — scroll up in chat to see what files were created and why.
- **Start a second project** — Emergent supports multiple concurrent builds (subject to your plan limits).

You do **not** need to stay focused on the chat window. The agent will complete the build and notify you when the preview URL is live.

## Prompting basics

Effective prompts lead to faster builds, lower credit usage, and fewer revision rounds. Here are four principles:

### 1. Be specific and detailed

The agent rewards clarity. Instead of "build a task app," write:

> Build a task app where users can create tasks with a title, due date, and priority level (low/medium/high). Show tasks in a list sorted by due date. Let users mark tasks complete with a checkbox.

Specific prompts reduce back-and-forth and help the agent make better architectural decisions.

### 2. Concise features beat mega-prompts

A prompt with **3–5 well-defined features** is more effective than a wall of text with 20 vague requirements.

**Why?**
- The agent can plan a coherent data model and UI flow.
- You spend fewer credits on rework when scope is clear.
- You can always add features in follow-up prompts after the initial build.

<Tip>
Think of your first prompt as an MVP (minimum viable product). You can iterate and expand once the core is working.
</Tip>

### 3. Ask the agent to explain before building

If you're uncertain about feasibility or want to review the plan, add this to your prompt:

> Explain how you'd build this—don't start coding yet.

The agent will walk you through the proposed tech stack, data schema, and page structure. You can then refine or approve before credits are spent.

### 4. Why pasting a ChatGPT plan underperforms

If you've drafted a detailed spec in ChatGPT (or another LLM) and paste it into Emergent, you may find the build less smooth than expected.

**Reasons:**
- External specs often include implementation details (file names, folder structure, library choices) that conflict with Emergent's conventions.
- ChatGPT-generated plans are optimized for *explanation*, not for *execution* in Emergent's agentic workflow.
- The Emergent agent works best when it can ask clarifying questions and make architectural decisions in context.

**Better approach:**
- Use your ChatGPT draft as a reference, then write a concise natural-language prompt describing *what* the app should do and *how* it should feel—not *how* to build it.
- Let the Emergent agent ask questions and propose the structure.

<Note>
If you have a detailed spec you want to preserve, consider sharing it as context when the agent asks for clarification, rather than as the initial prompt.
</Note>

## Voice mode

You can describe your app using voice input instead of typing. This is especially useful for:

- Rapid ideation and iteration
- Mobile builds (see [Building from the Emergent mobile app](/building-from-the-emergent-mobile-app))
- When you want to sketch an idea conversationally

**How voice works:**
1. Click the microphone icon in the chat input (desktop) or tap the voice button (mobile).
2. Speak your prompt naturally: "I want to build a book tracker where I can add books, rate them, and mark them as read or unread."
3. Review the transcription and edit if needed, then send.

The agent processes voice input the same way as text. You can mix voice and text throughout the build—use voice for high-level instructions and text for precise details like field names or design tweaks.

<Tip title="Voice is faster for exploration">
If you're not sure exactly what you want, voice mode lets you iterate quickly. Describe a rough idea, hear the agent's plan, then refine in follow-up voice messages.
</Tip>

For more on mobile voice builds, see [Building from the Emergent mobile app](/building-from-the-emergent-mobile-app).

---

## What's next

Once your first build is live:

<CardGroup cols={2}>
<Card title="Iterate on your build" icon="code" href="/what-is-a-job">
Ask the agent to add features, fix bugs, or adjust design. Each request creates a new job.
</Card>

<Card title="Understand the chat-to-deployment flow" icon="arrow-right" href="/the-chat-to-deployment-flow">
Learn how Emergent interprets prompts, generates code, tests, and deploys.
</Card>

<Card title="Explore integrations" icon="plug" href="/key-integrations-catalogue">
Connect to Stripe, SendGrid, third-party APIs, and more.
</Card>

<Card title="Learn about credits" icon="coins" href="/credit-expiry-recharging">
Understand how build credits work, when they expire, and how to recharge.
</Card>
</CardGroup>
your-first-build-walkthrough.description: 1. Pick a simple idea (e.g. book tracker); keep it small.

troubleshooting.title: Troubleshooting
troubleshooting.content:
## Build Failures

Mobile builds can fail for a variety of reasons. Most are fixable by checking credentials, dependencies, or build logs.

**Common causes and fixes:**

- **Expired or missing credentials** — EAS needs valid Apple Developer or Google Play Console credentials to sign your app. Check that your account is active and that you've uploaded the correct certificates and provisioning profiles. Re-run the credential setup if needed.
- **Insufficient EAS credits** — Builds consume credits on your Expo account. If you've exhausted your monthly allocation, the build will queue indefinitely or fail. Check your Expo dashboard and add credits if necessary.
- **Native dependency conflicts** — If your app uses a library that requires specific native modules or has incompatible peer dependencies, the build may fail during the dependency resolution step. Review the build logs for `npm` or `yarn` errors and update or remove the conflicting package.
- **Out-of-date `eas-cli`** — Ensure you're running a recent version of the EAS CLI. Run `npm install -g eas-cli` to update.
- **Incorrect `app.json` or `eas.json` configuration** — Typos in bundle identifiers, version codes, or build profiles will cause silent failures or validation errors. Double-check these files against the [Publishing to the stores](/publishing-to-the-stores) checklist.

<Tip title="Read the build logs">
Always expand the full build log in the Expo dashboard. The error is usually near the end and tells you exactly which step failed.
</Tip>

---

## Submission Rejected

Apple and Google both review submissions before your app goes live. Common rejection reasons include:

| Reason | Platform | Fix |
|--------|----------|-----|
| Missing privacy policy or terms of service | Both | Add a publicly accessible link in your app's store listing and in-app settings. |
| Sign in with Apple not implemented | iOS | If you offer any third-party sign-in (Google, Facebook), Apple requires you also offer Sign in with Apple. Add it or remove other social logins. |
| App crashes on launch | Both | Test on a physical device before submission. If using Expo Go for testing, note that production builds behave differently—always test a production `.ipa` or `.aab`. |
| Incomplete or misleading screenshots | Both | Use real app screenshots that accurately represent functionality. Avoid mockups or marketing graphics that don't match the actual UI. |
| Incorrect age rating | Both | Ensure your app's content rating matches what reviewers see. If your app allows user-generated content, declare it and implement moderation. See [App takedown & content moderation](/app-takedown-content-moderation). |
| Bundle ID or package name mismatch | Both | The identifier in your build must exactly match what you registered in App Store Connect or Google Play Console. Check `app.json` → `ios.bundleIdentifier` and `android.package`. |

<Warning title="Sign in with Apple audience validation">
A common iOS rejection occurs when Sign in with Apple is configured with the wrong audience (client ID). See the dedicated section below for the fix.
</Warning>

If your app is rejected, the store will provide specific feedback. Address each point, increment your build number, and resubmit.

---

## Updates Not Appearing

You've published an over-the-air (OTA) update using `eas update`, but users aren't seeing the new version.

**Why this happens:**

- **The update hasn't propagated yet** — OTA updates can take a few minutes to reach all edge servers. Wait 5–10 minutes and force-close/reopen the app.
- **Update channel mismatch** — Your build is configured to listen to a specific update channel (e.g., `production`). If you published to `preview` but your build expects `production`, the update won't load. Check `eas.json` and ensure the channel in your `eas update --channel X` command matches the build profile.
- **App not connected to the internet** — OTA updates require a network connection. If the device is offline or has restrictive firewall rules, updates can't download.
- **Native code changed** — OTA updates only work for JavaScript and asset changes. If you modified native dependencies, permissions, or anything in the `ios` or `android` folders, you must submit a new build to the stores.
- **Update policy set to `ON_LOAD` with long session** — By default, Expo checks for updates when the app launches. If a user never fully closes the app, they won't fetch the new update. Consider using `ON_ERROR_RECOVERY` or prompting users to restart.

<Steps>
<Step title="Verify the update was published">
Run `eas update:list --branch <your-branch>` and confirm the latest update ID matches what you just published.
</Step>
<Step title="Check the build's update channel">
Look in `eas.json` under the build profile you deployed (e.g., `preview` or `production`) and note the `channel` field. It must match the `--channel` you used in `eas update`.
</Step>
<Step title="Force a fresh launch">
Fully quit the app (swipe it away from the app switcher) and relaunch. The update should download on the next open if the channel is correct.
</Step>
</Steps>

<Info>
If you're testing in Expo Go, note that Expo Go does not respect EAS Update channels the same way standalone builds do. Always test OTA updates in a production or preview build installed via TestFlight or internal testing tracks.
</Info>

---

## Icons Show as Boxes on Android (Expo Go)

When testing on Android using Expo Go, vector icons from libraries like `@expo/vector-icons` or `react-native-vector-icons` render as empty boxes (sometimes called "tofu").

**Cause:** Expo Go's Android build does not bundle every possible icon font by default. The iOS version of Expo Go does, which is why the issue is Android-specific.

**Fix:**

<Steps>
<Step title="Use a production build for testing">
The simplest solution is to create a development or preview build with `eas build --profile preview` or `eas build --profile development`. These builds include all icon fonts your app declares.
</Step>
<Step title="Or switch to PNG/SVG assets">
If you must test in Expo Go, replace vector icons with static image assets (`.png` or `.svg` rendered via `react-native-svg`). This is not recommended for production, as vector icons scale better.
</Step>
</Steps>

<Tip>
This issue **only** affects Expo Go on Android. Once you build a standalone `.apk` or `.aab`, vector icons will render correctly.
</Tip>

---

## Sign in with Apple Rejection

**Symptom:** Your iOS app is rejected with a message like "Sign in with Apple does not work" or "Invalid client configuration," even though authentication works fine in testing.

**Root cause:** Sign in with Apple validates the **audience** (`aud`) claim in the ID token. If your backend or auth provider is configured to use the wrong client ID—often the **Services ID** instead of the **bundle identifier**—Apple's review team will see a validation error.

**How to fix:**

<Steps>
<Step title="Identify which identifier you're using">
Check your backend's Apple auth configuration or your Firebase/Auth0/Supabase settings. Look for the field labeled "Client ID," "Services ID," or "Audience."
</Step>
<Step title="Use the bundle ID, not the Services ID">
For native iOS apps, the `aud` claim in the ID token must match your app's **bundle identifier** (e.g., `com.yourcompany.yourapp`), **not** the Services ID you created in the Apple Developer portal.
</Step>
<Step title="Update your auth provider config">
- **Firebase:** Set the OAuth client ID to your bundle identifier.
- **Auth0 / Supabase / Custom backend:** Ensure the Apple connection or client config specifies the bundle ID as the audience.
</Step>
<Step title="Test with a production build">
Always test Sign in with Apple on a physical device using a build installed via TestFlight or direct `.ipa` sideload. Expo Go and simulators behave differently.
</Step>
<Step title="Resubmit">
Increment your build number, create a new build with the corrected config, and resubmit to App Store Connect.
</Step>
</Steps>

<Warning>
Do not share the same Services ID across web and native. Use the bundle ID for iOS and a separate Services ID for your web client if you have a browser-based flow.
</Warning>

---

## Quick Reference

An at-a-glance checklist for mobile publishing and troubleshooting.

### Pre-Submission Checklist

- [ ] Bundle ID (iOS) and package name (Android) match your store registrations
- [ ] App version and build number incremented in `app.json`
- [ ] App icon and splash screen assets present and correctly sized
- [ ] Privacy policy and terms of service URLs live and accessible
- [ ] Sign in with Apple implemented if you offer any third-party sign-in (iOS only)
- [ ] All required permissions declared and justified in store listing
- [ ] App tested on a production build (not Expo Go)
- [ ] Credentials uploaded to EAS (run `eas credentials` if unsure)

### Common Commands

| Task | Command |
|------|---------|
| Build for iOS (production) | `eas build --platform ios --profile production` |
| Build for Android (production) | `eas build --platform android --profile production` |
| Submit iOS to App Store | `eas submit --platform ios` |
| Submit Android to Play Store | `eas submit --platform android` |
| Publish an OTA update | `eas update --branch production --message "Bug fixes"` |
| List recent updates | `eas update:list --branch production` |
| Check build status | `eas build:list` |
| Configure credentials | `eas credentials` |
| View build logs | Open the build URL from `eas build:list` in your browser |

### Troubleshooting Decision Tree

```
Build failed?
├─ Check build logs for errors
├─ Verify credentials in EAS dashboard
└─ Ensure eas.json and app.json are valid

Submission rejected?
├─ Review rejection notice from Apple/Google
├─ Fix each listed issue
└─ Increment build number and resubmit

Update not appearing?
├─ Confirm update channel matches build profile
├─ Wait 5–10 minutes for propagation
└─ Fully quit and relaunch the app

Icons render as boxes (Android Expo Go)?
└─ Build a development/preview build instead

Sign in with Apple fails in review?
└─ Set audience to bundle ID, not Services ID
```

<Info>
For deeper context on how builds and deployments work, see [Publishing to the stores](/publishing-to-the-stores). For performance and stability issues, see [App slow, crashing or cold-starting](/app-slow-crashing-or-cold-starting).
</Info>

building-from-the-emergent-mobile-app.title: Building from the Emergent mobile app
building-from-the-emergent-mobile-app.content:
## Overview

The Emergent mobile app (iOS, Android and Progressive Web App) lets you build, preview and manage your projects on the go. You can chat with agents, watch builds in real time, test in-app previews, push OTA updates and navigate between projects—all from your phone or tablet.

The mobile experience is optimized for **iterating and monitoring** existing apps. For first-time project creation and advanced workflows (GitHub sync, [HIM mode](/him-human-in-middle-mode), VS Code integration), use the web workspace at [emergent.ai](https://emergent.ai).

---

## What you can do

<CardGroup cols={2}>
  <Card title="Chat & build" icon="message-square">
    Describe features, review agent changes and approve builds in the conversation thread.
  </Card>
  <Card title="In-app preview" icon="smartphone">
    See your app running natively—no waiting for a deploy or opening a browser.
  </Card>
  <Card title="OTA updates" icon="refresh-cw">
    Push over-the-air updates to published apps instantly from the mobile app.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Deep linking" icon="link">
    Jump directly into a project or preview from push notifications and shared links.
  </Card>
</CardGroup>

---

## Navigation tabs

The Emergent mobile app has four bottom tabs:

| Tab | Icon | What it does |
|-----|------|--------------|
| **Home** | house | Your workspace: recent projects, team activity, notifications. |
| **Projects** | folder | Filterable list of all your apps—open any to start building. |
| **Preview** | smartphone | Live native preview of the currently selected project (see [Preview vs Deployed](/preview-vs-deployed-separate)). |
| **Account** | user | Subscription, team settings, sign out. |

<Tip title="Swipe to switch projects">
In the **Preview** tab, swipe left or right to cycle through your most recent projects.
</Tip>

---

## Opening and building a project

<Steps>
  <Step title="Tap a project card">
    In **Projects** or from your **Home** feed, tap the app you want to work on.
  </Step>
  <Step title="Chat with agents">
    The conversation thread appears. Describe changes, ask questions or approve pending builds.
  </Step>
  <Step title="Review the build">
    When the agent finishes, tap **Preview** in the bottom bar to see the updated app running natively.
  </Step>
  <Step title="Iterate">
    Continue chatting to refine features; each approved build refreshes the preview automatically.
  </Step>
</Steps>

<Note>
The mobile app streams build logs and test results in real time, just like the web workspace.
</Note>

---

## In-app native preview

The **Preview** tab renders your app using **native mobile components** (React Native, Capacitor or Flutter, depending on your stack). This means:

- **Instant feedback**—no deploy step, no opening a browser.
- **True device features**—camera, GPS, push notifications, biometrics.
- **Offline-first testing**—check how your app behaves without a network connection.

<Warning>
The preview runs the **latest build** in the selected environment (usually `main`). To test a different environment, switch it in the project header before opening Preview.
</Warning>

If your app is slow or crashes in preview, see [App slow, crashing or cold-starting](/app-slow-crashing-or-cold-starting).

---

## Over-the-air (OTA) updates

Once you've published an app to the App Store or Play Store, you can push **instant updates** to live users without waiting for store review:

<Steps>
  <Step title="Build a new version">
    Chat with the agent and approve the build as usual.
  </Step>
  <Step title="Tap 'Push OTA Update'">
    In the project header menu (three dots), select **Push OTA Update**.
  </Step>
  <Step title="Confirm target environment">
    Choose `production`, `staging`, or another [environment](/clone-environment). The update goes live within seconds.
  </Step>
</Steps>

<Info>
OTA updates work for **JavaScript, assets and styling**. Native binary changes (new permissions, SDKs) still require a full App Store / Play Store release.
</Info>

For setup and limits, see [Push notifications](/push-notifications) and [Build generation for a pre-existing Play Store app](/build-generation-for-a-pre-existing-play-store-app).

---

## Deep linking

Emergent deep links let you jump into a specific project or preview from:

- **Push notifications**—when a build finishes or a team member comments.
- **Shared links**—a teammate sends you `emergent.app/p/<project-id>`.
- **QR codes**—scan a code on a laptop screen to open the same project on your phone.

<Tip>
If you're signed in to multiple Emergent accounts (personal + work), the app prompts you to choose which workspace to open.
</Tip>

---

## Feature limits (mobile vs web)

The mobile app is designed for **iteration and monitoring**. The following advanced workflows are **only available on the web**:

| Feature | Mobile | Web |
|---------|--------|-----|
| Create a new project | ❌ | ✅ |
| Maxx (full AI rebuild) | ❌ | ✅ |
| Fork / Clone project | ❌ | ✅ ([Clone environment](/clone-environment) is web-only) |
| Push to GitHub | ❌ | ✅ |
| [HIM mode](/him-human-in-middle-mode) (approve every file) | ❌ | ✅ |
| VS Code integration | ❌ | ✅ |
| Bulk environment management | ❌ | ✅ |
| In-chat preview (same window) | ❌ | ✅ |
| Native app preview (separate tab) | ✅ | ❌ (use browser preview) |

<Note>
You **can** chat, build, test and deploy from mobile—you just can't create brand-new projects or use GitHub/VS Code sync.
</Note>

---

## Installing the mobile app

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="iOS">
    Download from the [App Store](https://apps.apple.com/app/emergent) (requires iOS 15+).
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Android">
    Download from [Google Play](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=ai.emergent) (requires Android 8+).
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Progressive Web App">
    Visit [app.emergent.ai](https://app.emergent.ai) on any mobile browser and tap **Add to Home Screen**. The PWA offers most features but lacks deep native integrations (camera, biometrics).
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

---

## Switching between web and mobile

Your workspace **syncs instantly**:

1. Start a build on mobile.
2. Open the same project on the web—you'll see the build in progress.
3. Approve the next change on the web; your mobile preview refreshes automatically.

For a deep dive on how Emergent handles cross-platform state, see [Web ↔ Mobile conversion (canonical)](/web-mobile-conversion-canonical).

---

## Best practices

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Use mobile for quick tweaks, web for heavy lifting">
    Chat-based iteration works great on mobile. For major refactors, new project setup or GitHub workflows, switch to the web workspace.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Test on real devices">
    The native preview is the fastest way to catch UI glitches, performance bottlenecks and permission prompts before you ship.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Enable push notifications">
    Get notified when builds finish, teammates comment or your app is flagged for moderation (see [App takedown & content moderation](/app-takedown-content-moderation)).
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Keep the app updated">
    Emergent ships new mobile features weekly. Enable auto-updates in the App Store / Play Store to stay current.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

---

## Next steps

<CardGroup cols={2}>
  <Card title="A tour of the workspace" icon="compass" href="/a-tour-of-the-workspace">
    Explore tabs, panels and shortcuts in the web UI.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Preview vs Deployed" icon="eye" href="/preview-vs-deployed-separate">
    Understand the difference between in-app preview and live production URLs.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Push notifications" icon="bell" href="/push-notifications">
    Set up alerts for builds, deploys and team activity.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Database (MongoDB)" icon="database" href="/database-mongodb">
    Query and manage your app's data from mobile or web.
  </Card>
</CardGroup>
building-from-the-emergent-mobile-app.description: Build and manage apps from Emergent's own iOS/Android/PWA app - navigation tabs, in-app previews, OTA updates, deep linking. Note feature limits vs web (no project creation; no Max

glossary-of-emergent-terms.title: Glossary of Emergent terms
glossary-of-emergent-terms.content:
## Agentic development

**Agentic development** describes a workflow where autonomous AI agents write, test, debug and deploy code on behalf of the user. In Emergent, you describe what you want in natural language and agents handle the implementation—selecting frameworks, scaffolding components, wiring APIs and iterating on feedback.

---

## ECU (Emergent Compute Unit)

An **ECU** is Emergent's billing unit, similar to a credit. Building, testing and deploying apps consumes ECUs. Different operations cost different amounts: a simple front-end change may use a few ECUs, while generating video or refactoring a large codebase costs more. Your plan includes a monthly ECU allowance; extra usage is billed at your plan's overage rate.

<Info>
Most users on the Starter plan build 2–5 full-stack projects per month before hitting their ECU limit.
</Info>

---

## Job

A **Job** is a discrete task the agent executes—for example "add dark mode toggle," "create a login page," or "deploy to production." Jobs appear in the chat as the agent works. Larger requests are automatically split into multiple Jobs. You can monitor Job progress in the workspace sidebar and chat history.

---

## Redeploy vs Replace

- **Redeploy** pushes your latest code to the live production URL. The app's environment variables, custom domain, database and analytics remain unchanged. Use this for routine updates.
- **Replace** tears down the current deployment and creates a brand-new one from scratch—new URLs, new environment IDs, new database cluster if applicable. Existing custom domains and environment variables must be reconfigured. Use Replace only when instructed by support or when troubleshooting severe infrastructure issues.

<Warning title="Replace is destructive">
Replace deletes your current deployment endpoints and requires re-linking custom domains. Always Redeploy unless you have a specific reason to Replace.
</Warning>

---

## Universal LLM Key

The **Universal LLM Key** is a single API credential that routes requests to over 200 LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Cohere, Llama, Mistral and more) through a unified interface. Emergent apps can call any model without managing multiple API keys. The Universal Key is billed on actual LLM usage (measured in tokens/requests) with no markup; you see the cost breakdown in your project's billing panel.

Learn more in [The Universal LLM Key](/the-universal-llm-key).

---

## Maxx mode

**Maxx mode** gives agents extended autonomy: larger context windows, permission to refactor multiple files in parallel, and the ability to iterate without waiting for your approval at each step. Maxx mode consumes more ECUs but produces higher-quality results for complex requests. Enable it by toggling the "Maxx" switch in the chat composer when you want the agent to "go deep" on a feature.

<Tip>
Use Maxx mode for new features with unclear requirements or when you want the agent to explore multiple design options.
</Tip>

---

## Preview vs Deployed

- **Preview** is the live URL that updates every time the agent saves changes. Use it to test work-in-progress features. The Preview URL is publicly accessible but not indexed by search engines.
- **Deployed** (also called "Production") is the stable, published version of your app. It only updates when you explicitly click **Deploy**. This is the URL you share with real users and link to custom domains.

Read the full comparison in [Preview vs Deployed](/preview-vs-deployed-separate).

---

## Bundle Identifier (Bundle ID)

A **Bundle Identifier** is a unique reverse-domain string (for example `com.yourcompany.appname`) that identifies your mobile app on iOS and Android. You configure this once when converting a web app to mobile or creating a new mobile project. The Bundle ID must match across builds, code-signing certificates and app-store listings. Changing it later requires generating new builds and re-submitting to app stores.

<Note>
Choose your Bundle ID carefully. Convention is `com.<company>.<appname>` in lowercase with no spaces or special characters.
</Note>

---

## Custom domain

A **custom domain** lets you serve your Deployed app from your own URL (for example `app.yourcompany.com` or `yourcompany.com`). Emergent provides automatic HTTPS certificates. You configure DNS by adding a `CNAME` or `A` record in your domain registrar's dashboard, then link the domain in your workspace's Deployment settings.

See the step-by-step guide in [Custom domain](/custom-domain).

---

## MCP (Model Context Protocol)

**MCP** is an open standard for exposing data sources and tools to LLMs. Emergent supports MCP servers so your agents can query databases, SaaS APIs and internal systems without custom integration code. You can connect official MCP servers (Postgres, GitHub, Notion) or build your own. Configured MCP servers appear in the agent's tool picker when you chat.

Learn how to add them in [Custom & MCP integrations](/custom-mcp-integrations).

---

## Expo & EAS (Expo Application Services)

**Expo** is the React Native framework Emergent uses for mobile apps. **EAS** (Expo Application Services) is Expo's cloud build and submission platform. When you generate iOS or Android builds, Emergent triggers EAS Build behind the scenes. You will see references to EAS in build logs and may need an Expo account (free tier works) if you want direct access to build artifacts or advanced signing options.

<Info>
Emergent handles most EAS configuration automatically. You only need an Expo account if you want to download `.ipa`/`.apk` files directly or manage your own signing credentials.
</Info>

---

## Keystore (Android) & Certificates (iOS)

- **Keystore** (Android): A `.jks` or `.keystore` file containing cryptographic keys used to sign your APK or AAB. Required for publishing to Google Play. Emergent can generate one automatically or you can upload your own.
- **Certificates & Provisioning Profiles** (iOS): Apple-issued credentials that prove your identity and authorize the app to run on devices or be distributed via the App Store. Emergent manages these through EAS or you can provide your own from the Apple Developer portal.

<Warning>
Store keystore passwords and certificate files securely. Losing them means you cannot update your app on the respective store.
</Warning>

---

## Web ↔ Mobile conversion

**Web ↔ Mobile conversion** is Emergent's ability to transform a web app into iOS/Android (and vice versa) with minimal rework. The agent adapts components, navigation and styling to match platform conventions. Not all features convert automatically—native device APIs, camera access and push notifications may require additional Jobs.

Read the detailed guide in [Web ↔ Mobile conversion](/web-mobile-conversion-canonical).

---

## Database (MongoDB)

Every Emergent project includes an optional **MongoDB** cluster. Agents can create collections, define schemas and wire CRUD operations on your behalf. The database runs on managed infrastructure; connection strings and credentials are auto-injected as environment variables. You can inspect data in the workspace **Database** tab or connect with any Mongo client using the provided URI.

See [Database (MongoDB)](/database-mongodb) for schema design and querying tips.

---

## AI media generation

Emergent integrates **Replicate**, **Hugging Face**, **DALL·E**, **Stable Diffusion** and other models for generating images, videos and audio inside your app. Agents can wire generation endpoints, handle prompt engineering and cache outputs. Media generation Jobs consume ECUs based on model and resolution; exact costs appear in the Job summary.

Explore available models in [AI media generation](/ai-media-generation-image-video-audio).

---

## Custom agents

**Custom agents** are specialized assistants you configure for domain-specific tasks—for example a "Marketing Copy Agent" with tone guidelines and brand vocabulary, or a "Data Analyst Agent" with SQL templates. Custom agents appear in the agent picker and can be invoked mid-conversation or set as the default for a project.

Learn how to create them in [Custom agents](/custom-agents).

---

## Key integrations catalogue

The **Key integrations catalogue** lists pre-configured connectors (Stripe, Twilio, SendGrid, Firebase, Supabase, etc.) that agents can install and wire with a single command. Each integration includes authentication helpers, usage examples and common workflows. Browse the full list in [Key integrations catalogue](/key-integrations-catalogue).

---

## Environment variables

**Environment variables** store secrets (API keys, database URIs, OAuth client IDs) outside your code. Emergent auto-provisions variables for internal services (MongoDB, Universal Key) and lets you add custom ones in the workspace **Settings** panel. Variables are available to both Preview and Deployed builds; you can define separate values per environment.

<Tip>
Never hard-code secrets in chat prompts. Ask the agent to "read the API key from environment variables" instead.
</Tip>

---

## Workspace

The **workspace** is the web IDE where you review code, manage deployments, inspect logs and configure settings. It includes a file tree, live preview iframe, terminal, database browser and deployment controls. Tour the interface in [A tour of the workspace](/a-tour-of-the-workspace).
