credit-expiry-recharging.title: Credit expiry & recharging
credit-expiry-recharging.content:
## Monthly reset

Credits on Emergent operate on a **monthly billing cycle**. At the start of each cycle (the day your plan renews), your credit balance resets to the full amount included in your plan—you do not accumulate unused credits from previous months.

For example, if your plan includes 500 credits per month and you use only 200, the remaining 300 do not roll over. Your balance resets to 500 on the renewal date.

<Info title="Pro tip">
Check your current cycle and remaining credits in the workspace sidebar. The display shows both your balance and the days until reset.
</Info>

## Credit expiry

<Warning title="Credits expire—plan accordingly">
**Unused credits expire at the end of each billing cycle.** This catches many users by surprise, so it's important to understand:

- Monthly plan credits do **not** carry forward to the next month
- Any topped-up credits (purchased outside your plan) also expire after **90 days** from the purchase date
- There are no refunds for expired credits

If you regularly have credits left over, consider downgrading to a smaller plan and topping up only when needed for larger projects.
</Warning>

To avoid losing credits you've paid for:

- Monitor your balance regularly (visible in the workspace header)
- Use credits for experimentation, prototyping, or running extra agents before the cycle ends
- Set a calendar reminder a few days before renewal to use remaining balance

## Topping up & the two credit types

You can **add credits anytime** without waiting for your monthly reset. Emergent offers two distinct credit systems depending on how you want to power your AI agents:

### Emergent Credits (default)

These are the standard credits included in your plan and available for top-up purchase. They work with Emergent's managed LLM infrastructure—no API keys required, usage is metered automatically.

**To top up Emergent Credits:**

<Steps>
<Step title="Open billing settings">
Click your avatar in the workspace header, then select **Billing & Usage**.
</Step>

<Step title="Purchase a credit pack">
Choose a credit pack size (typically 100, 500, or 1,000 credits). Payment is processed immediately via Stripe.
</Step>

<Step title="Credits appear instantly">
Your new balance shows in the workspace sidebar within seconds. Topped-up credits have a **90-day expiry** from purchase.
</Step>
</Steps>

### Universal LLM Key credits

If you configure a [Universal LLM Key](/the-universal-llm-key) (your own OpenAI, Anthropic, or other provider API key), agents use **your key's budget** instead of Emergent Credits. This is a separate system:

- Emergent does **not** deduct credits when using your own key
- You are billed directly by your LLM provider (OpenAI, Anthropic, etc.)
- Usage limits and costs depend on your provider's account settings
- You can switch back to Emergent Credits anytime by removing the key

<Note>
The two credit types never mix. An agent run either consumes Emergent Credits (managed) **or** charges your external LLM account (Universal Key), never both. See [How credits work](/how-credits-work) for a detailed comparison.
</Note>

**When to top up vs. use your own key:**

| Scenario | Recommended approach |
|----------|---------------------|
| Occasional small projects | Use Emergent Credits; top up as needed |
| High-volume production apps | Configure Universal LLM Key for predictable provider billing |
| Testing new models | Universal Key gives you access to the latest provider releases immediately |
| Simplicity & no API management | Stick with Emergent Credits |

Top-ups are non-refundable and subject to the same 90-day expiry. Always check your current balance and cycle date before purchasing additional credits.

team-roles-permissions-collaboration.title: Team roles, permissions & collaboration
team-roles-permissions-collaboration.content:
## Understanding project roles

Every Emergent project has a **single owner** and can have any number of admins, members and viewers. Each role grants a different level of access to the project's resources, configuration and billing.

<Note title="Personal projects">
If you create a project on your own, you are the owner by default. You can invite collaborators at any time from the project settings.
</Note>

## Role capabilities

The table below shows what each role can do:

| Capability | Owner | Admin | Member | Viewer |
|------------|-------|-------|--------|--------|
| **View & test the app** | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| **Chat with the agent** | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | – |
| **Approve & deploy changes** | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | – |
| **Edit project settings** | ✓ | ✓ | – | – |
| **Invite or remove members** | ✓ | ✓ | – | – |
| **Manage the database** | ✓ | ✓ | – | – |
| **Configure custom domain** | ✓ | ✓ | – | – |
| **View & manage billing** | ✓ | – | – | – |
| **Transfer ownership** | ✓ | – | – | – |
| **Delete the project** | ✓ | – | – | – |

<Callout type="info" title="Viewers can test but not modify">
Viewers are ideal for stakeholders, clients or QA testers who need to see the live app and its history but should not make changes.
</Callout>

## Shared credit pool

All projects draw from a **shared credit pool** that belongs to the owner's account. Every collaborator—regardless of role—uses credits from that pool when they interact with the agent or deploy changes.

- The owner's [credit balance](/credit-expiry-recharging) funds all project activity.
- Team members do not need their own credits or subscriptions.
- Usage by any team member is attributed to the owner's account for billing purposes.

<Warning title="Monitor usage in multi-user projects">
Because all team members share the same credit pool, it's important to track usage if you have a large team or are working on multiple projects simultaneously.
</Warning>

## Inviting team members

<Steps>
<Step title="Open project settings">
Navigate to your project and click the **Settings** icon in the top navigation bar (or sidebar, depending on your view).
</Step>

<Step title="Go to the Team tab">
Select **Team** from the settings menu to see the current list of collaborators.
</Step>

<Step title="Send an invite">
Enter the email address of the person you want to invite, choose their role from the dropdown (**Admin**, **Member** or **Viewer**), then click **Invite**.

They will receive an email with a link to accept the invitation and join the project.
</Step>
</Steps>

<Tip title="Invite by email only">
Invitations are sent to email addresses. The recipient must have (or create) an Emergent account with that email to accept the invite.
</Tip>

## Changing a member's role

Owners and admins can update any team member's role at any time:

1. Open **Settings → Team**.
2. Locate the member in the list.
3. Click the role dropdown next to their name and select the new role.
4. The change takes effect immediately—no email confirmation required.

<Note>
You cannot change your own role if you are the owner. To step down, you must first transfer ownership to another team member.
</Note>

## Removing a team member

Owners and admins can remove any member (including other admins) from the project:

1. Open **Settings → Team**.
2. Click the **Remove** button next to the member's name.
3. Confirm the action in the dialog.

Removed members immediately lose access to the project, including the chat history, codebase and deployed app configuration. They can be re-invited later if needed.

<Warning title="Removing an admin">
Admins can remove other admins. If you have multiple admins, coordinate role changes carefully to avoid accidental lockouts.
</Warning>

## Transferring ownership

Only the current owner can transfer ownership to another team member. Ownership transfer is **irreversible** and immediately moves billing responsibility and full control to the new owner.

<Steps>
<Step title="Open Team settings">
Go to **Settings → Team** in your project.
</Step>

<Step title="Select the new owner">
Find the team member you want to promote and click **Transfer ownership** next to their name.
</Step>

<Step title="Confirm the transfer">
You will be prompted to confirm. Once confirmed:

- The selected member becomes the **Owner**.
- You become an **Admin** (or can be assigned a different role by the new owner).
- The new owner's account takes over billing and credit management for the project.
</Step>
</Steps>

<Danger title="Ownership transfer is permanent">
You cannot undo an ownership transfer. The new owner will have full control, including the ability to remove you from the project or delete it entirely.
</Danger>

## Best practices for team collaboration

- **Assign roles conservatively**: Grant the minimum permissions needed for each team member's responsibilities.
- **Use viewers for external stakeholders**: Clients, investors or non-technical collaborators can see progress without risking accidental changes.
- **Communicate before transferring ownership**: Ensure the new owner understands they will inherit billing and full administrative control.
- **Monitor the credit pool**: Keep an eye on usage if your team is large or actively iterating—credits are shared across all collaborators.

For more on how credits work and recharge policies, see [Credit expiry & recharging](/credit-expiry-recharging).
team-roles-permissions-collaboration.description: Four project roles (Owner/Admin/Member/Viewer) with a capability matrix, a shared credit pool, inviting members, changing roles, and transferring ownership.

file-storage-emergent-object-store.title: File storage (Emergent Object Store)
file-storage-emergent-object-store.content:
## Overview

Emergent provides S3-compatible object storage for every organization through **Emergent Object Store**, powered by Tigris. This lets your deployed apps handle user uploads, avatars, documents, and other files without connecting an external AWS account or managing buckets yourself.

<Callout type="info" title="Automatic provisioning">
Object storage is provisioned on-demand when you ask the agent to add file upload or storage capabilities to your app. You don't need to request it separately.
</Callout>

**Key characteristics:**

- **S3-compatible API** — standard `PutObject`, `GetObject`, `DeleteObject` operations work out of the box
- **5 GB quota per organization** — shared across all your apps and deployments
- **No credit cost** — storage operations (reads, writes, deletes) do not consume [deployment credits](/credit-expiry-recharging)
- **Secure by default** — buckets and credentials are scoped to your organization; the agent configures access automatically

---

## How to request storage

Simply describe file-handling requirements in chat, for example:

- *"Let users upload profile pictures"*
- *"Add a document upload form and store PDFs in object storage"*
- *"Store user-generated images in S3"*

The agent will:

1. Provision a bucket (or reuse your org's existing bucket)
2. Generate scoped credentials (`AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`, `S3_BUCKET`, `S3_ENDPOINT`)
3. Inject those credentials as environment variables in the deployment
4. Install the necessary SDK (`aws-sdk`, `boto3`, etc.) and write storage code

<Note>
You never see or manage raw bucket names or access keys directly — the agent handles configuration end-to-end.
</Note>

---

## Using storage in your code

Because Emergent Object Store is S3-compatible, you use standard AWS SDKs with a custom endpoint:

<CodeGroup>
```javascript Node.js (AWS SDK v3)
import { S3Client, PutObjectCommand } from '@aws-sdk/client-s3';

const s3 = new S3Client({
  endpoint: process.env.S3_ENDPOINT,
  region: 'auto',
  credentials: {
    accessKeyId: process.env.AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID,
    secretAccessKey: process.env.AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY,
  },
});

await s3.send(new PutObjectCommand({
  Bucket: process.env.S3_BUCKET,
  Key: 'uploads/avatar.jpg',
  Body: fileBuffer,
}));
```

```python Python (boto3)
import boto3
import os

s3 = boto3.client(
    's3',
    endpoint_url=os.environ['S3_ENDPOINT'],
    aws_access_key_id=os.environ['AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID'],
    aws_secret_access_key=os.environ['AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY'],
)

s3.put_object(
    Bucket=os.environ['S3_BUCKET'],
    Key='uploads/avatar.jpg',
    Body=file_data
)
```
</CodeGroup>

<Tip>
The agent will write code similar to the above when you ask for file uploads. You typically won't need to write S3 client code by hand.
</Tip>

---

## Quota and limits

| Resource       | Limit per organization |
|----------------|------------------------|
| **Total storage** | 5 GB                 |
| **Number of buckets** | 1 (shared)       |
| **API calls** | No hard limit (fair use) |

<Warning title="Approaching quota">
If your apps approach the 5 GB limit, new uploads may fail. Monitor usage via your object counts and file sizes; the platform does not yet surface a storage dashboard.
</Warning>

When you exceed quota, `PutObject` requests will return HTTP 507 (Insufficient Storage) or a similar error. The agent cannot automatically expand quota — contact support if you need more than 5 GB.

---

## Security and access control

- **Private by default** — objects are not publicly readable unless you explicitly generate signed URLs or set public ACLs (discouraged).
- **Scoped credentials** — each organization's access keys can only interact with that organization's bucket.
- **No cross-org access** — apps in different organizations cannot read each other's files.

<Callout type="tip" title="Serving files to users">
To let users download uploads, generate **pre-signed URLs** with a short expiry (e.g., 1 hour). This avoids exposing permanent credentials in the browser. Ask the agent: *"Generate signed URLs for uploaded files so users can download them securely."*
</Callout>

---

## Common use cases

<CardGroup cols={2}>
  <Card title="Profile avatars" icon="user-circle">
    Store and serve user-uploaded images; resize on upload or on-the-fly.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Document uploads" icon="file-text">
    Accept PDFs, spreadsheets, or text files; parse or index them server-side.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Media galleries" icon="image">
    Let users upload photos or videos; list and display thumbnails.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Export artifacts" icon="download">
    Generate CSVs, reports, or ZIP archives on the server and store them for async download.
  </Card>
</CardGroup>

---

## FAQ

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Can I bring my own S3 bucket or AWS account?">
    Not currently. Emergent Object Store is the only supported file storage backend. If you need to integrate with an existing S3 bucket, you can configure custom environment variables with your own credentials, but those operations *will* consume deployment runtime and are outside the included quota.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Do storage API calls count against deployment credits?">
    No. Reads, writes, and deletes against Emergent Object Store are free and do not consume [deployment credits](/credit-expiry-recharging). Only compute time (API requests, background jobs, etc.) counts.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="What happens to files when I delete a deployment?">
    Files remain in your organization's bucket. Deleting a deployment does *not* delete uploaded objects. You can ask the agent to write a cleanup script or manually purge objects via the S3 API.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Can I use a CDN in front of object storage?">
    Yes. Generate signed URLs with longer expiries and cache them at the edge (e.g., Cloudflare). The agent can help you implement URL signing and caching headers. Note that the S3 endpoint itself is globally distributed by Tigris, so a separate CDN is often unnecessary for read performance.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Is versioning or lifecycle management supported?">
    Not at this time. Emergent Object Store offers basic S3 operations (put, get, delete, list). Features like versioning, lifecycle policies, and replication are not exposed.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

---

## Related resources

<CardGroup cols={2}>
  <Card title="Database (MongoDB)" icon="database" href="/database-mongodb">
    Persistent NoSQL database included with every deployment.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Credit expiry & recharging" icon="coins" href="/credit-expiry-recharging">
    Understand which operations consume credits (storage operations do not).
  </Card>
</CardGroup>
file-storage-emergent-object-store.description: S3-compatible file storage powered by Tigris (5GB/org quota, no AWS account) for user uploads; requested via the agent, and storage operations do not consume credits.

what-and-how.title: What and How
what-and-how.content:
## What integrations are

An **integration** in Emergent is any connection between your app and a third-party service—a database, an authentication provider, a payment processor, an email API, a vector store, or an external API.

When you describe your app in chat, the agent decides which integrations are needed and configures them automatically. You don't manually wire up connection strings, OAuth flows, or SDK clients; the agent does that for you as part of the build.

Common examples:

- **Databases**: Supabase, Neon Postgres, Pinecone, Upstash Redis
- **Auth**: Clerk, Supabase Auth, or [Emergent Auth (built-in)](/emergent-auth-built-in)
- **Payments**: Stripe
- **Email**: Resend, SendGrid
- **AI/ML**: OpenAI, Anthropic, Replicate, ElevenLabs
- **Other APIs**: any REST or GraphQL endpoint your app needs

Browse the full set in the [Key integrations catalogue](/key-integrations-catalogue).

---

## How auth & keys are handled

Emergent takes care of the plumbing so you can focus on describing *what* your app should do, not *how* to wire it up.

### What Emergent does for you

<Steps>
<Step title="Detects the integration">
When you mention a feature—"users sign in with Google" or "store embeddings in Pinecone"—the agent identifies the service and adds the integration to your app.
</Step>

<Step title="Scaffolds the connection">
The agent installs the necessary SDK, injects environment variables, and writes the glue code (init clients, handle callbacks, manage sessions).
</Step>

<Step title="Prompts for keys when needed">
If a service requires an API key or secret, Emergent prompts you to provide it. You paste the key into the workspace UI; it's stored encrypted and injected at runtime.
</Step>
</Steps>

<Info title="Your keys stay private">
API keys and secrets you supply are encrypted at rest and never shared. Only your app's runtime environment can decrypt them.
</Info>

### What you supply

For most third-party services, **you bring your own account and API key**:

- Sign up with the service (Stripe, OpenAI, Clerk, etc.)
- Generate an API key or secret in their dashboard
- Paste it into Emergent when prompted

The agent will tell you exactly which key it needs and where to find it.

<Tip>
Some integrations (like [Emergent Auth](/emergent-auth-built-in)) are fully managed—no external account or key required.
</Tip>

---

## When keys are requested

You'll be asked to provide a key in two situations:

1. **During the build**: The agent pauses and prompts you in chat. Paste the key, then resume.
2. **After deploy**: If a key is missing or invalid, the app will fail at runtime. Check the logs, add the key via the workspace settings, and redeploy.

<Warning>
If you skip providing a required key, the agent may stub out the integration or the feature will break at runtime. Always supply keys when prompted.
</Warning>

---

## Environment variables & secrets

Under the hood, every integration key becomes an **environment variable** (e.g. `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY`). The agent:

- Declares the variable in your app's config
- Injects it at build and runtime
- Uses it in the code (e.g. `process.env.OPENAI_API_KEY`)

You can view and edit these variables in the workspace **Settings** panel. See [A tour of the workspace](/a-tour-of-the-workspace) for details.

---

## Next steps

<CardGroup cols={2}>
<Card title="Key integrations catalogue" icon="grid" href="/key-integrations-catalogue">
Browse supported services and their setup requirements
</Card>
<Card title="Emergent Auth (built-in)" icon="shield-check" href="/emergent-auth-built-in">
Use the platform's managed auth—no external account needed
</Card>
<Card title="Your data & ownership" icon="lock" href="/your-data-ownership">
Understand how your keys, data and code are stored and protected
</Card>
<Card title="Your first build (walkthrough)" icon="rocket" href="/your-first-build-walkthrough">
See integrations in action as you build your first app
</Card>
</CardGroup>
what-and-how.description: 1. What integrations are: how Emergent connects your app to third-party services.

deployment-issues.title: Deployment issues
deployment-issues.content:
## Overview

Deployment issues fall into two broad categories: **build-time failures** (the agent cannot bundle or prepare your app) and **runtime failures** (your app starts but behaves incorrectly or crashes). This page walks through the most common scenarios and how to resolve them.

<Callout type="tip" title="Check the deployment pipeline first">
Most build errors appear in the **deployment pipeline log**. See [Deployment pipeline failures](/deployment-pipeline-failures) for step-by-step diagnostics.
</Callout>

---

## Build-time failures

### Missing dependencies

**Symptom:** Build fails with `Module not found` or `Cannot find package`.

**Cause:** The agent has not added a required library to `package.json` (Node.js), `requirements.txt` (Python), or your framework's manifest.

**Fix:**

<Steps>
<Step title="Identify the missing package">
Read the build log; the error message names the import that failed.
</Step>

<Step title="Tell the agent in chat">
"Install `[package-name]` and re‑deploy." The agent will add the dependency and trigger a new build.
</Step>

<Step title="Verify the manifest">
In the **Files** pane, confirm the package appears in `package.json` or `requirements.txt` before the next deployment.
</Step>
</Steps>

---

### Incompatible Node / Python version

**Symptom:** Build fails with syntax errors or a message like `Unexpected token` (Node) or `invalid syntax` (Python).

**Cause:** The deployment runtime uses a different language version than the code expects (for example, async/await syntax in Node 12, or Python 3.11 match statements on a Python 3.9 runtime).

**Fix:**

1. Check the [Deployment types](/deployment-types) page for the runtime version your plan provides.
2. Ask the agent: *"Use syntax compatible with Node 16"* (or the version you have).
3. Re‑generate the code and re‑deploy.

<Callout type="info">
If you need a specific runtime version, consider upgrading your [Deployment plan level](/deployment-plan-levels) or switching to a Docker‑based deployment (if available on your plan).
</Callout>

---

### Build timeout

**Symptom:** Build aborts with `Timeout exceeded` or `Build killed`.

**Cause:** The build step (install dependencies, transpile, bundle) runs longer than the time limit for your plan.

**Fix:**

<Tabs>
<Tab title="Reduce dependencies">
Ask the agent to remove unused libraries or combine smaller packages. Fewer dependencies = faster install.
</Tab>

<Tab title="Optimize build config">
For Next.js or Vite apps, disable source maps in production or switch to a lighter bundler mode. Example: *"Set `productionBrowserSourceMaps: false` in `next.config.js`."*
</Tab>

<Tab title="Upgrade plan">
Higher [Deployment plan levels](/deployment-plan-levels) offer longer build windows and more CPU.
</Tab>
</Tabs>

---

### Out of memory during build

**Symptom:** Build crashes with `JavaScript heap out of memory` or `Killed`.

**Cause:** The build process (Webpack, Vite, TypeScript compiler) exceeds available RAM.

**Fix:**

- **Node apps:** Add `NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=4096` to your build environment (ask the agent to set this in the deployment config).
- **Simplify the build:** Split large bundles, enable tree‑shaking, or lazy‑load heavy modules.
- **Upgrade plan:** More RAM is available at higher tiers—see [Deployment plan levels](/deployment-plan-levels).

---

## Runtime failures

### App starts but shows a blank page

**Symptom:** Deployment succeeds; opening the URL displays a white screen or "Application error."

**Common causes & fixes:**

| Cause | How to diagnose | Fix |
|-------|-----------------|-----|
| Client‑side crash | Open browser DevTools → Console; look for uncaught exceptions. | Share the error with the agent: *"Fix runtime error: [paste stack trace]."* |
| Missing environment variable | App tries to read `process.env.API_KEY` but it's undefined. | Set the variable in the **Environment** pane and re‑deploy. See [How apps work here](/how-apps-work-here-mental-model#environment-variables). |
| Static‑asset 404 | CSS or JS files return 404; check Network tab in DevTools. | Ask the agent to fix the public path or output directory in the build config. |

---

### Database connection failures

**Symptom:** Logs show `MongoNetworkError`, `ECONNREFUSED`, or similar.

**Cause:** The app cannot reach the MongoDB instance—wrong connection string, firewall rule, or the database is not provisioned.

**Fix:**

<Steps>
<Step title="Verify the database is provisioned">
In the workspace sidebar, confirm a MongoDB database exists. If not, ask the agent: *"Add a MongoDB database to this project."*
</Step>

<Step title="Check the connection string">
The environment variable (usually `MONGODB_URI` or `DATABASE_URL`) must match the value shown in the **Environment** pane. Copy it exactly—include username, password, and database name.
</Step>

<Step title="Whitelist the deployment IP">
Some plans deploy from dynamic IPs. If your MongoDB host has an IP allowlist, add `0.0.0.0/0` (all IPs) or ask support for the deployment IP range.
</Step>
</Steps>

<Callout type="warning" title="Credentials in code">
Never hard‑code `mongodb://user:pass@host` in your source files. Always use environment variables and keep secrets out of version control.
</Callout>

Read more: [Database (MongoDB)](/database-mongodb).

---

### API or external service timeouts

**Symptom:** Requests to third‑party APIs (Stripe, OpenAI, etc.) hang or return `504 Gateway Timeout`.

**Possible causes:**

- **Rate limit:** Your API key has hit a quota.
- **Network policy:** The deployment environment blocks outbound HTTPS to certain domains (rare).
- **Slow endpoint:** The third‑party service is down or experiencing latency.

**Fix:**

1. **Check the third‑party status page** (e.g., `status.openai.com`).
2. **Increase timeout** in your HTTP client (Axios, Fetch): set `timeout: 30000` (30 seconds).
3. **Verify API key:** Confirm the key is valid and has sufficient quota; test it locally or in a tool like Postman.
4. **Review logs:** Look for `429 Too Many Requests` or `401 Unauthorized`—these point to credential or quota issues, not network problems.

---

### Deployment health check fails

**Symptom:** Deployment pipeline succeeds, but the platform marks the app as **unhealthy** and does not route traffic.

**Cause:** The health‑check endpoint (`/health` or `/`) does not return HTTP 200 within the timeout window.

**Fix:**

- **Add or fix the health route:** Ensure your app responds to `GET /health` (or the path configured in your deployment settings) with a 200 status and minimal logic (e.g., `res.json({ status: 'ok' })`).
- **Speed up startup:** Move heavy initialization (database seeding, large file reads) out of the main server bootstrap so the health check can succeed quickly.
- **Check the timeout setting:** Some plans allow you to configure the health‑check timeout—ask the agent to increase it if your app needs more time to warm up.

---

### Custom domain not resolving

**Symptom:** Visiting `app.yourdomain.com` shows a DNS error or "Site not found."

**Diagnosis:**

<Steps>
<Step title="Verify DNS records">
Run `dig app.yourdomain.com` or use an online DNS checker. The `CNAME` must point to the Emergent deployment hostname (shown in the **Custom domain** settings).
</Step>

<Step title="Wait for propagation">
DNS changes can take 1–48 hours to propagate globally. Test from multiple locations or use `8.8.8.8` as your resolver.
</Step>

<Step title="Check SSL certificate status">
In the workspace, navigate to **Custom domain** and confirm the SSL certificate is **Active**. If it shows **Pending**, wait a few more minutes; if **Failed**, double‑check the DNS `CNAME`.
</Step>
</Steps>

<Callout type="info">
Detailed setup instructions: [Custom domain](/custom-domain).
</Callout>

---

## Out of credits / quota exceeded

**Symptom:** Deployment is queued indefinitely or aborts with *"Insufficient credits."*

**Cause:** Your account has consumed its [credit allocation](/how-credits-work) for builds, compute time, or API calls.

**Fix:**

- **Check your balance:** Open the **Billing** or **Usage** dashboard (depending on your plan).
- **Upgrade or top up:** Purchase additional credits or move to a higher plan tier with more monthly allowance.
- **Optimize usage:** Reduce the number of deployments by batching changes; use preview builds sparingly.

---

## Image / video / audio generation failures

**Symptom:** AI‑generated media assets fail to appear or return errors.

**Cause:** Model unavailable, quota exceeded, or unsupported parameters.

**Fix:** See the dedicated page [AI media generation](/ai-media-generation-image-video-audio) for model‑specific troubleshooting and parameter guidance.

---

## Getting further help

If none of the above resolves your issue:

<CardGroup cols={2}>
<Card title="Ask the agent" icon="message-circle">
Paste the full error message into chat. The agent can read logs and often auto‑fix configuration mistakes.
</Card>

<Card title="Review the pipeline log" icon="list" href="/deployment-pipeline-failures">
Step‑by‑step guide to interpreting build and deploy logs.
</Card>

<Card title="Check platform status" icon="activity">
Rare outages or maintenance windows are announced on the Emergent status page (link in your workspace footer).
</Card>

<Card title="Contact support" icon="life-buoy">
Use the **Help** button in the workspace to open a ticket. Include your project ID and the timestamp of the failed deployment.
</Card>
</CardGroup>

<Callout type="success" title="Most issues resolve in chat">
The agent has access to your deployment logs and can iterate on fixes in real time—start there before opening a support ticket.
</Callout>
deployment-issues.description: Common deployment failures and how to fix them.

web-mobile-conversion-ref.title: Web <-> Mobile conversion (ref)
web-mobile-conversion-ref.content:
## Overview

Emergent lets you convert web apps to native mobile apps and vice versa—preserving your data, users, and functionality. This page is a reference for mobile builders; **for complete information on conversion workflows, constraints, and rollback procedures, see the canonical [Web <-> Mobile conversion](/web-mobile-conversion-canonical) page in the Going Live section.**

## When to convert

You might convert a project:

- **Web → Mobile** when you've validated a web MVP and want native distribution through app stores
- **Mobile → Web** when you need a web presence for marketing, SEO, or desktop users alongside your native app
- **Between platforms** when migrating to a new deployment target while keeping your backend, database, and authentication intact

<Note>
Conversions preserve your [MongoDB database](/database-mongodb), environment variables, and user accounts. Front-end code is regenerated to match the target platform's idioms (React Native for mobile, Next.js for web).
</Note>

## What's preserved vs. regenerated

| Component | Behavior |
|-----------|----------|
| Database & collections | **Preserved** — schema and data remain intact |
| User accounts & auth | **Preserved** — login works immediately post-conversion |
| Environment variables | **Preserved** — API keys, secrets carry over |
| Backend logic | **Regenerated** — rewritten for target platform, functionally equivalent |
| UI components | **Regenerated** — adapted to platform conventions (native mobile vs. responsive web) |
| Third-party integrations | **Reviewed** — agents assess compatibility; may require minor adjustments (e.g., web-only analytics SDKs) |

## How to convert

<Steps>
<Step title="Navigate to project settings">
In the workspace, open the **Settings** panel (gear icon in the left sidebar).
</Step>

<Step title="Choose conversion option">
Under **Platform**, select **Convert to Mobile** or **Convert to Web**. Confirm the target platform and deployment region.
</Step>

<Step title="Agents rebuild the front end">
Emergent agents analyze your existing app, then regenerate the UI and routing for the new platform. This typically takes 3–8 minutes depending on app complexity.
</Step>

<Step title="Test in the workspace">
Once conversion completes, use the preview pane to verify functionality. Check critical flows (login, data display, forms) before deploying.
</Step>

<Step title="Deploy">
When satisfied, deploy the converted app. For mobile, this creates a new build for TestFlight/internal testing or production submission. For web, it publishes to your existing or new [custom domain](/custom-domain).
</Step>
</Steps>

<Warning title="Original platform build is paused">
After conversion, the **original platform build is no longer updated**. If you need both web and mobile simultaneously, convert and maintain both projects separately (each with its own deployment pipeline).
</Warning>

## Platform-specific considerations

### Converting web → mobile

- **Responsive layouts** become native mobile components (ScrollView, FlatList, native navigation)
- **Web-only libraries** (e.g., certain charting or map libraries) are replaced with React Native equivalents
- **App store assets** (icons, screenshots, descriptions) must be configured post-conversion for submission

### Converting mobile → web

- **Native modules** (camera, geolocation, push notifications) are adapted to web APIs where possible; agents flag unsupported features
- **Mobile navigation** (tab bars, stack navigators) translates to web routing and menu structures
- **Touch gestures** become click/hover interactions

<Tip>
After converting mobile → web, review your [custom domain](/custom-domain) settings to ensure the web app is accessible at your preferred URL.
</Tip>

## Rollback and alternative paths

If a conversion doesn't meet your needs:

- **Rollback** — contact support to revert to the pre-conversion state (available within 7 days of conversion)
- **Parallel projects** — for long-term dual-platform support, maintain separate Emergent projects (one web, one mobile) sharing the same database connection string

For details on rollback procedures, downtime expectations, and edge cases, see the [canonical conversion documentation](/web-mobile-conversion-canonical).

## Related resources

</Card>

pull-from-github-with-caution.title: Pull from GitHub (with caution)
pull-from-github-with-caution.content:
<Callout type="warning" title="Risk of overwriting local changes">
When you pull code from GitHub into your Emergent workspace, the agent may modify or overwrite files it considers part of the core application logic. **Always keep a backup of your work elsewhere** before initiating a pull.
</Callout>

## What happens when you pull

Pulling from GitHub imports the repository's current state into your workspace. The Emergent agent then:

- Scans the incoming files for structural changes
- May refactor, reorganise or overwrite code to align with its understanding of the project
- Treats the pull as new input—similar to a fresh chat instruction

This behaviour is by design: the agent assumes you want it to interpret and integrate the changes. However, **it cannot distinguish between code you wrote manually and code it generated earlier**, so custom edits may be lost.

## Recommended workflow

<Steps>
<Step title="Commit and tag your workspace state">
Before pulling, use the GitHub integration to **push** your current Emergent workspace to a branch or tag. This creates a snapshot you can return to.
</Step>

<Step title="Clone a local copy (optional)">
If you've made manual edits outside Emergent, `git clone` the repository to your machine and keep that copy as a reference.
</Step>

<Step title="Pull cautiously">
Trigger the pull only when you're ready for the agent to process the incoming changes. Monitor the agent's activity in the chat log.
</Step>

<Step title="Review and test">
After the pull completes, inspect modified files in the editor and run your app to confirm functionality. See [A tour of the workspace](/a-tour-of-the-workspace) for navigation tips.
</Step>
</Steps>

## When pulling is safe

Pulling works well when:

- The repository contains **only agent-generated code** (no manual edits).
- You're syncing changes made by a teammate also using Emergent, and you trust the agent to reconcile them.
- You're importing a fresh starter template or example project.

## When to avoid pulling

<Info>
If you've hand-edited files—especially configuration, API routes or database schemas—**do not pull** without a backup. The agent may discard your changes in favour of its own interpretation.
</Info>

Consider these alternatives:

| Scenario | Alternative approach |
|----------|---------------------|
| You made manual edits in the Emergent editor | Push to GitHub first, then describe the desired merge behaviour in chat rather than pulling. |
| You edited files locally (outside Emergent) | Copy the diff into chat and ask the agent to integrate it, or manually paste changes into the editor. |
| You want to import a dependency or library | Describe the addition in chat; let the agent install and configure it. |

## Recovery if something goes wrong

If a pull overwrites critical work:

1. **Check your Git history** — if you pushed to GitHub beforehand, check out the earlier commit locally and copy back the lost code.
2. **Restore from backup** — if you cloned or exported the workspace, copy files from that snapshot.
3. **Describe the issue in chat** — paste any surviving fragments and ask the agent to reconstruct the feature. The agent can often regenerate logic from a brief description.

<Tip>
Emergent workspaces are ephemeral by design. For mission-critical projects, maintain a canonical repository outside the platform and treat Emergent as a **drafting and prototyping layer** rather than the source of truth.
</Tip>

## Related

<CardGroup cols={2}>
<Card title="Your data & ownership" icon="shield-check" href="/your-data-ownership">
Understand how code and data are stored
</Card>
<Card title="Glossary of Emergent terms" icon="book-open" href="/glossary-of-emergent-terms">
Definitions of workspace, agent and other key concepts
</Card>
</CardGroup>

how-apps-work-here-mental-model.title: How apps work here (mental model)
how-apps-work-here-mental-model.content:
## You describe, the agent builds

When you work with Emergent, you're collaborating with an AI agent that handles all the implementation details. Here's how the division of labor works:

**What the agent handles:**

- Writing all code (Python backend, React frontend, database schemas)
- Setting up project structure and dependencies
- Following web development best practices
- Fixing bugs and runtime errors
- Deploying and configuring infrastructure

**What you decide:**

- The app's purpose and core features
- User experience and interface choices
- Business logic and workflows
- When a feature is "done"
- Which direction to take when multiple options exist

<Tip title="Think of it as pair programming">
You're the product owner and architect; the agent is the developer who implements your vision. The clearer your requirements, the better the result.
</Tip>

This model lets you focus on *what* you want to build rather than *how* to build it. The agent translates your natural-language descriptions into working code, tests it, and deploys it — often in a single conversation.

For a concrete example of this workflow in action, see [Your first build (walkthrough)](/your-first-build-walkthrough).

## What's under the hood

Every Emergent app is a full-stack web application built with a consistent technology stack:

- **Backend**: FastAPI (Python) — handles API endpoints, business logic, and data operations
- **Frontend**: React — renders the user interface and manages client-side state
- **Database**: MongoDB — stores your application data with flexible schemas

<Info title="Why this matters">
Understanding the stack helps you communicate more effectively with the agent. When you say "add a REST endpoint" or "create a new collection," the agent knows exactly what you mean in the context of FastAPI and MongoDB.
</Info>

You don't need to write any of this code yourself, but knowing the foundation helps in a few situations:

- **Debugging**: When something doesn't work, you can describe the problem using technical terms the agent understands
- **Integrations**: If you want to connect external services, you'll know what capabilities the stack provides
- **Migration**: If you ever need to export your app, you'll have a standard FastAPI + React codebase

All code is generated according to modern best practices for each framework. The agent handles package management, routing, state management, and deployment configuration automatically.

For help troubleshooting issues, see [Debugging & testing with the agent](/debugging-testing-with-the-agent).

## What the AI knows vs what you think it knows

<Warning title="Common source of frustration">
The agent is powerful, but it cannot read your mind. It only knows what you've explicitly told it in the current conversation.
</Warning>

**The agent remembers:**

- Everything you've said in the current chat session
- The current state of your app's code and structure
- General web development knowledge and best practices
- Common patterns for similar features

**The agent does NOT automatically know:**

- Your industry-specific jargon or internal terminology
- Implicit requirements you assume are "obvious"
- Visual design preferences unless you describe them
- Data formats or business rules you haven't mentioned
- Context from previous projects or other apps

### Being explicit pays off

Instead of: *"Add the usual authentication"*  
Try: *"Add email/password authentication with a login page, signup page, and password reset flow. Store user sessions with JWT tokens."*

Instead of: *"Make it look professional"*  
Try: *"Use a clean layout with a white background, blue primary buttons, and cards with subtle shadows for each item."*

Instead of: *"Connect to the payment system"*  
Try: *"Integrate Stripe for payments. Users should be able to purchase credits with a card, and we need to store transaction history in a `payments` collection."*

<Tip>
When the agent asks clarifying questions, it's helping you be more specific. Answering these questions leads to better results faster than assuming the agent will "figure it out."
</Tip>

The more concrete and detailed your descriptions, the closer the first implementation will be to your vision. Vague instructions require more back-and-forth to get right.

For guidance on communicating effectively with the agent, see [Best Practices](/best-practices) and [What and How](/what-and-how).

deploying-web.title: Deploying (web)
deploying-web.content:
## What deployment does

When you deploy an app in Emergent, the platform provisions production infrastructure and makes your application live at a **public, permanent URL**. Unlike the preview environment (which spins up on demand and shuts down after inactivity), a deployed app runs **24/7** and can handle real user traffic.

Each deployment:

- Creates a stable, shareable URL (e.g. `https://your-app-name.emergent.app`)
- Provisions serverless compute, storage and any required services
- Runs health checks and keeps the app online continuously
- Routes traffic through a CDN for low-latency delivery

<Info title="First-time deployment">
The first deployment of an app can take **~15 minutes** while infrastructure is provisioned and your code is built. Subsequent updates are typically faster.
</Info>

---

## Cost of a deployed app

A deployed app costs **50 credits per month** while it remains live. This covers:

- Compute and storage for hosting
- Network egress and CDN delivery
- Health monitoring and logging
- Automatic scaling within platform limits

<Note>
Credits are deducted **monthly** from your account balance while the app is deployed. If you shut down the deployment, billing stops immediately. See [Credit expiry & recharging](/credit-expiry-recharging) for details on topping up.
</Note>

---

## Sharing your deployed app

Once deployment completes, share the public URL with anyone. No authentication is required unless your app implements its own login flow.

**Common use cases:**

- Share with friends or beta testers for feedback
- Embed in a portfolio or showcase
- Connect a custom domain (if supported by your plan)
- Use in production for low-to-moderate traffic

<Tip>
The deployed URL is permanent as long as the app remains live. You can redeploy updates at any time without changing the URL.
</Tip>

---

## Shutting down a deployment

You can shut down a deployed app **at any time** from the workspace. This:

- Stops the app and releases infrastructure
- Immediately halts the 50 credits/month charge
- Preserves your code and project history

To redeploy later, simply click **Deploy** again from the same project.

<Warning>
Shutting down a deployment **does not** delete any databases or external services your app may use (e.g. MongoDB). If you want to remove data, manually delete those resources separately. See [Database (MongoDB)](/database-mongodb) for details.
</Warning>

---

## Monitoring a deployed app

Emergent provides basic monitoring tools to check the health and performance of your live app.

### Checking uptime

From the workspace, the deployment status indicator shows:

- **Green (Live)** – app is healthy and responding
- **Yellow (Degraded)** – partial outage or slow response
- **Red (Down)** – app is unreachable

<Info>
The platform runs automated health checks every few minutes. If your app becomes unresponsive, you'll see a status change in the workspace and may receive an alert (depending on your notification settings).
</Info>

### Viewing logs

Click **Logs** in the deployment panel to stream real-time output from your app. Logs capture:

- HTTP requests and responses
- Console output (`console.log`, `print`, etc.)
- Uncaught exceptions and stack traces
- Framework-level warnings

Use logs to debug unexpected behavior or trace user-reported issues.

### Production errors

If your app crashes or throws unhandled errors, Emergent surfaces them in the **Errors** tab. Each entry includes:

- Timestamp and affected route or endpoint
- Full stack trace
- Request context (URL, headers, user agent)

<Tip title="Proactive debugging">
Check the Errors tab regularly, especially after pushing updates. Catching issues early helps maintain a smooth experience for your users.
</Tip>

For performance issues (slow load times, cold starts), see [App slow, crashing or cold-starting](/app-slow-crashing-or-cold-starting).

---

## Next steps

<CardGroup cols={2}>
  <Card title="Credit expiry & recharging" icon="coins" href="/credit-expiry-recharging">
    Understand how credits work and how to top up
  </Card>
  <Card title="App takedown & content moderation" icon="shield-alert" href="/app-takedown-content-moderation">
    Learn the platform's content policies and enforcement
  </Card>
</CardGroup>

app-slow-crashing-or-cold-starting.title: App slow, crashing or cold-starting
app-slow-crashing-or-cold-starting.content:
## Why apps slow down, crash or cold-start

Emergent apps run on **KEDA-powered Kubernetes clusters** with event-driven auto-scaling and scale-to-zero when idle. This architecture keeps costs low and resources efficient, but it means some performance characteristics differ from always-on hosting.

### Scale-to-zero and cold starts

When your app receives **no requests for several minutes**, KEDA scales it down to zero running pods. The next request will experience a **cold start** — typically 5–15 seconds — while Kubernetes provisions a new pod, pulls the container image and boots your application.

Cold starts are normal and expected for low-traffic apps. High-traffic apps remain warm because continuous requests keep at least one pod running.

<Tip title="Keep critical apps warm">
If cold starts impact user experience, consider upgrading to a tier with a higher minimum replica count or configuring a health-check ping from an external monitor (e.g. UptimeRobot) every 2–3 minutes.
</Tip>

### Pod Disruption Budgets by tier

Emergent applies **Pod Disruption Budgets (PDBs)** to ensure availability during cluster maintenance, upgrades and node rotations. The guarantees vary by subscription tier:

| Tier       | Minimum available pods | Impact                                  |
|------------|------------------------|-----------------------------------------|
| Free       | 0                      | App may go offline during maintenance   |
| Starter    | 1                      | At least one pod always running         |
| Pro        | 2                      | Zero-downtime rolling updates           |
| Enterprise | Custom                 | Configurable per SLA                    |

<Warning>
Free-tier apps may experience **brief downtime** during platform updates. For production workloads, use Starter tier or higher.
</Warning>

### Auto-scaling behaviour (KEDA)

KEDA monitors **HTTP request rate, CPU and memory** metrics. When demand increases, KEDA automatically provisions additional pods. When demand drops, pods scale back down.

**Scaling thresholds:**
- Scale up when **average CPU >70%** or **request queue depth >10**
- Scale down after **5 minutes** of low load
- Scale to zero after **no requests for 10 minutes** (configurable per tier)

<Info>
Auto-scaling reacts to *sustained* load, not instant spikes. A sudden traffic burst may briefly slow response times until new pods become ready (typically 10–20 seconds).
</Info>

## Common causes of slow performance

### Memory or CPU limits exceeded

Each tier allocates specific resource limits per pod. If your app exceeds these, Kubernetes **throttles CPU** or **kills the pod** (OOMKilled) and restarts it.

**Check your app's resource usage:**
1. Open the **Workspace** and navigate to your app
2. Click **Metrics** in the sidebar
3. Review the CPU and memory graphs for spikes or sustained high usage

If you consistently hit limits, either optimise your code (see below) or upgrade to a tier with higher per-pod resources.

<Steps>
<Step title="Identify resource bottlenecks">
Look for repeated pod restarts or CPU throttling events in the Metrics panel.
</Step>
<Step title="Profile your application">
Use `console.time()` (Node.js), `cProfile` (Python) or framework-specific profilers to find slow functions or database queries.
</Step>
<Step title="Optimise or upgrade">
Refactor expensive operations, add caching or move to a higher tier if the workload is legitimate.
</Step>
</Steps>

### Slow database queries

MongoDB is shared infrastructure; poorly optimised queries can slow your app and impact other users.

**Common culprits:**
- **Missing indexes** on frequently queried fields
- **Large result sets** fetched without pagination (`limit` / `skip`)
- **Unbounded regex queries** or full collection scans

<Tip>
Use MongoDB's `.explain()` method to inspect query plans. Add indexes for fields used in `find()`, `sort()` and aggregation pipelines. See [Database (MongoDB)](/database-mongodb) for indexing guidance.
</Tip>

### Blocking I/O or unoptimised dependencies

Heavy synchronous operations — file I/O, image processing, PDF generation — block the event loop in Node.js or the main thread in Python, stalling all other requests.

**Solutions:**
- Move heavy tasks to background workers or queues
- Use streaming APIs for large file uploads/downloads
- Lazy-load large dependencies only when needed
- Replace heavy libraries with lighter alternatives (e.g. `dayjs` instead of `moment`)

### Cold dependency fetches

If your app fetches external resources (fonts, CSS frameworks, third-party APIs) on every request, network latency compounds. Cache responses or bundle assets at build time.

## Common causes of crashes

### Unhandled promise rejections / exceptions

Emergent's runtime restarts crashed pods automatically, but repeated crashes trigger **CrashLoopBackOff** — the pod won't restart until you fix the code.

<CodeGroup>
```javascript Node.js
process.on('unhandledRejection', (reason, promise) => {
  console.error('Unhandled Rejection:', reason);
  // Log to monitoring, do NOT exit the process
});
```

```python Python (Flask)
@app.errorhandler(Exception)
def handle_exception(e):
    app.logger.error(f"Unhandled exception: {e}")
    return {"error": "Internal server error"}, 500
```
</CodeGroup>

<Warning title="CrashLoopBackOff">
If logs show repeated crashes within seconds of startup, you have a **boot-time error** (missing env var, broken import, failed DB connection). Fix the root cause — the pod won't stabilise until the error is resolved.
</Warning>

### Out-of-memory kills (OOMKilled)

When a pod exceeds its memory limit, Kubernetes terminates it immediately. You'll see `OOMKilled` in the Metrics panel.

**Common causes:**
- In-memory caching of large datasets (use Redis or MongoDB instead)
- Memory leaks (closures holding references, event listeners not cleaned up)
- Large request payloads without streaming

**Mitigation:**
1. Add memory profiling (Node.js: `--inspect`, Python: `memory_profiler`)
2. Implement response streaming for large data exports
3. Use external storage (MongoDB, S3-compatible object storage) instead of in-memory buffers
4. Upgrade tier if legitimate high-memory workload

### Missing or incorrect environment variables

If your app expects an API key, database URL or config value that isn't set, it may crash on boot or on first use.

<Note>
Emergent automatically injects `MONGODB_URI` and `PORT`. Custom env vars must be set in the app's **Settings** panel. The [Universal LLM Key](/the-universal-llm-key) is injected only if enabled.
</Note>

## Debugging workflow

<AccordionGroup>
<Accordion title="How do I view real-time logs?">
Open your app in the Workspace, click **Logs** in the sidebar. Logs stream in real time and persist for 7 days (30 days on Pro/Enterprise).
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="My app works locally but crashes in production">
Check for missing environment variables, file-system paths (containers are read-only except `/tmp`), or dependencies that rely on native binaries not present in the container image.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Metrics show high CPU but logs are silent">
Your app may be stuck in an infinite loop, performing expensive synchronous operations, or running a hot regex. Add `console.time()` / `console.timeEnd()` around suspect code paths, redeploy and check logs.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Cold starts are too slow (>20 seconds)">
Large container images take longer to pull. Minimise dependencies, use multi-stage Docker builds (if custom Dockerfile), and ensure your app framework starts quickly (avoid heavy initialisation logic at boot).
</Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

## Quick performance checklist

<Steps>
<Step title="Add database indexes">
Use `.createIndex()` for fields in `find()`, `sort()` and aggregation `$match` stages.
</Step>
<Step title="Enable response caching">
Cache expensive computations, API responses or rendered HTML for a few seconds or minutes using in-memory LRU cache or Redis.
</Step>
<Step title="Paginate large result sets">
Never fetch entire collections. Use `limit()` and `skip()` or cursor-based pagination.
</Step>
<Step title="Wrap async code in try/catch">
Prevent unhandled rejections from crashing the app. Log errors and return user-friendly messages.
</Step>
<Step title="Monitor memory and CPU trends">
Check the Metrics panel weekly. Gradual increases suggest a memory leak; sudden spikes indicate inefficient operations.
</Step>
<Step title="Test under realistic load">
Use `autocannon` (Node.js) or `locust` (Python) to simulate concurrent users and identify bottlenecks before they hit production.
</Step>
</Steps>

<Info title="Still experiencing issues?">
If performance problems persist after applying these fixes, describe your symptoms in chat and agents will profile your app, suggest optimisations or recommend a tier upgrade if resource limits are the bottleneck.
</Info>
app-slow-crashing-or-cold-starting.description: KEDA event-driven auto-scaling, scale-to-zero cold starts, Pod Disruption Budgets by tier, and performance optimisation for slow/crashing deployed apps.

notion.title: Notion
notion.content:
## Overview

The Notion integration allows your Emergent app to read from and write to Notion databases, pages, and blocks. You can query databases, create pages, update content, and sync data between your app and your Notion workspace.

<Note title="Authentication required">
You'll need a Notion integration token with appropriate permissions for the pages and databases you want to access.
</Note>

## Prerequisites

Before setting up the Notion integration in Emergent, you'll need:

- A Notion account with workspace admin access (to create internal integrations)
- The pages or databases you want to integrate already created in Notion
- Permissions to share those resources with an integration

## Setting up your Notion integration

<Steps>

<Step title="Create a Notion integration">
Navigate to [Notion's integration settings](https://www.notion.so/my-integrations) and click **New integration**.

Give your integration a name (for example, "Emergent App"), select the workspace, and choose the capabilities you need:

- **Read content** – query databases and read page content
- **Update content** – modify existing pages and database entries
- **Insert content** – create new pages and database records

Click **Submit** to create the integration and reveal your **Internal Integration Token**.
</Step>

<Step title="Copy the integration token">
Copy the token that starts with `secret_`. You'll need this in the next step.

<Warning>
Keep this token secure. Anyone with access to it can read or modify your Notion data according to the permissions you granted.
</Warning>
</Step>

<Step title="Share Notion pages with your integration">
Open each Notion page or database you want your app to access. Click the **···** menu in the top right, select **Add connections**, and choose your integration by name.

Without this step, your integration won't be able to see the page — even with a valid token.
</Step>

<Step title="Add the token to Emergent">
In your Emergent workspace, open the **Settings** panel (bottom left) and navigate to **Integrations**. Find **Notion** in the list and click **Connect**.

Paste your Internal Integration Token into the field and click **Save**.
</Step>

<Step title="Test the connection">
In Chat, describe a simple query to verify the integration works:

> "Fetch the titles of all entries in my Tasks database in Notion"

If the integration is configured correctly, the agent will retrieve and display the data.
</Step>

</Steps>

## Common use cases

<CardGroup cols={2}>

<Card title="Task sync" icon="list-checks">
Pull tasks from a Notion database, display them in your app, and push updates back when users complete them.
</Card>

<Card title="Content publishing" icon="file-text">
Use Notion as a headless CMS — query a database of blog posts or docs and render them in your app.
</Card>

<Card title="Form submissions" icon="inbox">
Write form responses from your app directly into a Notion database for review and triage.
</Card>

<Card title="Knowledge base search" icon="search">
Query your team's Notion wiki or documentation pages and surface answers in-app.
</Card>

</CardGroup>

## Working with Notion databases

Notion databases are queryable collections with properties (columns). When you describe a query in Chat, the agent will:

1. Identify the database by name or ID
2. Apply any filters you specify (status, date range, tags, etc.)
3. Return the properties you request (or all properties by default)

<Tip>
Reference databases by their user-friendly name in Chat. The agent will resolve the database ID automatically once the page is shared with your integration.
</Tip>

### Example queries

- "Show me all tasks in the Marketing database where Status is 'In Progress'"
- "Create a new entry in the Contacts database with name 'Alice' and email 'alice@example.com'"
- "Update the Status property of the task titled 'Design review' to 'Done'"

## Permissions and access control

Your Notion integration can only access pages and databases that have been explicitly shared with it. If you add a new database or page later, remember to share it via **Add connections** in Notion.

<Info>
If you revoke the integration's access in Notion or regenerate the token, you'll need to update the token in Emergent's integration settings.
</Info>

## Troubleshooting

<AccordionGroup>

<Accordion title="I get an 'object not found' error">
The page or database hasn't been shared with your integration. Open the page in Notion, click **···** → **Add connections**, and select your integration.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="The agent can't find my database by name">
Try sharing the database page with the integration, then re-describe your request in Chat. If the issue persists, you can provide the database ID directly (find it in the URL when viewing the database in Notion).
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Properties aren't updating">
Verify that your integration has **Update content** capability. You may need to edit the integration in Notion's settings and re-save the token in Emergent.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="I want to revoke access">
In [Notion's integration settings](https://www.notion.so/my-integrations), find your integration and click **Delete integration**. Then remove the token from Emergent's integration settings.
</Accordion>

</AccordionGroup>

## Next steps

- Explore the [Database (MongoDB)](/database-mongodb) integration to combine Notion data with your app's internal database
- Use [The Universal LLM Key](/the-universal-llm-key) to add AI-powered search over your Notion content
- Visit the [Glossary of Emergent terms](/glossary-of-emergent-terms) for definitions of workspace, agent, and integration concepts

deployment-plan-levels.title: Deployment plan levels
deployment-plan-levels.content:
## Overview

Every deployment on Emergent runs on a **plan level** — a CPU and memory tier that determines the compute resources available to your application. Choosing the right plan ensures your app has enough headroom to handle its workload without over-provisioning.

Plan levels range from light (suitable for static sites and low-traffic services) to heavy (for compute-intensive backends and high-concurrency APIs).

---

## Available plan levels

Emergent offers four tiers:

| Plan      | CPU   | Memory | Typical use cases                                    |
|-----------|-------|--------|------------------------------------------------------|
| **Micro** | 0.5   | 512 MB | Static sites, documentation, marketing pages         |
| **Small** | 1     | 1 GB   | Low-traffic APIs, hobby projects, internal tools     |
| **Medium**| 2     | 2 GB   | Production web apps, REST APIs, moderate concurrency |
| **Large** | 4     | 4 GB   | High-traffic services, background workers, ML inference |

<Note>
All plans include HTTPS, automatic scaling within the tier, and zero-downtime deployments.
</Note>

---

## How to choose the right plan

### Start with your app's workload

Ask yourself:

- **Traffic volume**: How many concurrent users or requests per second do you expect?  
- **Data processing**: Does the app handle large files, images, or compute-heavy operations?  
- **Background jobs**: Do you run scheduled tasks, email sends, or queue workers?  
- **Dependencies**: Do your runtime libraries (Node.js packages, Python deps) have high memory overhead?

<Tip title="Start small, scale up">
If you're unsure, deploy on **Small** and monitor resource usage. You can upgrade to a higher tier anytime from the deployment settings.
</Tip>

### When to use Micro

Choose **Micro** if your app:

- Serves **static HTML/CSS/JS** with no server-side logic  
- Runs a simple SSG (static site generator) like Hugo, Eleventy, or a docs site  
- Expects **fewer than 100 concurrent visitors**

<Warning>
Micro plans are **not suitable** for Node.js servers, Python Flask/Django apps, or anything with a persistent runtime. Use Small or higher for dynamic backends.
</Warning>

### When to use Small

Choose **Small** if your app:

- Is a **lightweight REST API** or a simple web server  
- Handles **low-to-moderate traffic** (hundreds of requests per hour)  
- Runs a hobby project, internal tool, or proof-of-concept  
- Uses a minimal framework (Express, FastAPI, Sinatra)

### When to use Medium

Choose **Medium** if your app:

- Serves a **production web application** with moderate concurrency  
- Processes form submissions, image uploads, or external API calls  
- Runs a database-backed app (PostgreSQL, MongoDB) with typical query loads  
- Expects **hundreds to low thousands of concurrent users**

This is the **most common tier** for production services.

### When to use Large

Choose **Large** if your app:

- Handles **high traffic** or compute-intensive workloads  
- Runs ML inference, video processing, or large data transformations  
- Operates background workers or queue consumers alongside the main service  
- Needs **4+ GB of memory** for dependencies or in-memory caching

---

## Monitoring and upgrading

Once deployed, you can view real-time CPU and memory usage in the **deployment details** panel.

<Steps>
<Step title="Open the deployment">
Navigate to your app's **Deployments** tab and select the active deployment.
</Step>

<Step title="Check resource metrics">
Scroll to the **Resources** section to see current usage and historical graphs.
</Step>

<Step title="Upgrade if needed">
If you're consistently hitting 80%+ usage, click **Change Plan** and select a higher tier. The upgrade applies instantly with no downtime.
</Step>
</Steps>

<Info>
Plan downgrades are also supported. If your app is over-provisioned, you can scale down to save on deployment costs.
</Info>

---

## Pricing and credits

Each plan level consumes a different number of [credits](/how-credits-work) per hour of uptime. Higher tiers cost more per hour but provide better performance and reliability.

Check the **Billing** page in your workspace for the current credit rate per plan.
