deployment-pipeline-failures.title: Deployment pipeline failures
deployment-pipeline-failures.content:
## Overview

Deployment failures in Emergent typically fall into one of six categories: build-time errors, database migration timeouts, environment-secret issues, container crashes, webhook conflicts, and failed health checks. This page walks through each failure mode, its symptoms, and how to resolve it.

<Callout type="tip" title="Deploy logs are your friend">
The deployment panel shows real-time logs for each stage—build, migrate, deploy. When a deployment fails, scroll to the error message and look for the stack trace or last successful step.
</Callout>

---

## Build errors

Build failures occur during the TypeScript compile, linting, or dependency-resolution phase. Emergent runs `npm install` (or the equivalent for your package manager) then compiles your code; any error here halts the pipeline before containers are started.

### Common causes

- **TypeScript errors** – Type mismatches, missing imports, or incorrect generics introduced by a recent code generation.
- **ESLint violations** – The build enforces your project's linting rules; a new unused variable or disallowed pattern will block deployment.
- **Dependency conflicts** – Incompatible package versions, missing peer dependencies, or a corrupted `package-lock.json`.

### Resolution steps

<Steps>
<Step title="Read the build log">
Open the deployment panel and expand the **Build** stage. The last few lines will show the exact file and line number.
</Step>

<Step title="Fix locally first">
Reproduce the error in your local workspace (`npm run build` or `npm run lint`). Fix the issue, commit, and push.
</Step>

<Step title="Dependency conflicts">
If the error mentions peer-dependency warnings or version mismatches, run `npm install` locally to regenerate lock files, then commit the updated `package-lock.json`.
</Step>

<Step title="Retry the deployment">
Once you've pushed the fix, trigger a new deploy from the workspace or let the automatic deployment pick up the latest commit.
</Step>
</Steps>

<Callout type="warning" title="Auto-generated code">
If the agents introduced the error during a recent generation, describe the issue in chat (e.g. *"Build is failing with TS error on line 42 of `api/users.ts`"*) and the agent will propose a corrective change.
</Callout>

---

## Database migration timeouts

When your app includes schema changes (new collections, indexes, or data transforms), Emergent runs a migration step before starting the new containers. If the migration script takes too long or cannot connect to MongoDB, the deploy will time out.

### Symptoms

- Deploy logs show `Running migrations…` for several minutes, then fail with a timeout or connection error.
- No new containers are started; the previous version continues to run.

### Common causes

| Cause | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| **Large data transform** | Migration script loops over millions of documents; exceeds the timeout window. |
| **Database unreachable** | Network issue or incorrect connection string prevents the migrator from reaching MongoDB. |
| **Lock contention** | Another process holds a write lock on the collection being migrated. |

### Resolution steps

<Steps>
<Step title="Check migration logs">
Look for connection errors or slow query warnings in the deploy panel's **Migrate** stage.
</Step>

<Step title="Optimize the migration">
If the script is slow, refactor it to batch updates or use bulk operations. Ask the agent to rewrite the migration for better performance.
</Step>

<Step title="Verify connection secrets">
Ensure `MONGODB_URI` is correctly set in your environment secrets. See [Database (MongoDB)](/database-mongodb) for connection-string format.
</Step>

<Step title="Increase timeout (if available)">
Contact support if your migration legitimately requires more than the default window; the Emergent team can adjust the timeout for your workspace.
</Step>
</Steps>

<Callout type="info">
If the migration is a one-time backfill, consider running it manually via a script in your workspace, then removing the migration step and deploying again.
</Callout>

---

## Secret-export issues

Deployments can fail if required environment variables are missing, malformed, or contain invalid characters that break the container's shell environment.

### Symptoms

- Deploy succeeds but the app immediately crashes with `Missing required env var` or similar.
- Logs show escaped characters or truncated secret values.

### Common causes

- A new feature expects an API key (e.g. `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY`) that hasn't been added to the workspace secrets.
- Secret value contains unescaped quotes, newlines, or special shell characters.
- Copy-paste error introduced invisible characters or trailing whitespace.

### Resolution steps

<Steps>
<Step title="Audit required secrets">
Check your code for `process.env.VARIABLE_NAME` references and ensure each is defined in the workspace's **Secrets** panel.
</Step>

<Step title="Re-enter the secret">
Delete and re-add the secret in the UI to eliminate hidden characters. Paste the value directly from the provider (no intermediate text editor).
</Step>

<Step title="Test locally">
Export the secret in your local shell (`export VAR=value`) and run the app to confirm it parses correctly.
</Step>

<Step title="Redeploy">
Once all secrets are present and valid, trigger a new deployment. The containers will pick up the updated environment.
</Step>
</Steps>

<Callout type="tip" title="Universal LLM Key">
If your app uses AI features, remember to set [The Universal LLM Key](/the-universal-llm-key) in secrets—many AI generation failures stem from a missing or expired key.
</Callout>

---

## CrashLoopBackOff and OOM kills

After a successful build, containers may crash repeatedly (CrashLoopBackOff) or be killed by the orchestrator for exceeding memory limits (OOM kill). Both prevent the deployment from reaching a healthy state.

### CrashLoopBackOff

The container starts but exits within seconds, triggering an automatic restart loop.

**Common causes:**

- Uncaught exception during startup (missing secret, database connection failure).
- Port mismatch—app listens on a port different from the one the health check expects.
- Syntax error or runtime crash in initialization code.

**Resolution:**

<Steps>
<Step title="Read container logs">
The deploy panel's **Runtime** tab shows stdout/stderr from the crashed container. Look for the stack trace or last log line before the crash.
</Step>

<Step title="Fix the error">
Address the root cause (add missing secret, correct the listen port, fix the exception). Commit and redeploy.
</Step>

<Step title="Verify health-check endpoint">
Ensure your app exposes the health-check route (`/health` or `/api/health`) and it returns `200 OK` when the app is ready.
</Step>
</Steps>

### OOM kills

The container is terminated because it consumed more memory than allocated.

**Symptoms:**

- Logs end abruptly with no stack trace.
- Deploy panel shows `OOMKilled` or `Exit code 137`.

**Resolution:**

<Steps>
<Step title="Identify memory-hungry code">
Profile the app locally or add logging to track memory usage. Common culprits: large in-memory caches, file uploads held in RAM, unbounded data fetches.
</Step>

<Step title="Optimize or paginate">
Refactor to stream large responses, paginate queries, or offload processing to a background job.
</Step>

<Step title="Request a memory increase">
If the app legitimately needs more RAM, contact support to raise the container's memory limit for your workspace.
</Step>
</Steps>

<Callout type="warning" title="Mobile WebView apps">
Apps converted from web to mobile via [Web ↔ Mobile conversion](/web-mobile-conversion-canonical) may bundle larger assets; ensure image/video assets are optimized or served from CDN rather than embedded.
</Callout>

---

## Telegram 409 conflicts

If your app integrates a Telegram bot, deployments may fail with a `409 Conflict` error when setting the webhook. This happens when another instance (or a previous deployment) is already registered to receive updates at a different URL.

### Cause

Telegram allows only **one** webhook URL per bot token at a time. If you deploy to a new domain or the agent attempts to register a second webhook before deleting the old one, Telegram rejects the request.

### Resolution

<Steps>
<Step title="Delete the existing webhook">
Use the Telegram Bot API to clear the current webhook:

```bash
curl https://api.telegram.org/bot<YOUR_BOT_TOKEN>/deleteWebhook
```
</Step>

<Step title="Redeploy">
Trigger a new deployment. The app will register the correct webhook URL on startup.
</Step>

<Step title="Ensure single deployment">
Avoid running multiple instances of the same bot (e.g. staging + production with the same token). Use separate bot tokens for each environment.
</Step>
</Steps>

<Callout type="info">
If you recently changed your [custom domain](/custom-domain), the old webhook URL may still be registered. Deleting it resolves the conflict.
</Callout>

---

## Health-check failures

Emergent waits for your app to respond successfully to health-check probes before marking the deployment as live. If the checks time out or return non-2xx status codes, the deployment is rolled back.

### Symptoms

- Deploy progresses past build and migrate, then stalls at **Starting containers…**
- Logs show repeated `GET /health` or `GET /api/health` requests, all failing or timing out.

### Common causes

| Cause | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| **Missing route** | No handler defined for the health-check path. |
| **Database dependency** | Health check queries MongoDB, but DB is unreachable or slow, causing timeouts. |
| **Incorrect listen address** | App binds to `127.0.0.1` instead of `0.0.0.0`, making it unreachable from the orchestrator. |
| **Slow startup** | App takes longer to initialize than the probe's initial-delay setting. |

### Resolution steps

<Steps>
<Step title="Implement a lightweight health endpoint">
Ensure your app exposes a route that returns `200 OK` without heavy logic:

<CodeGroup>
```typescript Express
app.get('/health', (req, res) => {
  res.status(200).json({ status: 'ok' });
});
```

```typescript Fastify
fastify.get('/health', async () => {
  return { status: 'ok' };
});
```
</CodeGroup>

Do **not** query the database or external APIs in the health check—keep it instant.
</Step>

<Step title="Bind to 0.0.0.0">
Verify your server listens on all interfaces:

```typescript
app.listen(PORT, '0.0.0.0', () => {
  console.log(`Server ready on port ${PORT}`);
});
```
</Step>

<Step title="Check readiness logic">
If your app must wait for DB or cache to initialize, expose a separate `/ready` endpoint and ensure the health check uses `/health` (which always returns 200).
</Step>

<Step title="Review probe timing">
Contact support if your app's startup genuinely requires more time than the default initial delay; the team can adjust probe settings for your workspace.
</Step>
</Steps>

<Callout type="success" title="Fast health checks = faster rollouts">
A quick, dependency-free health endpoint ensures deployments complete in seconds and rollbacks are instant if something goes wrong.
</Callout>

---

## Next steps

<CardGroup cols={2}>
<Card title="Database (MongoDB)" icon="database" href="/database-mongodb">
Connection strings, scaling, and backup strategies
</Card>

<Card title="Custom domain" icon="globe" href="/custom-domain">
Point your own domain at a deployed app
</Card>

<Card title="Glossary of Emergent terms" icon="book" href="/glossary-of-emergent-terms">
Definitions of workspace, agent, vibe-coding, and more
</Card>

<Card title="A tour of the workspace" icon="map" href="/a-tour-of-the-workspace">
Overview of the Emergent interface and panels
</Card>
</CardGroup>
deployment-pipeline-failures.description: Specific failure modes: build errors (TS/ESLint/dependency), DB migration timeouts, secret-export issues, CrashLoopBackOff/OOM kills, Telegram 409, health-check failures.

previewing-iterating.title: Previewing & iterating
previewing-iterating.content:
## Using the preview

As the AI agent builds your app, Emergent automatically generates a **live preview**. This preview updates in real time as the agent writes code, installs dependencies, and configures features—no manual refresh required in most cases.

The preview runs in a sandboxed environment separate from your eventual production deployment. It's designed for rapid iteration: you can test each feature, explore the UI, and verify behavior before you ever commit to deploying.

### Testing and iterating

Once the agent pauses (either because it completed your request or hit a stop reason—see [How the agent runs](/how-the-agent-runs-workflow-stop-reasons)), open the preview and interact with your app as a real user would:

- Click through flows, submit forms, trigger actions.
- Check responsive layouts on different screen sizes (resize the preview pane or open in a new tab).
- Verify integrations like authentication, database reads/writes, or external API calls.

When you spot something that needs to change—whether it's a bug, a design tweak, or a missing feature—simply **describe the change in chat**. The agent will read your feedback, modify the relevant code, and the preview will update automatically. This cycle repeats as many times as you need.

<Tip title="Be specific in your change requests">
Instead of "the button looks wrong," try "move the Sign In button to the top-right corner and make it blue." Clear instructions help the agent iterate faster.
</Tip>

### Sharing the preview

You can share the preview URL with teammates or stakeholders to gather feedback before deploying. Keep in mind that the preview environment may reset or become unavailable if the workspace is idle for an extended period, so it's not suitable for long-term public access.

<Warning title="Preview is NOT your deployed app">
The preview environment and your deployed app are **completely separate**. Changes you see in the preview do *not* automatically appear in production.

- The preview uses temporary infrastructure that spins up and down as you build.
- Deployment is a deliberate step that provisions persistent infrastructure, locks in a specific version of your code, and assigns a production domain.

Until you explicitly deploy (or redeploy), your live app will continue running the last deployed version—even if the preview shows something totally different. For details on how these environments differ, see [Preview vs Deployed](/preview-vs-deployed-separate).
</Warning>

## When you're ready to deploy

Once you're satisfied with what you see in the preview, you can move to deployment. Deployment packages your app, provisions infrastructure according to your [Deployment plan level](/deployment-plan-levels), and publishes it at a stable URL.

Check the [Deployment types](/deployment-types) page to understand your options, and see [A tour of the workspace](/a-tour-of-the-workspace) for the deploy button location and workflow.

data-leakage.title: Data leakage
data-leakage.content:
## We treat your data with the same care you would

When you build on Emergent, you're trusting us with app code, database records, API keys, and sometimes sensitive business logic. We've architected every layer of the platform to prevent accidental exposure or leakage.

<Callout type="success" title="Your data stays yours">
Emergent does **not** train AI models on your code, prompts, or database content. We do not share your project data with third parties outside the AI providers required to run agents and generate media. Your secrets, database records, and deployed apps remain isolated to your workspace.
</Callout>

---

## What gets sent to AI providers

Emergent uses third-party language models (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, etc.) to power agents and Wingman. Here's what those providers see:

| Data type | Sent to AI | Purpose |
|-----------|-----------|---------|
| Your chat messages & prompts | Yes | Instruction and context for the agent |
| Generated code files | Yes | So the agent can read, edit, and reason about your app |
| Database schema | Yes | To help the agent write queries and understand data structure |
| Database **records** | Only if you explicitly paste them into chat | Agent needs to see sample data to debug or build features |
| Environment variable **names** | Yes | Agent can reference `process.env.STRIPE_KEY` in code |
| Environment variable **values** | **No** | Secrets are injected at runtime; agents never see the actual API key |
| Job & deployment logs (stdout/stderr) | Partially | If the agent is debugging a failing build, recent logs may be included in context |

<Note>
AI providers process this data to respond to your request but—per their terms—do not train public models on API traffic from enterprise/commercial use.
</Note>

---

## Secrets & environment variables

When you add an API key or secret in the **Env** panel, it is:

- Encrypted at rest in our database
- Injected into your app's runtime **only** (not visible in code)
- Never included in chat context sent to the AI

The agent can *write* code that references `process.env.YOUR_SECRET`, but it never sees the plaintext value. This prevents accidental logging, copy-paste errors, or model memorization.

<Warning>
If you **paste** a secret directly into the chat (e.g., "use API key `sk-12345…`"), that text *will* be sent to the AI provider. Always add secrets via the Env panel instead.
</Warning>

---

## Database isolation

Every Emergent workspace includes a dedicated MongoDB instance. Your database is:

- **Not shared** across workspaces or users
- Accessible only via the platform's scoped connection (the agent and your deployed app)
- Encrypted in transit and at rest

The agent can read and write collections to build features, but it does not have shell access or admin privileges beyond standard CRUD operations.

<Tip>
If you're connecting an **external** database (via a connection string in Env), standard network security applies—ensure you've whitelisted Emergent's IP range and use credentials with least-privilege access.
</Tip>

---

## Code & deployment artifacts

All source code, build logs, and deployment artifacts live in isolated storage tied to your workspace. Emergent staff do not browse your code unless you explicitly grant support access during a troubleshooting session.

Your app is deployed to a sandboxed container with:

- Ephemeral filesystem (writes don't persist between jobs)
- No access to other users' processes or data
- Rate-limited egress to prevent abuse

<Info>
Deployed apps are publicly accessible by URL, so **do not hard-code sensitive data** in client-side JavaScript or HTML. Use environment variables and server-side logic to protect secrets.
</Info>

---

## What we log & retain

Emergent retains:

- **Chat transcripts** – to preserve your workspace history and allow agents to reference past context
- **Job run metadata** – timestamps, credit usage, stop reasons
- **Error logs** – to help you (and us) debug failed builds

We do **not** retain:

- Full HTTP request/response bodies from your deployed app
- Database query results (beyond what the agent writes to the DB itself)
- Media files uploaded by your app's end users (unless you explicitly store them in your own MongoDB or external storage)

<Callout type="note" title="Data retention for troubleshooting">
If you delete a workspace, all associated code, chat history, and database records are **permanently removed** within 30 days. Aggregated usage metrics (credit spend, job count) are retained for billing and analytics but are not tied to identifiable project content.
</Callout>

---

## Compliance & best practices

While Emergent is designed for rapid prototyping and production-grade apps, you remain responsible for:

- **Not storing PII or regulated data** (HIPAA, PCI DSS) unless you've architected appropriate safeguards (encryption, access controls) in your own app logic
- **Reviewing generated code** for accidental logging of secrets or sensitive user data
- **Using environment variables** for all API keys, database credentials, and OAuth secrets

<Tip>
For production apps handling sensitive data, consider adding a middleware layer (auth tokens, field-level encryption) in your app code. Emergent gives you full control over your stack—use it to enforce your own security policies.
</Tip>

---

## Reporting a concern

If you believe your data has been exposed or you've discovered a vulnerability, email **security@emergent.ai** immediately. We triage security reports within 24 hours and will work with you to remediate any confirmed issues.

For general data or privacy questions, see our **Privacy Policy** (linked in the workspace footer) or reach out to support via the in-app chat.
data-leakage.description: Safeguards against leakage; what is / isn't exposed and how it's protected.

slack.title: Slack
slack.content:
## Overview

Connect your Emergent app to Slack to send notifications, receive commands, and build interactive chat experiences. This integration enables your app to post messages to channels, respond to user interactions, and leverage Slack's rich messaging features.

Common use cases include deployment notifications, error alerts, approval workflows, and conversational interfaces for your application logic.

## Prerequisites

Before integrating Slack, ensure you have:

- A Slack workspace where you have permission to install apps
- An active Emergent project
- Administrative access to your Emergent app's environment variables

## Setting up a Slack app

<Steps>
<Step title="Create a new Slack app">
Navigate to [api.slack.com/apps](https://api.slack.com/apps) and click **Create New App**. Choose **From scratch**, provide an app name (e.g., "My Emergent App"), and select the workspace where you want to install it.
</Step>

<Step title="Configure OAuth & permissions">
In your app's settings, go to **OAuth & Permissions** in the sidebar. Scroll down to **Bot Token Scopes** and add the permissions your app needs:

- `chat:write` — post messages to channels
- `chat:write.public` — post to channels without joining
- `channels:read` — view basic channel info
- `groups:read` — view private channel info (if needed)
- `im:read` and `im:write` — send direct messages
- `commands` — handle slash commands (if applicable)

Add any additional scopes required by your specific integration.
</Step>

<Step title="Install the app to your workspace">
At the top of the **OAuth & Permissions** page, click **Install to Workspace**. Slack will prompt you to authorize the app. Once approved, you'll receive a **Bot User OAuth Token** starting with `xoxb-`. Copy this token — you'll need it in the next section.
</Step>

<Step title="Configure event subscriptions (optional)">
If your app needs to respond to Slack events (messages, reactions, button clicks), enable **Event Subscriptions** in the sidebar.

Set the **Request URL** to your Emergent app's webhook endpoint (e.g., `https://your-app.emergent.run/api/slack/events`). Slack will verify this URL with a challenge request.

Subscribe to the bot events you need, such as `message.channels`, `app_mention`, or `message.im`.
</Step>

<Step title="Set up slash commands (optional)">
To handle slash commands like `/deploy` or `/status`, go to **Slash Commands** and click **Create New Command**.

Provide the command name, request URL (e.g., `https://your-app.emergent.run/api/slack/command`), and a brief description. Save your changes.
</Step>
</Steps>

<Note>
Slack will only send events to publicly accessible URLs. If you're developing locally, use a tool like ngrok to create a temporary tunnel, or deploy your app to Emergent's hosted environment first.
</Note>

## Adding credentials to Emergent

Your Emergent app needs the Slack bot token and signing secret to authenticate requests.

<Steps>
<Step title="Copy your credentials">
From your Slack app settings:

- Copy the **Bot User OAuth Token** from **OAuth & Permissions** (`xoxb-...`)
- Copy the **Signing Secret** from **Basic Information** under **App Credentials**
</Step>

<Step title="Set environment variables">
In your Emergent project chat, describe the environment variables you need:

```
Add these environment variables:
SLACK_BOT_TOKEN=xoxb-your-token-here
SLACK_SIGNING_SECRET=your-signing-secret
```

The AI agents will securely store these as encrypted environment variables in your app.
</Step>

<Step title="Use the credentials in code">
Reference the environment variables in your application logic:

<CodeGroup>
```javascript Node.js
const { WebClient } = require('@slack/web-api');
const client = new WebClient(process.env.SLACK_BOT_TOKEN);

await client.chat.postMessage({
  channel: '#general',
  text: 'Deployment successful! 🚀'
});
```

```python Python
from slack_sdk import WebClient
import os

client = WebClient(token=os.environ['SLACK_BOT_TOKEN'])
client.chat_postMessage(
    channel='#general',
    text='Deployment successful! 🚀'
)
```
</CodeGroup>
</Step>
</Steps>

## Common integration patterns

<CardGroup cols={2}>
<Card title="Notification workflows" icon="bell">
Send alerts when deployments complete, errors occur, or user actions require attention. Post rich messages with buttons and attachments.
</Card>

<Card title="Approval flows" icon="circle-check">
Request approvals via interactive messages. Users click buttons to approve or reject, triggering webhooks back to your app.
</Card>

<Card title="Command interfaces" icon="terminal">
Implement slash commands that execute app logic directly from Slack, such as triggering builds or querying status.
</Card>

<Card title="Event-driven automation" icon="zap">
Listen for Slack events (mentions, reactions, new messages) and respond programmatically or trigger workflows.
</Card>
</CardGroup>

## Verifying webhook requests

<Warning>
Always verify that incoming webhook requests are genuinely from Slack using the signing secret. This prevents unauthorized parties from sending fake events to your app.
</Warning>

Slack signs each request with a timestamp and HMAC signature. Use the official SDKs or implement verification manually:

<CodeGroup>
```javascript Node.js
const crypto = require('crypto');

function verifySlackRequest(req) {
  const signature = req.headers['x-slack-signature'];
  const timestamp = req.headers['x-slack-request-timestamp'];
  const body = JSON.stringify(req.body);
  
  const hmac = crypto.createHmac('sha256', process.env.SLACK_SIGNING_SECRET);
  const [version, hash] = signature.split('=');
  hmac.update(`${version}:${timestamp}:${body}`);
  
  return crypto.timingSafeEqual(
    Buffer.from(hash, 'hex'),
    hmac.digest()
  );
}
```

```python Python
import hmac
import hashlib

def verify_slack_request(request):
    signature = request.headers['X-Slack-Signature']
    timestamp = request.headers['X-Slack-Request-Timestamp']
    body = request.get_data(as_text=True)
    
    base = f"v0:{timestamp}:{body}"
    expected = 'v0=' + hmac.new(
        os.environ['SLACK_SIGNING_SECRET'].encode(),
        base.encode(),
        hashlib.sha256
    ).hexdigest()
    
    return hmac.compare_digest(expected, signature)
```
</CodeGroup>

## Troubleshooting

<AccordionGroup>
<Accordion title="Messages aren't appearing in channels">
Verify that your bot has been added to the target channel. Either invite the bot manually (`/invite @YourBot`) or use the `chat:write.public` scope to post without joining.

Check that the channel ID or name is correct. Channel IDs start with `C` for public channels and `G` for private channels.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Webhook URL verification fails">
Ensure your endpoint responds to Slack's challenge request immediately with the `challenge` parameter in the response body. Do not perform long operations during verification.

If using Emergent's serverless functions, confirm the endpoint is deployed and publicly accessible.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Events aren't triggering">
Confirm that **Event Subscriptions** is enabled and the correct bot events are subscribed. Check your app's event logs in the Slack API dashboard for delivery failures.

Verify your request URL is returning HTTP 200 within three seconds. Slack will disable your endpoint after repeated timeouts.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Interactive components don't work">
Enable **Interactivity & Shortcuts** in your app settings and provide a **Request URL** for interaction payloads. This is separate from the events URL.

Ensure your endpoint can parse `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` payloads and respond within three seconds to acknowledge the interaction.
</Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

## Next steps

<CardGroup cols={2}>
<Card title="Database (MongoDB)" icon="database" href="/database-mongodb">
Store Slack user mappings and interaction state in your app's database.
</Card>

<Card title="Custom domain" icon="globe" href="/custom-domain">
Use a branded domain for your Slack webhook endpoints.
</Card>
</CardGroup>

## Additional resources

- [Slack API documentation](https://api.slack.com/)
- [Building Slack apps guide](https://api.slack.com/start)
- [Block Kit builder](https://api.slack.com/block-kit) for designing rich messages

resend.title: Resend
resend.content:
## Overview

Resend is a modern email API that makes it easy to send transactional and marketing emails from your Emergent app. With its developer-friendly interface and reliable delivery, Resend is ideal for password resets, welcome emails, notifications, and more.

This guide walks you through integrating Resend into your Emergent project so your AI agents can send emails on behalf of your application.

<Note>
Resend requires an API key, which you'll obtain from their dashboard. The free tier includes generous limits for development and small production workloads.
</Note>

## Prerequisites

Before you begin, you'll need:

- An Emergent project (or start a new one by describing your app idea)
- A Resend account — sign up at [resend.com](https://resend.com)
- A verified sending domain (Resend provides a sandbox domain for testing)

## Getting your Resend API key

<Steps>
<Step title="Create a Resend account">
Visit [resend.com](https://resend.com) and sign up. Verify your email address to activate your account.
</Step>

<Step title="Add and verify a domain">
In the Resend dashboard, navigate to **Domains** and add your domain (e.g., `yourdomain.com`). Follow the DNS verification steps—typically adding TXT and CNAME records.

For testing, you can use Resend's built-in sandbox domain (`onboarding@resend.dev`) without verification, though it has sending limits.
</Step>

<Step title="Generate an API key">
Go to **API Keys** in the Resend dashboard and click **Create API Key**. Give it a descriptive name (e.g., "Emergent Production") and copy the key—it will only be shown once.
</Step>
</Steps>

## Configuring Resend in Emergent

<Steps>
<Step title="Open your Emergent project">
Navigate to the project where you want to send emails.
</Step>

<Step title="Add the API key as an environment variable">
In the Emergent chat, tell the agent to add your Resend API key:

> "Add a secret environment variable called `RESEND_API_KEY` with the value `re_abc123...`"

The agent will securely store this credential and make it available to your application code.

<Tip>
Use descriptive variable names. If you have multiple services, consider `RESEND_API_KEY` for clarity rather than a generic `API_KEY`.
</Tip>
</Step>

<Step title="Install the Resend SDK">
Ask the agent to install the Resend library for your stack:

> "Install the Resend Node.js SDK"

or for Python:

> "Install the resend Python package"

The agent will add the dependency and ensure it's available in your runtime environment.
</Step>
</Steps>

## Sending your first email

Once configured, you can ask the Emergent agent to implement email sending in your app. Here are some example prompts:

<Tabs>
<Tab title="Transactional email">
> "When a user signs up, send them a welcome email via Resend. Use the template: subject 'Welcome to [AppName]', body with a friendly greeting and a link to getting started."
</Tab>

<Tab title="Password reset">
> "Add a forgot password flow. When triggered, generate a reset token, save it to the database, and send a password reset email via Resend with a link containing the token."
</Tab>

<Tab title="Notification digest">
> "Every Monday at 9am, query all users with pending notifications and send each a summary email via Resend listing their unread items."
</Tab>
</Tabs>

The agent will write the necessary code, configure email templates, and handle error cases like invalid recipient addresses.

## Testing email delivery

<AccordionGroup>
<Accordion title="How do I test without spamming real users?">
Use Resend's sandbox domain (`onboarding@resend.dev` as the "from" address) to send test emails to your own address. Emails from the sandbox domain won't count against your production quota and are clearly marked as tests.

Alternatively, tell the agent: "In development mode, send all emails to `mytest@example.com` instead of real recipients."
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Can I preview emails before sending?">
Yes—ask the agent to add an admin endpoint or page that renders email templates without actually sending them. For example:

> "Add a `/admin/preview-email?template=welcome` route that shows what the welcome email looks like."
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="How do I check delivery status?">
Resend provides webhook events for delivery, bounces, and complaints. You can ask the agent:

> "Set up a webhook endpoint to receive Resend delivery events and log them to the database."

Or check the Resend dashboard under **Logs** to see recent email activity.
</Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

## Common use cases

<CardGroup cols={2}>
<Card title="User onboarding" icon="user-plus">
Welcome emails, email verification links, and getting-started guides sent automatically when users sign up.
</Card>

<Card title="Transactional alerts" icon="bell">
Order confirmations, shipping updates, payment receipts, and account security notifications.
</Card>

<Card title="Scheduled digests" icon="calendar">
Daily or weekly summaries, activity reports, and content recommendations sent on a schedule.
</Card>

<Card title="Team collaboration" icon="users">
Invitations, mentions, comment notifications, and shared document alerts within your app.
</Card>
</CardGroup>

## Best practices

- **Verify your domain** for production use—emails from verified domains have better deliverability and avoid sandbox limits.
- **Use environment variables** for API keys and never commit them to your codebase.
- **Handle errors gracefully**—ask the agent to retry failed sends or log them for manual review.
- **Personalize emails**—include the recipient's name and relevant context to improve engagement.
- **Monitor bounce rates**—if Resend reports high bounces, check your recipient list quality and unsubscribe flow.

<Warning>
Resend enforces rate limits based on your plan tier. If you're sending high volumes, coordinate with the agent to implement queueing or batch sending to stay within limits.
</Warning>

## Troubleshooting

| Issue | Solution |
|-------|----------|
| "Invalid API key" error | Double-check the `RESEND_API_KEY` variable value in your Emergent project. Regenerate the key in Resend if needed. |
| Emails not arriving | Check your spam folder. Verify your sending domain in the Resend dashboard. Review Resend's **Logs** for delivery errors. |
| Rate limit exceeded | Ask the agent to add retry logic with exponential backoff, or upgrade your Resend plan for higher limits. |
| "From" address rejected | Ensure the sender address matches your verified domain. Sandbox emails must use `onboarding@resend.dev`. |

## Next steps

- **Customize email templates**: Ask the agent to use HTML templates with your brand colors and logo.
- **Track opens and clicks**: Enable Resend's tracking features and have the agent log engagement data.
- **Integrate with workflows**: Combine Resend with database triggers or scheduled jobs—see [Database (MongoDB)](/database-mongodb) for persistence options.
- **Set up webhooks**: Capture delivery events and update user records when emails bounce or are opened.

<Info>
Resend's API is RESTful and well-documented. If you need advanced features (like batch sending or A/B testing subject lines), describe your goal to the Emergent agent and it will implement the appropriate API calls.
</Info>

paypal.title: PayPal
paypal.content:
## Overview

PayPal is one of the most widely-used payment processors worldwide, supporting credit cards, debit cards, and PayPal account payments. Integrating PayPal into your Emergent app enables you to accept payments from customers in over 200 markets and 25+ currencies.

This guide walks you through setting up PayPal for your Emergent project, from creating a developer account to processing your first transaction.

<Note>
PayPal offers both **Standard** (redirect-based) and **Advanced** (in-context checkout) integrations. Emergent supports both patterns — describe your preferred checkout flow in chat and the platform will scaffold the appropriate implementation.
</Note>

## Before you begin

You'll need:

- A PayPal Business account (or a PayPal Developer sandbox account for testing)
- Your app deployed or running locally in Emergent
- Basic understanding of your app's payment flow

<Tip>
If you don't have a PayPal Business account yet, you can start with a free Developer account at [developer.paypal.com](https://developer.paypal.com) — it includes sandbox credentials for testing without processing real money.
</Tip>

## Get your PayPal API credentials

<Steps>
<Step title="Log in to the PayPal Developer Dashboard">
Navigate to [developer.paypal.com](https://developer.paypal.com) and sign in with your PayPal account. If this is your first time, you'll be prompted to accept the developer agreement.
</Step>

<Step title="Create an app">
1. Go to **My Apps & Credentials** in the dashboard
2. Click **Create App**
3. Enter an app name (e.g., "Emergent Payment Integration")
4. Select the account type — choose **Sandbox** for testing or **Live** for production
5. Click **Create App**

PayPal will generate a **Client ID** and **Secret** for your application.
</Step>

<Step title="Copy your credentials">
On the app details page, copy:
- **Client ID** — your public identifier
- **Secret** — your private API key (keep this secure)

You'll use these in the next section to configure Emergent.
</Step>

<Step title="Enable required features">
Scroll down to **Features** and ensure the following are enabled:
- **Accept Payments** — core checkout functionality
- **Webhooks** (optional but recommended) — receive real-time payment notifications

Click **Save** if you make any changes.
</Step>
</Steps>

## Configure PayPal in Emergent

<Steps>
<Step title="Add credentials to your environment">
In your Emergent chat, describe where you need PayPal configured. For example:

> "Add PayPal checkout to the pricing page. Use the Client ID and Secret from my environment variables."

Emergent will prompt you for the credentials if they're not already set.
</Step>

<Step title="Set environment variables">
Provide your PayPal credentials as environment variables:

```bash
PAYPAL_CLIENT_ID=your_client_id_here
PAYPAL_SECRET=your_secret_here
PAYPAL_MODE=sandbox  # or 'live' for production
```

<Warning>
Never commit your `PAYPAL_SECRET` to version control. Emergent stores environment variables securely and injects them at runtime.
</Warning>
</Step>

<Step title="Verify the integration">
Ask Emergent to implement a test checkout flow. For example:

> "Create a button that charges $10 via PayPal and shows a success message on completion."

Emergent will scaffold the PayPal SDK integration, handle the OAuth token exchange, and create the necessary API calls.
</Step>
</Steps>

## Testing your integration

<Tabs>
<Tab title="Sandbox testing">
PayPal provides test accounts pre-configured in your sandbox:

1. Go to **Sandbox → Accounts** in the Developer Dashboard
2. Use the **Personal** (buyer) account credentials to complete test purchases
3. Check the **Business** (seller) account to verify funds were received

All sandbox transactions use fake money and cards — no real charges occur.
</Tab>

<Tab title="Live testing">
Before going live:

1. Switch `PAYPAL_MODE` to `live` in your environment variables
2. Replace sandbox credentials with your live Client ID and Secret
3. Process a small real transaction (e.g., $0.50) to verify end-to-end flow
4. Check your PayPal Business account dashboard for the incoming payment

<Info>
PayPal charges a transaction fee (typically 2.9% + $0.30 per transaction in the US). Fees vary by region and transaction volume — see [PayPal's pricing page](https://www.paypal.com/pricing) for details.
</Info>
</Tab>
</Tabs>

## Common payment flows

<CardGroup cols={2}>
<Card title="One-time payments" icon="credit-card">
Standard checkout for products, services, or donations. User completes payment and returns to your app.
</Card>

<Card title="Subscriptions" icon="repeat">
Recurring billing for memberships or SaaS. Requires PayPal Billing Plan setup in your dashboard.
</Card>

<Card title="Invoicing" icon="file-text">
Send payment requests via email. Useful for B2B or custom quotes.
</Card>

<Card title="Refunds & disputes" icon="undo">
Process refunds programmatically or handle buyer disputes through the PayPal Resolution Center.
</Card>
</CardGroup>

Describe your desired flow to Emergent (e.g., *"Add a monthly subscription plan for $29/month with PayPal"*) and the platform will implement the appropriate PayPal API calls.

## Webhooks (optional)

Webhooks notify your app about payment events in real time — completed payments, refunds, disputes, subscription cancellations, etc.

<Steps>
<Step title="Enable webhooks in PayPal">
In the Developer Dashboard:
1. Go to your app's settings
2. Scroll to **Webhooks**
3. Click **Add Webhook**
4. Enter your webhook URL: `https://your-app.emergent.app/api/webhooks/paypal`
5. Select the events you want to receive (at minimum: `PAYMENT.CAPTURE.COMPLETED`)
</Step>

<Step title="Implement the webhook handler">
Tell Emergent to create the endpoint:

> "Add a webhook at /api/webhooks/paypal that verifies PayPal signatures and updates order status in the database."

Emergent will scaffold signature verification, event parsing, and database updates.
</Step>

<Step title="Test webhook delivery">
Use the **Webhook Simulator** in the PayPal dashboard to send test events to your endpoint and verify correct handling.
</Step>
</Steps>

<Tip>
Webhooks are essential for subscription apps — they let you know when a renewal succeeds or fails without polling the API.
</Tip>

## Security best practices

- **Never expose your Secret** — keep it in environment variables, not in code
- **Verify webhook signatures** — PayPal signs all webhook requests; reject unsigned calls
- **Use HTTPS in production** — PayPal requires secure endpoints for live webhooks
- **Validate amounts server-side** — never trust payment amounts sent from the client

Emergent's generated code includes signature verification and server-side validation by default.

## Troubleshooting

<AccordionGroup>
<Accordion title="Payment fails with 'INSTRUMENT_DECLINED'">
This is a PayPal error indicating the buyer's payment method was declined by their bank. Ask the buyer to:
- Verify their card details
- Contact their bank to authorize international transactions (if applicable)
- Try a different payment method

In sandbox mode, ensure you're using a valid test card from PayPal's test account list.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Webhooks not arriving">
Check that:
- Your webhook URL is publicly accessible (not `localhost`)
- The endpoint returns a `200 OK` status within 10 seconds
- Your app is running and not rate-limited by PayPal

View delivery attempts and retry failed webhooks in the PayPal dashboard under **Webhooks → Recent Deliveries**.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="'Client ID not found' error">
You're likely using sandbox credentials in live mode (or vice versa). Verify:
- `PAYPAL_MODE` matches your credential type (`sandbox` or `live`)
- You copied the correct Client ID for the selected mode

Each mode has separate credentials — sandbox keys won't work in production.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Refund fails with 'TRANSACTION_LIMIT_EXCEEDED'">
PayPal limits the number of refunds you can issue within a time window. If you hit this limit:
- Wait 24 hours and retry
- Contact PayPal Support to request a limit increase
- For high-volume refunds, use batch refund APIs
</Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

## Going live checklist

Before switching to production:

- [ ] Replace sandbox credentials with live Client ID and Secret
- [ ] Set `PAYPAL_MODE=live` in environment variables
- [ ] Update webhook URLs to your production domain
- [ ] Test a small real transaction end-to-end
- [ ] Review PayPal's [Go Live Checklist](https://developer.paypal.com/api/rest/production/)
- [ ] Ensure your business details are correct in your PayPal Business account

<Warning title="Data handling compliance">
If you store payment data or user information, ensure your app complies with PCI-DSS, GDPR, and other applicable regulations. PayPal handles sensitive card data, but you're responsible for protecting customer information in your database.
</Warning>

## Next steps

<CardGroup cols={2}>
<Card title="Database (MongoDB)" icon="database" href="/database-mongodb">
Store order history and customer data in your Emergent MongoDB instance
</Card>

<Card title="Custom domain" icon="globe" href="/custom-domain">
Connect a custom domain for production checkout pages
</Card>
</CardGroup>

For advanced scenarios — multi-currency pricing, marketplace splits, or custom branding — describe your requirements in chat and Emergent will guide you through the PayPal Advanced Checkout APIs.

build-generation-for-a-pre-existing-play.title: Build generation for a pre-existing Play Store app
build-generation-for-a-pre-existing-play.content:
## Overview

When you have an existing app already published on the Google Play Store or Apple App Store, Emergent can generate new builds that preserve your app's identity and signing credentials. This allows you to update your app through Emergent while maintaining continuity with your existing store listing.

To do this, you'll need to provide Emergent with the signing credentials from your original app. This page walks through extracting the required credential files for both Android and iOS.

<Note>
If you're creating a brand new app (not updating an existing store listing), Emergent will generate signing credentials automatically. This guide is only for apps already published to the stores.
</Note>

## Generate a .pem file from your signing key

For Android apps on the Play Store, you'll need to convert your existing signing key into a `.pem` file that Emergent can use.

<Steps>
<Step title="Locate your keystore file">
Find the `.jks` or `.keystore` file you used to sign your original app. This is typically stored securely on your development machine or in your team's credential vault.
</Step>

<Step title="Extract the certificate">
Use the `keytool` command (included with Java JDK) to export the certificate:

```bash
keytool -export -rfc -keystore your-keystore.jks -alias your-key-alias -file certificate.pem
```

You'll be prompted for your keystore password and key alias. If you don't remember the alias, you can list all aliases with:

```bash
keytool -list -keystore your-keystore.jks
```
</Step>

<Step title="Verify the PEM file">
Open `certificate.pem` in a text editor. It should contain text starting with `-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----` and ending with `-----END CERTIFICATE-----`.
</Step>

<Step title="Upload to Emergent">
In your Emergent workspace, navigate to your mobile app build settings and upload the `.pem` file in the Android signing section. You'll also need to provide your keystore password and key alias.
</Step>
</Steps>

<Warning title="Keep your keystore file secure">
Never commit your keystore file or passwords to version control. If you lose your keystore, you cannot update your existing Play Store app — you would need to publish as a completely new app.
</Warning>

## Generate a .p8 key from Apple Developer account

For iOS apps on the App Store, you need to generate an App Store Connect API key in `.p8` format.

<Steps>
<Step title="Log in to App Store Connect">
Navigate to [App Store Connect](https://appstoreconnect.apple.com) and sign in with your Apple Developer account credentials.
</Step>

<Step title="Access Users and Access">
Click your name in the top-right corner, then select **Users and Access** from the dropdown menu.
</Step>

<Step title="Navigate to Keys">
In the left sidebar, under the **Integrations** section, click **Keys**.
</Step>

<Step title="Generate a new key">
Click the **+** button or **Generate API Key**. Give your key a descriptive name (for example, "Emergent Build Key") and assign the **App Manager** role or higher.
</Step>

<Step title="Download the .p8 file">
After creating the key, click **Download API Key**. This downloads a `.p8` file.

<Callout type="warning" title="Download immediately">
Apple only allows you to download the `.p8` file once. If you lose it, you'll need to revoke the key and create a new one.
</Callout>

Record the **Issuer ID** (visible at the top of the Keys page) and the **Key ID** (shown next to your newly created key). You'll need both values along with the `.p8` file.
</Step>

<Step title="Upload to Emergent">
In your Emergent workspace, go to your iOS app build settings and upload the `.p8` file. Enter the Issuer ID and Key ID in the corresponding fields.
</Step>
</Steps>

<Info>
The `.p8` key provides API access to your App Store Connect account. Emergent uses it to manage provisioning profiles, certificates, and submit builds on your behalf — all without needing your Apple ID password.
</Info>

## Next steps

Once you've uploaded your signing credentials, Emergent can generate builds that update your existing store listings. For a walkthrough of the full build process, see [Your first build (walkthrough)](/your-first-build-walkthrough).

<CardGroup cols={2}>
<Card title="A tour of the workspace" icon="compass" href="/a-tour-of-the-workspace">
Learn how to navigate the Emergent interface and manage your projects
</Card>
<Card title="Custom domain" icon="globe" href="/custom-domain">
Point your own domain to your Emergent-built web app
</Card>
</CardGroup>
