paystack.title: Paystack
paystack.content:
## Overview

Paystack is a modern payment gateway that makes it easy to accept payments from customers across Africa. This guide shows you how to integrate Paystack into your Emergent app so you can collect payments, manage subscriptions, and handle transactions.

When you connect Paystack, your app can process card payments, bank transfers, mobile money, and other local payment methods supported across African markets.

## Before you begin

You'll need:

- A [Paystack account](https://paystack.com) (sign up is free)
- Your Paystack API keys (available in your Paystack dashboard under Settings → API Keys & Webhooks)
- An Emergent app that needs payment functionality

<Info>
Paystack provides both **test keys** (for development) and **live keys** (for production). Start with test keys while building and testing your integration.
</Info>

## Add Paystack to your app

<Steps>
<Step title="Tell Emergent you want to use Paystack">
In your app's chat, describe what you want to build:

> "Add Paystack payment integration. I want to accept card payments and generate payment links for customers."

Be specific about your use case — for example, one-time payments, subscriptions, or donation flows.
</Step>

<Step title="Provide your API keys">
Emergent will prompt you for your Paystack keys. You'll need:

- **Public key** — safe to expose in your frontend code
- **Secret key** — kept secure on the backend; never expose this in client-side code

Copy these from your Paystack dashboard (Settings → API Keys & Webhooks) and paste them when prompted.

<Warning>
Always use **test keys** during development. Switch to **live keys** only when you're ready to accept real payments in production.
</Warning>
</Step>

<Step title="Configure webhook endpoints">
Paystack sends notifications (webhooks) when payment events occur — successful charges, failed transactions, subscription renewals, etc.

Emergent will generate a webhook URL for your app. Copy this URL and add it in your Paystack dashboard:

1. Go to Settings → API Keys & Webhooks
2. Scroll to **Webhook URL**
3. Paste your Emergent webhook URL
4. Save changes

This ensures your app receives real-time updates about payment status.
</Step>

<Step title="Test the integration">
Use Paystack's test card numbers to verify everything works:

- **Successful payment**: `4084 0840 8408 4081` (any future expiry, any CVV)
- **Declined payment**: `5060 6666 6666 6666 64`

Process a test transaction in your app and confirm that payment status updates correctly.
</Step>

<Step title="Go live">
When you're ready for production:

1. Replace your test keys with live keys in your app's environment variables
2. Ensure your Paystack account is fully activated (business verification complete)
3. Confirm your webhook URL is configured with your live keys
4. Process a small real transaction to verify end-to-end flow
</Step>
</Steps>

## Common use cases

<Tabs>
<Tab title="One-time payments">
For selling products or services with a single charge:

- Initialize a transaction with an amount and customer email
- Redirect the customer to Paystack's secure checkout
- Handle the callback when payment succeeds or fails
- Confirm transaction status via webhook before fulfilling the order
</Tab>

<Tab title="Subscription billing">
For recurring revenue models:

- Create a **Plan** in your Paystack dashboard (defines amount and billing interval)
- Subscribe customers to the plan via your app
- Paystack automatically charges the customer on each billing cycle
- Handle `subscription.create`, `charge.success`, and `subscription.disable` webhooks
</Tab>

<Tab title="Payment links">
For no-code payment collection:

- Generate a Paystack payment link in your app
- Share the link via email, SMS, or messaging apps
- Customers pay without needing to visit your website
- Track payments in your Paystack dashboard or via webhooks
</Tab>

<Tab title="Split payments">
For marketplaces or platforms with multiple vendors:

- Set up **Subaccounts** for each vendor in Paystack
- Route a percentage of each transaction to the subaccount
- Paystack handles the splits automatically
- Each vendor can withdraw their balance independently
</Tab>
</Tabs>

## Supported payment methods

Paystack supports a wide range of payment options across African markets:

| Method | Availability | Notes |
|--------|--------------|-------|
| Debit/Credit Cards | All markets | Visa, Mastercard, Verve |
| Bank Transfer | Nigeria, Ghana, South Africa | Instant or pending confirmation |
| Mobile Money | Ghana, Kenya | MTN, Vodafone, Airtel, M-Pesa |
| USSD | Nigeria | Dial codes for all major banks |
| QR Code | Nigeria, Ghana | Scan-to-pay at physical locations |
| Bank Account | Nigeria | Direct debit for subscriptions |

<Tip>
Enable multiple payment methods to maximize conversion. Customers can choose their preferred option at checkout.
</Tip>

## Webhook events

Your app receives these common events from Paystack:

<AccordionGroup>
<Accordion title="charge.success">
Fired when a payment is successfully completed. Use this to fulfill orders, grant access, or trigger downstream workflows. Always verify the transaction amount and status before taking action.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="charge.failed">
Sent when a payment attempt fails (insufficient funds, incorrect PIN, etc.). You might want to notify the customer or offer alternative payment methods.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="transfer.success">
Triggered when you send money to a customer (refunds, payouts, etc.). Useful for confirming disbursements in marketplace or payout scenarios.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="subscription.create">
Fired when a customer is subscribed to a plan. Update your database to reflect active subscription status.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="subscription.disable">
Sent when a subscription is canceled (by the customer or due to failed payments). Revoke access or notify the customer as appropriate.
</Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

<Info>
Paystack webhooks include a signature header (`x-paystack-signature`) for verification. Emergent validates this automatically to ensure events are authentic.
</Info>

## Testing and troubleshooting

### Test mode vs. live mode

Always develop and test with **test keys**. Test mode has no financial impact — transactions are simulated and no real money moves. When you switch to **live keys**, every transaction is real.

### Common issues

<AccordionGroup>
<Accordion title="Webhook not receiving events">
- Confirm the webhook URL in your Paystack dashboard matches the one Emergent provided
- Check that your app is deployed and accessible (webhooks can't reach local development servers unless you use a tunnel)
- Verify the webhook signature validation is enabled
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Transactions showing as pending">
- Bank transfers and some mobile money payments require manual confirmation
- Check the Paystack dashboard for transaction status
- Set up webhook listeners for `charge.success` to know when payment clears
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Payment page not loading">
- Ensure your public key is correctly configured in the frontend
- Check browser console for JavaScript errors
- Verify the transaction amount is valid (Paystack requires amounts in kobo/pesewas — smallest currency unit)
</Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

### Testing tools

Paystack provides a **Test Mode Dashboard** where you can:

- View all test transactions
- Manually trigger webhook events
- Simulate different payment outcomes (success, decline, timeout)
- Inspect API requests and responses

Use these tools to verify your integration handles all scenarios correctly before going live.

## Security best practices

<CardGroup cols={2}>
<Card title="Protect your secret key" icon="key">
Never commit secret keys to version control or expose them in client-side code. Emergent stores them securely as environment variables.
</Card>

<Card title="Validate webhooks" icon="shield-check">
Always verify the `x-paystack-signature` header on incoming webhooks. This prevents malicious actors from spoofing payment events.
</Card>

<Card title="Confirm on the backend" icon="server">
After a customer completes checkout, verify the transaction status by querying Paystack's API from your backend — don't trust frontend callbacks alone.
</Card>

<Card title="Use HTTPS" icon="lock">
Ensure your webhook endpoint uses HTTPS. Paystack will not send events to insecure HTTP URLs in live mode.
</Card>
</CardGroup>

## Pricing and fees

Paystack charges a percentage of each successful transaction. Fees vary by country and payment method:

- **Nigeria**: 1.5% capped at ₦2,000
- **Ghana**: 1.95% (no cap)
- **South Africa**: 2.9% (no cap)

Additional fees may apply for international cards or specific payment methods. Check [Paystack's pricing page](https://paystack.com/pricing) for current rates.

<Note>
There are no setup fees, monthly charges, or hidden costs. You only pay when you successfully collect a payment.
</Note>

## Next steps

<CardGroup cols={2}>
<Card title="Custom domain" icon="globe" href="/custom-domain">
Set up a custom domain for a professional checkout experience
</Card>

<Card title="Database (MongoDB)" icon="database" href="/database-mongodb">
Store customer and transaction data for reporting and analytics
</Card>
</CardGroup>

## Resources

- [Paystack Documentation](https://paystack.com/docs)
- [Paystack API Reference](https://paystack.com/docs/api)
- [Test Cards and Accounts](https://paystack.com/docs/payments/test-payments)
- [Webhook Event Reference](https://paystack.com/docs/payments/webhooks)

web-mobile-conversion-canonical.title: Web <-> Mobile conversion (canonical)
web-mobile-conversion-canonical.content:
## What is platform conversion?

Emergent lets you **convert any app between web and mobile** at any time. When you convert, the platform rebuilds your app for the target platform — translating UI frameworks, layout patterns, navigation and platform-specific idioms — while preserving your app's logic, data and functionality.

Conversion is **non-destructive**: your original app remains intact until you confirm the converted version works as expected.

<Info>
Conversion works in both directions: web → mobile and mobile → web. The process is identical; the platform automatically detects your current deployment target and offers the opposite.
</Info>

---

## How conversion works

<Steps>
<Step title="Choose Convert from the deployment menu">
Open your app, click the **Deploy** dropdown in the top bar and select **Convert to [Mobile/Web]**.
</Step>

<Step title="The platform analyzes your app">
Emergent inspects your codebase, data schema, API routes, authentication flows and UI components to understand what needs to change.
</Step>

<Step title="Agent rebuilds for the target platform">
A dedicated conversion job runs — rewriting components, restructuring navigation, swapping frameworks (e.g. React web → React Native, or vice versa) and adjusting layout for the new form factor.
</Step>

<Step title="Review and test the converted app">
The converted app opens in preview mode. Test thoroughly — UI, navigation, data persistence, authentication and integrations — before deploying live.
</Step>

<Step title="Deploy when satisfied">
If everything works, deploy the converted app. If issues arise, iterate in chat ("the login button is misaligned on mobile") or revert to your original deployment.
</Step>
</Steps>

<Tip title="Conversion is a Job">
Like any build task, conversion runs as a [Job](/what-is-a-job) and consumes credits. You can watch progress, pause or cancel if needed.
</Tip>

---

## Will I lose data or functionality?

**Short answer:** No — with caveats for platform-specific features.

### What carries over seamlessly

- **Database schema and data**: tables, relations, indexes and all stored records remain intact.
- **Authentication & user accounts**: login methods (email, OAuth providers) and user sessions persist.
- **API routes & server logic**: backend endpoints, webhooks and integrations continue working unchanged.
- **Environment variables & secrets**: all config, API keys and feature flags transfer.
- **File uploads & storage**: user-uploaded assets remain accessible (paths may adjust for mobile).

### What adapts automatically

- **UI components**: buttons, forms, modals and lists rebuild using platform-native patterns (e.g. web `<button>` → React Native `<Pressable>`).
- **Navigation**: web routing (URL-based) converts to mobile navigation stacks/tabs; deep links are preserved where possible.
- **Responsive layout**: desktop multi-column layouts condense to mobile-friendly single-column or tabs.
- **Form validation & input types**: web HTML5 inputs map to appropriate mobile keyboard types and pickers.

<Note>
The agent preserves **business logic** and **user flows** — the *what* of your app — while rewriting *how* it renders and navigates on the new platform.
</Note>

### What may require adjustment

<Warning title="Platform-specific features need review">
Capabilities unique to one platform (browser APIs, mobile sensors, OS-level integrations) may not translate directly. Test these carefully.
</Warning>

| Feature | Web → Mobile | Mobile → Web |
|---------|--------------|--------------|
| **Camera/microphone** | Works on mobile; may need permission prompts added | Web uses `getUserMedia` API; works in modern browsers |
| **Push notifications** | Needs mobile push service (FCM/APNs) configured | Web uses service workers; requires HTTPS |
| **Geolocation** | Native mobile APIs are faster/more reliable | Web `navigator.geolocation` works but less precise |
| **File system access** | Mobile uses app-sandboxed storage | Web limited to downloads folder or File System API (Chromium) |
| **Print/PDF export** | Not a mobile pattern; may need redesign | Works natively in browsers |
| **Right-click menus** | Touch-and-hold patterns replace | Standard context menus supported |
| **Hover states** | Touch doesn't have hover; replaced with press/active states | Hover works normally |

<Info>
If your app relies heavily on a platform-specific feature, mention it explicitly in chat during conversion: *"Keep the QR scanner working on mobile"* or *"Preserve the print invoice button for web."*
</Info>

---

## Common conversion scenarios

<AccordionGroup>
<Accordion title="I built a dashboard on web. Can I convert it to mobile?">
Yes. Multi-column layouts will condense to scrollable single-column or tabbed views. Charts and tables adapt to smaller screens (the agent may introduce horizontal scroll for wide tables or summary cards for dense data).
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="My mobile app uses camera scanning. Will that work on web?">
The web version will use the browser's camera API (`getUserMedia`). It works on HTTPS sites in modern browsers but won't have the same native feel. Test thoroughly; you may want to hide the feature on web or offer an upload alternative.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="What happens to my analytics/tracking code?">
Third-party scripts (Google Analytics, Mixpanel) typically carry over. Web tags remain in `<head>`; mobile SDKs are added to the native shell. Verify events fire correctly after conversion.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Can I convert back if I don't like the result?">
Yes. Conversion doesn't delete your original deployment. If the converted app isn't right, continue working on your original or start a new conversion job with clearer instructions.
</Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

---

## Best practices for smooth conversion

- **Test edge cases**: empty states, long text, landscape orientation (mobile), narrow browser windows (web).
- **Check authentication flows**: login, signup, password reset and OAuth redirects must work on the new platform.
- **Verify file uploads**: ensure camera roll access (mobile) or drag-and-drop (web) works as expected.
- **Review navigation**: make sure every screen is reachable and back/close buttons behave correctly.
- **Test on real devices**: simulators are helpful, but real iOS/Android devices (or real browsers for web) catch platform quirks.

<Tip>
After conversion, open the app in preview and click through every major user flow. If something feels off, describe the issue in chat — the agent can fine-tune layout, navigation or component behavior.
</Tip>

---

## Related pages

<CardGroup cols={2}>
<Card title="Web ↔ Mobile conversion reference" icon="arrows-left-right" href="/web-mobile-conversion-ref">
Technical details: frameworks used, file structure changes, troubleshooting conversion issues.
</Card>
<Card title="How apps work here (mental model)" icon="brain" href="/how-apps-work-here-mental-model">
Understand Emergent's build system and how the agent structures your app.
</Card>
<Card title="What is a Job?" icon="list-checks" href="/what-is-a-job">
Learn how build tasks (including conversion) run and how to monitor progress.
</Card>
<Card title="Deploy & preview" icon="rocket" href="/deploy-and-preview">
Deploying your app live after conversion (or rolling back if needed).
</Card>
</CardGroup>

which-prompt-window-should-i-use.title: Which prompt window should I use?
which-prompt-window-should-i-use.content:
## Why this choice matters Emergent offers three prompt windows—**Starter**, **Pro**, and **Infinite**—each with different capabilities and resource limits. Picking the right one **before** you begin a build saves rework: the Starter window cannot access certain tools (databases, external APIs, custom domains) that Pro and Infinite unlock, and an app scaffolded in Starter may need significant refactoring if you later migrate to Pro. Choose deliberately at the outset. You can always upgrade mid-build, but doing so cleanly often means starting fresh or manually porting changes. --- ## Quick decision guide **Starter** — Fast iterations, no database, no external calls. Perfect for MVPs and learning the platform. **Pro** — Full-stack apps with MongoDB, third-party integrations, and custom domains. **Infinite** — Unlimited context, handles large refactors and multi-agent orchestration without token caps. Start **Starter** for quick exploration, then upgrade when you hit a limit (database, domain, or complexity). --- ## Detailed comparison | Feature | Starter | Pro | Infinite | |---------|---------|-----|----------| | **Use case** | Prototypes, learning, single-page apps | Production apps, databases, integrations | Large refactors, complex architectures | | **Context window** | Standard (~8k tokens) | Extended (~32k tokens) | Unlimited | | **Database (MongoDB)** | ❌ Not available | ✅ Full access | ✅ Full access | | **External API calls** | ❌ Not available | ✅ Allowed | ✅ Allowed | | **Custom domain** | ❌ Not available | ✅ Allowed | ✅ Allowed | | **Authentication** | Basic (demo mode) | Full OAuth, JWT | Full OAuth, JWT | | **Deployment** | Instant preview | Production-ready | Production-ready | | **Typical build time** | Minutes | Minutes to hours | Hours to days | | **Cost** | Free tier available | Pay-per-build | Premium pricing | All three windows share the same [chat-to-deployment flow](/the-chat-to-deployment-flow) and [workspace interface](/a-tour-of-the-workspace). The differences are purely resource and capability boundaries. --- ## Common pitfall: starting Starter when you'll need Pro A frequent stumbling block: you describe a simple UI in Starter, iterate to a working prototype, *then* realize you need user accounts or a database. At that point you have two options: Switch the same chat thread to Pro. The agents will scaffold database schemas and auth, but may need to rewrite routing, state management, and component structure to accommodate persistence. Copy your design notes and open a new Pro window. Describe the full feature set (including database and auth) from the start, so the agents architect correctly the first time. Option 2 (fresh start) is usually faster and cleaner for non-trivial apps. Migrating state-heavy UIs to a database-backed architecture mid-build generates significant diff churn. --- ## When to choose each window ### Starter
**Best for:** - Static landing pages - Client-side calculators or tools - Portfolio projects with no backend - Learning Emergent's workflow - Rapid throwaway experiments
**Limitations:** - No persistent data (refreshing the page loses state) - Cannot call external APIs or webhooks - No custom domains (deploys to `*.emergent.app`) - Limited context for very long builds
### Pro
**Best for:** - SaaS apps with user accounts - CRUD tools (task managers, CRMs, dashboards) - Integrations with Stripe, Twilio, SendGrid, etc. - Production deployments on your own domain - Typical business applications
**Includes:** - [MongoDB database](/database-mongodb) (shared cluster) - [Custom domain](/custom-domain) support - OAuth & JWT authentication - External API access (rate-limited per plan) - [Universal LLM Key](/the-universal-llm-key) for AI features
### Infinite
**Best for:** - Enterprise platforms with complex domain models - Multi-agent builds requiring deep context - Large-scale refactors (rewriting entire modules) - Apps with 50+ routes or microservices architecture - Long iterative sessions (days of refinement)
**Advantages:** - No token-window limits (agents see full conversation history) - Handles massive codebases without context loss - Premium multi-agent orchestration - All Pro features included - Priority support and SLA
Infinite is overkill for most projects. Reserve it for builds where you know you'll iterate extensively or where the architecture is genuinely complex (multi-tenant, microservices, heavy integrations). --- ## Switching windows mid-build If you start in Starter and later need Pro features: Download the workspace code (three-dot menu → **Export**) so you have a snapshot. Click **New Build** and select **Pro**. Paste your original prompt plus any refinements. Tell the agents which Pro features you need ("add MongoDB for user profiles," "integrate Stripe checkout," etc.). The agents will rebuild the app with database schemas, API routes, and auth. Compare against your Starter export and port over any custom logic manually. This workflow is smoother for small apps. If your Starter build has grown beyond a few components, starting fresh in Pro with a complete spec often yields a better architecture. --- ## FAQ Technically yes—open the code in a Starter window—but you'll lose database access, API calls, and custom domains. Any features depending on those will break. Downgrading is rarely useful except for stripping an app down to a static demo. Yes. Infinite pricing is premium tier. Check your account dashboard for current rates; it's designed for complex or long-running projects where the unlimited context justifies the cost. Start **Starter**. You'll know within a few prompts if you need a database or external APIs. Upgrading early (before you have dozens of components) is straightforward. No. The runtime environment enforces the window's capabilities. Starter builds cannot make outbound HTTP calls or connect to MongoDB, even if you manually add the code. The deployment sandbox will block those operations. --- ## Next steps Understand how prompts become deployed apps in any window. Learn how Pro and Infinite apps use persistent data. Definitions for prompt window, build, workspace, and more. Navigate the interface common to all three windows.
which-prompt-window-should-i-use.description: 1. Why the choice matters up front: each window has different capabilities & limitations; wrong choice = rework.

works-in-preview-but-breaks-in-productio.title: Works in preview but breaks in production
works-in-preview-but-breaks-in-productio.content:
## Why it happens

An app that runs flawlessly in preview can break the moment you deploy. This is almost always caused by **environmental differences** between the two runtimes — preview and production each have their own isolated environment, filesystem, and configuration.

<Info>
Preview and production are **completely separate containers**. A change in one does not automatically propagate to the other. See [Preview vs Deployed](/preview-vs-deployed-separate) for details.
</Info>

---

## Common culprits

### Environment variables not set in production

The most frequent cause. If your code reads `process.env.STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` and that variable exists in preview but not production, the app will fail.

**What to check:**

- Open the **Environment** panel in your workspace
- Confirm every variable your app needs is present in **both** Preview *and* Production columns
- Redeploy after adding missing variables

<Tip>
Agents often set variables in preview during development. You must explicitly copy or re-create them in production.
</Tip>

---

### Hardcoded `localhost` or preview URLs

Code that references `http://localhost:3000` or your preview URL (`*.preview.emergent.run`) will break in production because those addresses are unreachable from the live deployment.

**Examples:**

- API base URLs: `const API = "http://localhost:8000"`
- Webhook callbacks: `callbackUrl: "https://my-app.preview.emergent.run/hook"`
- OAuth redirect URIs hardcoded to preview

**Fix:**

Use environment variables for all URLs:

```javascript
const API_BASE = process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL || "http://localhost:3000";
```

Set `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL` differently in preview vs production.

---

### CORS configuration pointing to the wrong origin

If your backend explicitly allows only your preview domain:

```python
allowed_origins = ["https://my-app.preview.emergent.run"]
```

…production requests from `https://my-app.emergent.run` (or your custom domain) will be blocked.

**Fix:**

- Use an environment variable for allowed origins
- Or allow both domains
- Or use a wildcard pattern if security allows

---

### Files written at runtime disappear

Production containers use an **ephemeral filesystem**. Any file your app writes to disk (uploads, generated PDFs, cached images) will be lost on restart or scale-out.

**Symptoms:**

- User uploads work initially, then vanish
- Generated files return 404 after a few hours
- SQLite databases lose data

**Fix:**

Use [Emergent Object Store](/file-storage-emergent-object-store) for persistent file storage. Never rely on the local filesystem for data that must survive restarts.

<Warning title="Do not use local disk for persistence">
The container filesystem is wiped on every redeploy and can be cleared at any time during autoscaling.
</Warning>

---

### Missing system dependencies

Preview may have been running on a container that happened to have a system tool installed, but production does not.

**Common examples:**

| Tool         | Used for                           | Symptom in production                     |
|--------------|------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------|
| `ffmpeg`     | Video encoding, audio extraction   | "ffmpeg: command not found"               |
| Playwright   | Browser automation, screenshots    | Chromium binary missing                   |
| ImageMagick  | Image resizing, format conversion  | "convert: not found"                      |
| wkhtmltopdf  | HTML-to-PDF rendering              | PDF generation fails silently             |

**Fix:**

Declare dependencies in your project:

- Add `playwright install` to your build script
- Use a Docker base image that includes the tool
- Or ask the agents to install it via system packages

If the tool was present in preview by chance, you must explicitly require it for production.

---

### Webhooks still pointing to preview

External services (Stripe, Twilio, GitHub) may still have webhook URLs pointing to your preview instance.

**What happens:**

- Payment confirmations arrive in preview but not production
- SMS replies are processed in the wrong environment
- OAuth flows redirect to the old URL

**Fix:**

- Log into each third-party service
- Update webhook/callback URLs to your production domain
- Test the flow end-to-end in production

<Tip title="Use environment-specific webhook secrets">
Store separate webhook signing secrets for preview and production so you can safely test webhooks without triggering real side effects.
</Tip>

---

## Debugging checklist

<Steps>
<Step title="Compare environment variables">
Open the Environment panel and ensure every variable in preview also exists in production with the correct value.
</Step>

<Step title="Check logs">
View production logs in the workspace. Look for missing-variable errors, connection timeouts, or "command not found."
</Step>

<Step title="Search for hardcoded URLs">
Grep your codebase for `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `.preview.emergent.run` and replace with environment variables.
</Step>

<Step title="Verify CORS origins">
Ensure your backend allows requests from your production domain (or custom domain if configured).
</Step>

<Step title="Audit file writes">
If your app writes files, confirm they go to [Object Store](/file-storage-emergent-object-store), not `/tmp` or the project directory.
</Step>

<Step title="Confirm system dependencies">
If preview worked but production crashes on a missing binary, declare that dependency in your build configuration.
</Step>

<Step title="Update external webhooks">
Check every third-party integration and point webhooks to your live domain.
</Step>
</Steps>

---

## Still broken?

<CardGroup cols={2}>
<Card title="App slow or crashing" icon="gauge-high" href="/app-slow-crashing-or-cold-starting">
Performance and startup issues
</Card>
<Card title="Missing functionality" icon="wrench" href="/missing-functionality">
Feature worked in preview, now absent
</Card>
</CardGroup>

If none of the above applies, describe the exact error message in chat — agents can compare your preview and production configurations and identify the mismatch.
works-in-preview-but-breaks-in-productio.description: Why an app works in preview but breaks live: separate env vars, hardcoded localhost, CORS, ephemeral filesystem losing runtime files, missing system tools (ffmpeg/Playwright), webh

lemon-squeezy.title: Lemon Squeezy
lemon-squeezy.content:
## Overview

Lemon Squeezy is a merchant-of-record payment platform that handles billing, tax compliance, fraud prevention, and subscriptions for digital products and SaaS applications. When you integrate Lemon Squeezy with your Emergent app, you can accept payments, manage subscriptions, and handle customer billing without building payment infrastructure from scratch.

This guide walks you through connecting Lemon Squeezy to your Emergent project, configuring webhooks, and implementing checkout flows.

## Prerequisites

Before you begin, ensure you have:

- An active [Lemon Squeezy account](https://www.lemonsqueezy.com)
- At least one product or subscription plan created in your Lemon Squeezy dashboard
- Your Emergent app deployed (webhooks require a public URL)

<Note>
Lemon Squeezy provides test mode for development. You can create test products and process test transactions without handling real money during development.
</Note>

## Getting Your API Credentials

<Steps>
<Step title="Navigate to API settings">
Log in to your Lemon Squeezy dashboard and go to **Settings** → **API** from the main navigation.
</Step>

<Step title="Create an API key">
Click **Create API Key**, give it a descriptive name (e.g., "Emergent Production"), and copy the generated key immediately. Lemon Squeezy will only show the full key once.
</Step>

<Step title="Note your Store ID">
While in the dashboard, navigate to **Settings** → **Stores** and copy your Store ID. You'll need this to create checkout sessions and query products programmatically.
</Step>

<Step title="Add credentials to Emergent">
In your Emergent chat, tell the AI to add the API key and Store ID as environment variables:

```
Add these environment variables:
LEMON_SQUEEZY_API_KEY=your_api_key_here
LEMON_SQUEEZY_STORE_ID=your_store_id_here
```

The AI will securely store these values and make them available to your backend code.
</Step>
</Steps>

<Warning>
Never commit API keys directly in your code. Always use environment variables. Emergent automatically manages secrets and excludes them from version control.
</Warning>

## Implementing Checkout

The typical Lemon Squeezy integration follows this pattern: your app creates a checkout session server-side, then redirects the user to Lemon Squeezy's hosted checkout page.

### Creating a Checkout Endpoint

Ask the Emergent AI to create a checkout endpoint:

```
Create a /api/checkout endpoint that:
1. Takes a variantId (product variant) from the request
2. Creates a Lemon Squeezy checkout session
3. Returns the checkout URL to redirect the user

Use the LEMON_SQUEEZY_API_KEY and LEMON_SQUEEZY_STORE_ID environment variables.
```

The AI will generate server-side code that calls the Lemon Squeezy API to create checkout sessions. The response includes a `url` field where you redirect users to complete payment.

### Frontend Integration

For the client-side purchase flow:

```
Add a "Buy Now" button on the pricing page that:
1. Calls /api/checkout with the selected plan's variantId
2. Redirects the user to the returned checkout URL
```

<Tip>
Pass custom data (like user IDs or metadata) in the checkout session's `custom_data` field. This data will be included in webhook events, making it easy to associate purchases with users in your database.
</Tip>

## Setting Up Webhooks

Webhooks notify your app when payments succeed, subscriptions renew, or customers update their billing information.

<Steps>
<Step title="Create a webhook endpoint">
Instruct the AI to create a webhook handler:

```
Create a /api/webhooks/lemon-squeezy endpoint that:
1. Verifies the webhook signature
2. Handles order_created and subscription_updated events
3. Updates user records in the database when payments succeed
```

The AI will implement signature verification to ensure webhooks come from Lemon Squeezy.
</Step>

<Step title="Configure the webhook in Lemon Squeezy">
In your Lemon Squeezy dashboard:

1. Go to **Settings** → **Webhooks**
2. Click **Add Webhook**
3. Set the URL to `https://your-app.emergent.dev/api/webhooks/lemon-squeezy`
4. Copy the **Signing Secret** provided
</Step>

<Step title="Add the signing secret">
Tell the AI:

```
Add environment variable LEMON_SQUEEZY_WEBHOOK_SECRET with value: your_signing_secret_here
```
</Step>

<Step title="Select events">
In the Lemon Squeezy webhook settings, subscribe to the events your app needs. Common choices:

- `order_created` – one-time purchases complete
- `subscription_created` – new subscription starts
- `subscription_updated` – plan changes, renewals
- `subscription_payment_success` – recurring payment succeeds
- `subscription_cancelled` – user cancels subscription
</Step>
</Steps>

<Info>
Deploy your app before adding webhooks. Lemon Squeezy will attempt to verify the endpoint immediately, which requires a live URL. See [Custom domain](/custom-domain) for deploying with a production domain.
</Info>

## Handling Webhook Events

A typical webhook handler updates your database when payment events occur:

<CodeGroup>
```javascript Example webhook logic
// Pseudo-code for order_created event
if (event.type === 'order_created') {
  const customData = event.data.custom_data;
  const userId = customData.user_id;
  
  await updateUser(userId, {
    subscription: 'premium',
    subscriptionId: event.data.id,
    subscriptionStatus: 'active'
  });
}
```

```python Python example
# Pseudo-code for subscription_updated event
if event["type"] == "subscription_updated":
    subscription_id = event["data"]["id"]
    status = event["data"]["status"]
    
    db.users.update_one(
        {"subscriptionId": subscription_id},
        {"$set": {"subscriptionStatus": status}}
    )
```
</CodeGroup>

Instruct the AI with your specific data model:

```
When the order_created webhook fires, find the user by the user_id in custom_data and set their plan field to "pro" in MongoDB.
```

See [Database (MongoDB)](/database-mongodb) for details on database operations in Emergent.

## Testing Payments

Lemon Squeezy provides a test mode for safe development:

<Steps>
<Step title="Enable test mode">
In your Lemon Squeezy dashboard, toggle **Test Mode** on. All products, checkouts, and webhooks will use test mode until you toggle it off.
</Step>

<Step title="Use test card numbers">
Lemon Squeezy accepts standard test card numbers. For example:

- **4242 4242 4242 4242** – successful payment
- **4000 0000 0000 0002** – card declined

Any future expiry date and any CVV will work in test mode.
</Step>

<Step title="Verify webhook delivery">
After a test purchase, check the **Webhooks** section in Lemon Squeezy to see delivery logs. You can resend events if your endpoint wasn't ready.
</Step>
</Steps>

<Tip>
Use Emergent's built-in logs to debug webhook issues. Ask the AI: "Show me the last 10 requests to /api/webhooks/lemon-squeezy" to see incoming webhook payloads and your handler's responses.
</Tip>

## Common Integration Patterns

<Accordion title="Subscription status gating">
Store the user's subscription status in your database. In protected routes, check the status before rendering premium features:

```
Add middleware to /api/premium/* routes that checks if the current user's subscriptionStatus is "active". Return 403 if not.
```
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Customer portal links">
Generate customer portal URLs so users can manage their subscriptions (update payment methods, cancel, etc.):

```
Add a "Manage Subscription" button that calls /api/customer-portal and redirects to the Lemon Squeezy customer portal URL for the current user's subscription.
```
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Usage-based billing">
For metered billing, record usage in your database and report it to Lemon Squeezy:

```
When a user consumes a credit, decrement their credits field in MongoDB. At the end of each billing cycle, send the usage total to Lemon Squeezy via the API.
```

Consult the Lemon Squeezy API docs for the exact endpoint and payload format for usage reporting.
</Accordion>

## Going Live

<Steps>
<Step title="Switch to production mode">
In Lemon Squeezy, toggle **Test Mode** off. Ensure your products, pricing, and tax settings are configured for live transactions.
</Step>

<Step title="Update environment variables">
If your production API key differs from your test key, update `LEMON_SQUEEZY_API_KEY` in Emergent:

```
Update LEMON_SQUEEZY_API_KEY to the production key
```
</Step>

<Step title="Verify webhook endpoint">
Confirm your webhook URL points to your production domain and that the signing secret matches your production webhook configuration in Lemon Squeezy.
</Step>

<Step title="Test a live transaction">
Make a small real purchase to verify the end-to-end flow: checkout, payment, webhook delivery, and database update.
</Step>
</Steps>

<Warning title="Tax and compliance">
Lemon Squeezy acts as the merchant of record and handles VAT, sales tax, and invoicing. Ensure your product descriptions, pricing, and terms are accurate before going live, as Lemon Squeezy will enforce compliance based on the information you provide.
</Warning>

## Troubleshooting

<AccordionGroup>
<Accordion title="Webhook signature verification fails">
Double-check that `LEMON_SQUEEZY_WEBHOOK_SECRET` matches the signing secret shown in your Lemon Squeezy webhook settings. Re-copy it if uncertain—secrets are case-sensitive.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Checkout session creation returns 401">
Verify that `LEMON_SQUEEZY_API_KEY` is set correctly and that the key has not been revoked. Test mode keys differ from production keys; ensure you're using the right one for your current mode.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="User not updated after payment">
Check the webhook logs in Lemon Squeezy to confirm delivery. If the webhook was delivered but your database wasn't updated, add logging to your webhook handler to see the event payload and any errors.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Custom data not appearing in webhooks">
Ensure you're passing `custom_data` when creating the checkout session. The field must be a JSON object. Verify the data is present in the Lemon Squeezy order details before debugging your webhook handler.
</Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

## Additional Resources

- [Lemon Squeezy API Documentation](https://docs.lemonsqueezy.com/api)
- [Lemon Squeezy Webhooks Reference](https://docs.lemonsqueezy.com/api/webhooks)
- [Database (MongoDB)](/database-mongodb) – storing subscription data in Emergent
- [Custom domain](/custom-domain) – deploying your app with a production URL for webhooks

<Success>
You've successfully integrated Lemon Squeezy with your Emergent app. Users can now purchase products, subscribe to plans, and manage billing—all handled by Lemon Squeezy's merchant-of-record infrastructure.
</Success>

google-auth.title: Google auth
google-auth.content:
## Overview

Google authentication enables your Emergent app to let users sign in with their Google accounts. This integration uses OAuth 2.0 and requires credentials from the Google Cloud Console.

<Info>
Google auth is handled through Emergent's managed authentication system. Once configured, your app can request user profile data, email addresses, and optional scopes like Google Calendar or Drive access.
</Info>

## Prerequisites

Before you begin, ensure you have:

- A Google account with access to [Google Cloud Console](https://console.cloud.google.com)
- An Emergent app where you want to enable Google sign-in
- Appropriate billing enabled in Google Cloud (required for OAuth consent screen configuration)

## Setting up Google OAuth credentials

<Steps>
<Step title="Create a Google Cloud project">
Navigate to the [Google Cloud Console](https://console.cloud.google.com) and create a new project or select an existing one. Give it a descriptive name that matches your Emergent app.
</Step>

<Step title="Enable the Google+ API">
In your Google Cloud project, go to **APIs & Services > Library**. Search for "Google+ API" and click **Enable**. This API is required for basic profile information access.
</Step>

<Step title="Configure the OAuth consent screen">
Go to **APIs & Services > OAuth consent screen**:

- Choose **External** for user type (unless you have a Google Workspace organization)
- Fill in the required fields:
  - App name
  - User support email
  - Developer contact email
- Add your app's logo (optional but recommended)
- Click **Save and Continue**

For scopes, add the basic Google profile scopes:
- `userinfo.email`
- `userinfo.profile`

<Tip>
If your app needs additional Google services (Calendar, Drive, etc.), add those scopes here. You'll need to submit your app for verification if requesting sensitive scopes.
</Tip>
</Step>

<Step title="Create OAuth 2.0 credentials">
Navigate to **APIs & Services > Credentials** and click **Create Credentials > OAuth 2.0 Client ID**.

Select **Web application** as the application type, then configure:

- **Name**: A descriptive identifier (e.g., "Emergent Production")
- **Authorized JavaScript origins**: Add your Emergent app's URL:
  ```
  https://your-app-name.emergent.build
  ```
- **Authorized redirect URIs**: Add the callback URL:
  ```
  https://your-app-name.emergent.build/api/auth/callback/google
  ```

<Warning>
The redirect URI must match exactly. Include both your production domain and any custom domains you've configured.
</Warning>

Click **Create** and save the **Client ID** and **Client Secret** that appear.
</Step>

<Step title="Add credentials to Emergent">
In the Emergent chat interface, tell the agent to configure Google authentication:

```
Add Google authentication using:
Client ID: YOUR_CLIENT_ID
Client Secret: YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET
```

The agent will securely store these credentials and configure your app's authentication routes.

<Note>
Credentials are encrypted at rest. You can update them anytime by providing new values through chat.
</Note>
</Step>

<Step title="Test the integration">
Ask the agent to add a sign-in button to your app, then preview the app and click **Sign in with Google**. You should be redirected to Google's consent screen, then back to your app upon successful authentication.
</Step>
</Steps>

## Accessing user data

Once a user authenticates, your app can access their Google profile information. The typical data available includes:

- Email address
- Full name
- Profile picture URL
- Google user ID

<CodeGroup>
```typescript Example: Accessing user session
// In your app code
const session = await getSession();
if (session?.user) {
  const { email, name, image } = session.user;
  console.log(`Signed in as ${name} (${email})`);
}
```

```python Example: Backend route
# Python backend accessing authenticated user
from emergent import get_current_user

@app.route('/profile')
def profile():
    user = get_current_user()
    return {
        'email': user.email,
        'name': user.name,
        'picture': user.picture
    }
```
</CodeGroup>

## Additional scopes

If your app needs access to Google services beyond basic profile data, request additional OAuth scopes.

<Tabs>
<Tab title="Common scopes">
| Scope | Access |
|-------|--------|
| `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/calendar.readonly` | Read calendar events |
| `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive.file` | Access files created by the app |
| `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/gmail.send` | Send email on user's behalf |
| `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/userinfo.email` | Email address (included by default) |
| `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/userinfo.profile` | Basic profile info (included by default) |
</Tab>

<Tab title="Requesting scopes">
Tell the agent which scopes your app needs:

```
Update Google auth to request calendar read access and Gmail send permissions
```

The agent will modify the OAuth configuration and prompt users to grant additional permissions on next sign-in.

<Warning>
Sensitive or restricted scopes require Google's app verification process, which can take several weeks. Plan accordingly if you need scopes like full Gmail access or Drive file modification.
</Warning>
</Tab>
</Tabs>

## Multiple environments

When working with staging or development environments, add their redirect URIs to your Google Cloud OAuth client:

<Steps>
<Step title="Add development URLs">
In Google Cloud Console, edit your OAuth 2.0 client and add:

- `https://your-app-name-staging.emergent.build/api/auth/callback/google`
- `http://localhost:3000/api/auth/callback/google` (for local testing)
</Step>

<Step title="Use the same credentials">
You can reuse the same Client ID and Secret across environments, or create separate OAuth clients for better isolation and monitoring.
</Step>
</Steps>

## Troubleshooting

<AccordionGroup>
<Accordion title="Error: redirect_uri_mismatch">
The callback URL in your Google Cloud Console doesn't match the one your app is using. Double-check that:

- The protocol is `https://` (not `http://`) for production
- The domain matches exactly, including subdomains
- The path is `/api/auth/callback/google`
- There are no trailing slashes or typos
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Users see 'This app isn't verified'">
This warning appears when requesting scopes beyond basic profile. Options:

1. Add test users in Google Cloud Console (up to 100) who won't see the warning
2. Submit your app for verification if you need public access
3. Users can click "Advanced > Go to [app name]" to proceed anyway

For internal apps, adding specific users as testers is usually sufficient.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Authentication works but user data is missing">
Ensure your app is requesting the correct scopes. The default scopes include email and basic profile. If you need additional data, explicitly request those scopes and have users re-authenticate to grant the new permissions.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Can I use Google auth with a custom domain?">
Yes. When you configure a custom domain for your Emergent app, add the custom domain's callback URL to your Google OAuth client's authorized redirect URIs:

```
https://yourdomain.com/api/auth/callback/google
```

See the [custom domain](/custom-domain) guide for more details.
</Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

## Security considerations

<Callout type="warning" title="Keep credentials secure">
Never commit your Client Secret to version control or expose it in client-side code. Emergent stores these securely and only uses them server-side during the OAuth flow.
</Callout>

Best practices:

- **Rotate credentials** periodically, especially if you suspect exposure
- **Limit scopes** to only what your app genuinely needs
- **Monitor usage** in Google Cloud Console to detect unusual activity
- **Use different OAuth clients** for production and development environments when handling sensitive data

## Next steps

<CardGroup cols={2}>
<Card title="Database (MongoDB)" icon="database" href="/database-mongodb">
Store authenticated user data and preferences
</Card>

<Card title="Custom domain" icon="globe" href="/custom-domain">
Configure a custom domain for your app
</Card>
</CardGroup>

what-is-wingman.title: What is Wingman
what-is-wingman.content:
## Overview

**Wingman** is Emergent's standalone personal AI assistant with persistent memory. It is a separate product from Emergent's app-building platform and is designed to help you with everyday tasks, questions, and conversations while remembering context across sessions.

Wingman is available on multiple platforms:

- **Web** – [getwingman.com](https://getwingman.com)
- **Android** – Google Play Store
- **iOS** – Apple App Store

<Note>
Wingman is **not** the AI that builds your apps inside Emergent. It is a personal assistant you can use for general productivity, brainstorming, research, and more.
</Note>

## Key features

- **Persistent memory** – Wingman remembers your preferences, past conversations, and context over time, making interactions more personalized and efficient.
- **Multi-platform sync** – Start a conversation on your phone and continue it on the web, with memory carried across devices.
- **General-purpose assistant** – Ask questions, get summaries, draft content, or receive help with a wide range of everyday tasks.

## How it differs from Emergent's app builder

| Feature | Emergent App Builder | Wingman |
|---------|---------------------|---------|
| **Purpose** | Build, test and deploy apps via chat | Personal AI assistant for general tasks |
| **Memory** | Project-specific workspace context | Cross-conversation persistent memory |
| **Access** | Emergent platform workspace | Standalone web app & mobile apps |
| **Output** | Deployed web/mobile applications | Conversational assistance & answers |

## Getting started

<Steps>
<Step title="Choose your platform">
Visit [getwingman.com](https://getwingman.com), or download the app from the Play Store (Android) or App Store (iOS).
</Step>

<Step title="Sign in">
Create an account or sign in with your existing credentials. Your memory and conversation history will sync across all platforms where you're logged in.
</Step>

<Step title="Start chatting">
Ask Wingman anything—questions, tasks, ideas—and it will remember your preferences and context for future conversations.
</Step>
</Steps>

<Tip>
Wingman's persistent memory means you don't need to re-explain your preferences or background every time you chat. The more you use it, the more tailored your experience becomes.
</Tip>

## Privacy & memory

Wingman's memory is designed to enhance your experience by retaining context. You remain in control:

- Memory is tied to your account and syncs across your devices.
- You can manage or clear stored memory at any time through the app settings.
- Conversations and memory are not shared with other users or used to train Emergent's app-building models.

<Info>
For questions about data handling and privacy, refer to Wingman's privacy policy available in-app and on the website.
</Info>
what-is-wingman.description: Emergent's standalone personal AI assistant with persistent memory - separate from the app builder; available on web (getwingman.com), the Play Store and the App Store.

airtable.title: Airtable
airtable.content:
## Overview

Airtable is a cloud collaboration platform that combines the simplicity of a spreadsheet with the power of a database. Connect your Emergent app to Airtable to read, write, and sync data across bases, tables, and views.

<Note>
You'll need an Airtable account and a personal access token to complete this integration. Free Airtable accounts support basic API access.
</Note>

## When to use Airtable

Airtable works well for:

- **Content management** — Store blog posts, FAQs, or marketing copy that non-technical teammates can edit
- **Product catalogs** — Sync inventory, pricing, or feature flags from a structured base
- **User-generated data** — Collect form submissions, feature requests, or survey responses
- **Collaboration** — Share data with stakeholders who prefer a visual spreadsheet interface over raw JSON

If you need high-throughput transactional storage or complex relational queries, consider using the [MongoDB integration](/database-mongodb) instead.

## Before you begin

<Steps>
<Step title="Create or identify an Airtable base">
Log in to [Airtable](https://airtable.com) and create a new base (or locate an existing one). Note the base ID — it appears in the URL when you open the base:

```
https://airtable.com/appXXXXXXXXXXXXXX/...
                      ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
                         base ID
```
</Step>

<Step title="Generate a personal access token">
1. Go to [https://airtable.com/create/tokens](https://airtable.com/create/tokens)
2. Click **Create new token**
3. Give it a descriptive name (e.g., "Emergent integration")
4. Under **Scopes**, select:
   - `data.records:read` (to read records)
   - `data.records:write` (to create/update records)
   - `schema.bases:read` (to list tables and fields)
5. Under **Access**, choose the specific base(s) this token can access
6. Click **Create token** and copy the token immediately — you won't see it again
</Step>
</Steps>

<Warning title="Keep your token secure">
Treat your Airtable personal access token like a password. Anyone with this token can read or modify data in the bases you granted access to.
</Warning>

## Connect Airtable to Emergent

<Steps>
<Step title="Open the integrations panel">
In the Emergent workspace, click **Integrations** in the left sidebar (or press `I`).
</Step>

<Step title="Add Airtable">
Scroll to **Media & productivity** and click **Airtable**. Click **Connect**.
</Step>

<Step title="Paste your token">
In the **Personal Access Token** field, paste the token you generated. Click **Save**.
</Step>

<Step title="Verify the connection">
Emergent will test the token by fetching your account metadata. If successful, you'll see a green checkmark and "Connected" status.
</Step>
</Steps>

## Using Airtable in your app

Once connected, you can describe Airtable operations in chat and the AI agents will generate the integration code.

### Example prompts

<CardGroup cols={2}>
<Card title="Read records" icon="table">
"Fetch all records from the 'Products' table in my Airtable base and display them as cards."
</Card>
<Card title="Create a record" icon="plus">
"When the user submits this form, create a new record in the 'Leads' table with their name and email."
</Card>
<Card title="Update a record" icon="pencil">
"Add a button that marks a task as complete by updating the 'Status' field in Airtable."
</Card>
<Card title="Filter & sort" icon="filter">
"Show only records where 'Published' is true, sorted by 'Date' descending."
</Card>
</CardGroup>

### Common patterns

<Tabs>
<Tab title="Read & display">
Fetch records from a table and render them in your UI:

```javascript
// The AI agent will generate code similar to:
const records = await airtable.base('appXXXXXX').table('Products').select().all();
const products = records.map(r => ({ id: r.id, ...r.fields }));
```

Describe the desired UI (grid, list, table) and the agent will map the fields to components.
</Tab>

<Tab title="Create records">
Capture user input and write it to Airtable:

```javascript
await airtable.base('appXXXXXX').table('Leads').create({
  Name: formData.name,
  Email: formData.email,
  Source: 'Website form'
});
```

The agent infers field names from your Airtable schema when you describe the operation.
</Tab>

<Tab title="Update records">
Modify existing records by ID:

```javascript
await airtable.base('appXXXXXX').table('Tasks').update(recordId, {
  Status: 'Complete',
  CompletedAt: new Date().toISOString()
});
```

Describe the trigger (button click, form submit) and the fields to change.
</Tab>
</Tabs>

## Field types & mapping

Airtable supports many field types. The AI agent automatically maps them to JavaScript values:

| Airtable field type | JavaScript type | Notes |
|---------------------|----------------|-------|
| Single line text    | `string`       | Plain text |
| Long text           | `string`       | Multi-line, markdown supported |
| Number              | `number`       | Integer or decimal |
| Checkbox            | `boolean`      | `true` / `false` |
| Single select       | `string`       | One option from a predefined list |
| Multiple select     | `string[]`     | Array of selected options |
| Date                | `string`       | ISO 8601 format (`YYYY-MM-DD`) |
| Attachment          | `object[]`     | Array of `{ url, filename, ... }` |
| Link to another record | `string[]`  | Array of linked record IDs |

<Info>
When you describe a field in chat (e.g., "the product's price"), the agent inspects your Airtable schema and uses the correct field name and type.
</Info>

## Best practices

<AccordionGroup>
<Accordion title="Use views to pre-filter data">
Create an Airtable view with filters and sorting, then fetch from that view by name. This reduces API overhead and keeps complex logic in Airtable's UI.

```javascript
.table('Products').select({ view: 'Published items' })
```
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Cache frequently read data">
If a table changes infrequently (e.g., a settings table), cache the results in your app state and refresh periodically rather than fetching on every page load.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Handle rate limits gracefully">
Airtable's API is rate-limited (5 requests per second per base). For high-traffic apps, batch operations or use a background sync pattern. Describe the requirement in chat and the agent will implement retry logic.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Validate before writing">
Always validate user input before creating or updating records. The agent will add validation when you describe constraints (e.g., "email must be valid," "price must be positive").
</Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

## Troubleshooting

<AccordionGroup>
<Accordion title="'Invalid token' or 403 errors">
**Cause:** The personal access token is missing, expired, or lacks the required scopes.

**Solution:**
1. Regenerate the token at [https://airtable.com/create/tokens](https://airtable.com/create/tokens)
2. Ensure you selected `data.records:read`, `data.records:write`, and `schema.bases:read`
3. Confirm the token has access to the specific base
4. Re-enter the token in Emergent's integrations panel
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="'Table not found' errors">
**Cause:** The table name in your code doesn't match the table name in Airtable (names are case-sensitive).

**Solution:** Double-check the table name in Airtable. In chat, say "use the exact table name 'Products'" to ensure the agent uses the correct casing.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Records missing expected fields">
**Cause:** Empty fields are omitted from the API response by default.

**Solution:** The agent handles this automatically by using optional chaining (`record.fields.FieldName ?? defaultValue`). Describe default values in chat if needed.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Attachment URLs expire">
**Cause:** Airtable attachment URLs are temporary and expire after a few hours.

**Solution:** Download and re-host attachments in your app's storage, or fetch fresh URLs each time. Describe the desired behavior and the agent will implement it.
</Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

## Limits & pricing

- **Free plan:** 1,200 records per base, 2 GB attachment storage per base, 5 requests/second API rate limit
- **Paid plans:** Higher record limits, longer revision history, and advanced features

Check [Airtable's pricing page](https://airtable.com/pricing) for current details. Emergent does not charge extra for Airtable integrations.

## Next steps

<CardGroup cols={2}>
<Card title="AI media generation" icon="image" href="/ai-media-generation-image-video-audio">
Generate images, videos, or audio from text prompts
</Card>
<Card title="Database (MongoDB)" icon="database" href="/database-mongodb">
Use MongoDB for transactional or high-volume data storage
</Card>
<Card title="Custom domain" icon="globe" href="/custom-domain">
Deploy your app on your own domain
</Card>
<Card title="Glossary" icon="book" href="/glossary-of-emergent-terms">
Learn platform-specific terminology
</Card>
</CardGroup>

deployment-types.title: Deployment types
deployment-types.content:
## Overview

Emergent supports three deployment types, each suited to different stages of development and collaboration. The platform automatically selects the appropriate type based on your workflow, but understanding when each applies helps you plan testing, feedback and releases.

## The three deployment types

<CardGroup cols={3}>
<Card title="Development" icon="flask">
Fast, ephemeral deploys triggered by chat iterations during active building.
</Card>
<Card title="Preview" icon="eye">
Stable, shareable deploys created when you publish a checkpoint or share a build with collaborators.
</Card>
<Card title="Production" icon="rocket">
The live, publicly accessible version of your app, promoted from a preview deployment.
</Card>
</CardGroup>

## Development deployments

Development deployments are created automatically as you iterate in the [chat-to-deployment flow](/the-chat-to-deployment-flow). Every time the AI agents finish a build cycle, they deploy a new version to a transient development URL.

**Characteristics:**

- **Ephemeral** — each new iteration overwrites the previous development deploy
- **Fast** — optimized for quick turnaround during iteration
- **Private** — accessible only to you via a unique, unguessable URL
- **Not indexed** — search engines cannot discover development deploys

**When to use:**

- Active feature development and experimentation
- Rapid testing of UI changes or new functionality
- Debugging issues discovered in chat

<Note>
Development deployments do not persist. If you want to preserve a working build for later reference or share it with others, create a preview deployment instead.
</Note>

## Preview deployments

Preview deployments are stable, immutable snapshots of your app. They are created when you:

- Publish a checkpoint from the workspace
- Share a build with team members or stakeholders
- Use the **Create Preview** action in [the workspace](/a-tour-of-the-workspace)

**Characteristics:**

- **Immutable** — the code and assets never change once deployed
- **Stable URL** — each preview gets a unique, permanent URL (e.g., `your-app-preview-abc123.emergent.app`)
- **Shareable** — perfect for gathering feedback or QA testing
- **Multiple previews** — you can maintain several previews in parallel

**When to use:**

- Collecting feedback from stakeholders before going live
- Running QA or user-acceptance testing on a specific build
- Comparing multiple feature branches side-by-side
- Archiving a known-good state before risky changes

<Tip>
Preview deployments are the recommended way to share your app with collaborators. They remain accessible indefinitely (subject to your [deployment plan](/deployment-plan-levels)) and do not interfere with your production site.
</Tip>

## Production deployments

Production is the canonical, live version of your app — the one your end users visit. You promote a preview deployment to production when you are ready to release publicly.

**Characteristics:**

- **Single canonical URL** — your app's primary domain (e.g., `your-app.emergent.app` or a [custom domain](/custom-domain))
- **Promoted from preview** — production is always based on a tested, immutable preview
- **Public and indexed** — production deployments are discoverable by search engines (unless you configure otherwise)
- **Rollback-friendly** — you can re-promote a previous preview to production if an issue arises

**When to use:**

- Releasing a new version of your app to end users
- Updating the live site after successful QA
- Deploying a hotfix by promoting a known-good preview

<Steps>
<Step title="Promote a preview to production">
In the workspace, select the preview deployment you want to release and click **Promote to Production**.
</Step>
<Step title="Confirm the deployment">
The platform swaps the production environment to point to the selected preview build. Traffic begins flowing to the new version immediately.
</Step>
<Step title="Monitor and rollback if needed">
If issues arise, promote a different preview (or the previous production build) to roll back.
</Step>
</Steps>

## Comparison table

| Aspect | Development | Preview | Production |
|--------|-------------|---------|------------|
| **Lifecycle** | Ephemeral (replaced on next build) | Immutable, persists indefinitely | Immutable, promoted from preview |
| **URL** | Transient development URL | Unique, stable preview URL | Primary app domain |
| **Visibility** | Private (unguessable link) | Private (shareable link) | Public (indexed by default) |
| **Typical use** | Active iteration and debugging | QA, feedback, demos | Live release to end users |
| **Rollback** | Not applicable | Not applicable | Promote a different preview |

## Environment variables and secrets

All three deployment types share the same environment configuration (API keys, database credentials, etc.) defined in your workspace settings. This ensures consistency across development, preview and production without duplicating secrets.

If you need environment-specific configuration (e.g., separate Stripe keys for test vs. live), use the platform's [environment variable scoping](/database-mongodb#environment-variables) feature (available on higher deployment plans).

<Info>
The [Universal LLM Key](/the-universal-llm-key) is available in all deployment types, so you can test AI features in development and preview without providing your own API keys.
</Info>

## Deployment plan considerations

The number of concurrent preview deployments, production uptime guarantees and rollback history depend on your [deployment plan level](/deployment-plan-levels). Higher tiers unlock additional preview slots, custom domains and enhanced support.

If you encounter issues during any deployment type, consult the [deployment issues](/deployment-issues) and [deployment pipeline failures](/deployment-pipeline-failures) troubleshooting guides.

## Related pages

<CardGroup cols={2}>
<Card title="The chat-to-deployment flow" icon="comments" href="/the-chat-to-deployment-flow">
See how development deployments fit into the iterative build process.
</Card>
<Card title="Deployment plan levels" icon="layer-group" href="/deployment-plan-levels">
Compare plan features, preview limits and production SLAs.
</Card>
<Card title="Custom domain" icon="globe" href="/custom-domain">
Configure a custom domain for your production deployment.
</Card>
<Card title="Deployment issues" icon="triangle-exclamation" href="/deployment-issues">
Troubleshoot common deployment errors and failures.
</Card>
</CardGroup>
