monetisation-in-app-purchases-subscripti.title: Monetisation: in-app purchases & subscriptions
monetisation-in-app-purchases-subscripti.content:
## Overview

Emergent supports **native in-app purchases** (IAP) and **subscriptions** for both iOS and Android, letting you monetise mobile apps with minimal setup. Revenue flows through Apple App Store and Google Play Store, with platform fees deducted automatically.

For cross-platform subscription management and entitlement sync, Emergent integrates **RevenueCat**. For direct payment links in India, you can use **Razorpay** web checkout flows.

---

## Platform fees & revenue share

<Note>
Apple and Google collect their fees directly from customer payments before remitting revenue to your developer account.
</Note>

| Store | Standard rate | Small Business rate | Eligibility |
|-------|---------------|---------------------|-------------|
| **Apple App Store** | 30% | 15% | Developers earning <$1M/year across all apps |
| **Google Play** | 30% | 15% | First $1M per year per developer account |

Subscriptions on both platforms drop to **15%** after the customer's first year.

---

## Apple In-App Purchase (IAP)

### How it works

1. Define consumable, non-consumable or auto-renewable subscription products in **App Store Connect**.
2. Emergent's iOS build includes `StoreKit` integration; your agent can wire up product IDs and purchase flows.
3. Receipts are validated server-side to unlock entitlements.

<Steps>
<Step title="Create IAP products in App Store Connect">
Log into [App Store Connect](https://appstoreconnect.apple.com/) → **My Apps** → your app → **In-App Purchases** → **+**. Configure product ID, pricing and localisations.
</Step>

<Step title="Add product IDs to your Emergent project">
Tell your agent which product IDs to implement (e.g. `premium_monthly`, `coins_100`). The agent will generate the StoreKit purchase code and UI.
</Step>

<Step title="Test with sandbox accounts">
Create sandbox test users in App Store Connect → **Users and Access** → **Sandbox Testers**. Sign in with that account on your test device to trial purchases without real charges.
</Step>

<Step title="Validate receipts server-side">
Your Emergent backend verifies receipts with Apple's validation API and grants entitlements in your [database](/database-mongodb).
</Step>
</Steps>

<Warning title="Sandbox vs production receipts">
Apple issues different receipt signatures for sandbox and production. Your validation logic must target the correct endpoint (`buy.itunes.apple.com` for production, `sandbox.itunes.apple.com` for testing).
</Warning>

---

## Google Play Billing

### How it works

Google Play Billing works similarly: define products in the Play Console, integrate the Billing Library in your Android app, and validate purchases server-side via the Play Developer API.

<Steps>
<Step title="Set up products in Google Play Console">
**Monetize** → **Products** → **Create product**. Choose one-time, consumable or subscription, assign a SKU and set pricing.
</Step>

<Step title="Integrate Play Billing Library">
Emergent's Android builds include the `com.android.billingclient` dependency. Describe the purchase flow to your agent (e.g. "Show a paywall for `premium_yearly`").
</Step>

<Step title="Test with license testers">
Add test Google accounts under **Setup** → **License Testing** in the Play Console. These accounts can make real purchase flows that don't charge a card.
</Step>

<Step title="Verify purchase tokens">
After a successful purchase, send the token to your backend. Call the [Play Developer API](https://developers.google.com/android-publisher) to confirm validity and grant access.
</Step>
</Steps>

<Tip>
Enable **real-time developer notifications** (RTDN) in the Play Console to receive webhook events when subscriptions renew, cancel or expire.
</Tip>

---

## Cross-platform entitlements with RevenueCat

**RevenueCat** is a third-party service that unifies IAP logic across iOS, Android and web. It handles receipt validation, webhook delivery, and customer entitlement state—so you query one API instead of maintaining separate Apple and Google integrations.

### Why use RevenueCat?

<CardGroup cols={2}>
<Card title="Single source of truth" icon="database">
Check a user's subscription status with one REST call, regardless of which store they purchased from.
</Card>

<Card title="Webhooks for lifecycle events" icon="bell">
Receive real-time notifications on purchase, renewal, cancellation, refund or billing issue.
</Card>

<Card title="Paywall experiments" icon="flask">
A/B test pricing and messaging without app updates (requires RevenueCat Paywalls SDK).
</Card>

<Card title="Analytics & churn metrics" icon="chart-line">
Built-in dashboard for MRR, LTV, churn cohorts and trial conversion.
</Card>
</CardGroup>

### Integration steps

<Steps>
<Step title="Create a RevenueCat account">
Sign up at [revenuecat.com](https://www.revenuecat.com/) and create a new project.
</Step>

<Step title="Add platform credentials">
Under **Project Settings**, upload your Apple Shared Secret (from App Store Connect) and Google Service Account JSON (from Play Console → API access).
</Step>

<Step title="Define entitlements">
In the RevenueCat dashboard, create entitlements like `premium` or `pro` and map your App Store / Play Store product IDs to them.
</Step>

<Step title="Install the RevenueCat SDK">
Tell your Emergent agent to integrate the RevenueCat SDK (iOS: `RevenueCat`, Android: `purchases`). The agent will initialise the SDK with your public API key and wire up purchase methods.
</Step>

<Step title="Check entitlements in your app">
Call `Purchases.shared.getCustomerInfo()` (iOS) or `Purchases.sharedInstance.customerInfo` (Android) to see which entitlements the user has. Your backend can also query the [REST API](https://www.revenuecat.com/docs/api-v1) if you prefer server-side checks.
</Step>
</Steps>

<Info>
RevenueCat's free tier supports up to **$10k monthly tracked revenue**. Beyond that, pricing is 1% of tracked revenue. See [RevenueCat pricing](https://www.revenuecat.com/pricing/) for details.
</Info>

---

## Razorpay payment links for India

For **web-based checkout flows** or payment links (particularly useful in India), you can integrate [Razorpay](/razorpay).

<Note>
Razorpay checkout is a **web experience**—best for one-time purchases, donations or manual top-ups. For recurring mobile subscriptions tied to app store accounts, use Apple IAP or Google Play Billing instead.
</Note>

### When to use Razorpay

- **Direct payment links**: Send a customer a Razorpay link via SMS, email or in-app browser.
- **UPI, cards, wallets**: Support popular Indian payment methods outside the app stores.
- **Lower fees**: Razorpay charges ~2% vs 30% on app stores (but you lose the store's trust signals and one-tap purchase UX).

See the [Razorpay](/razorpay) page for setup instructions and webhook handling.

---

## Compliance & policies

<Warning title="App store review guidelines">
Both Apple and Google prohibit **alternative payment mechanisms** for digital goods (e.g. coins, premium features) sold inside the app. You **must** use IAP/Play Billing for such items. Razorpay links are only acceptable for physical goods, services or donations.
</Warning>

<AccordionGroup>
<Accordion title="Can I offer a cheaper subscription on my website?">
Yes, but you cannot advertise or link to it from the iOS/Android app (Apple/Google rules). Users who find your site independently can subscribe there, then sign in to the app to unlock features.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="What about promotional codes?">
Both stores support **promo codes** (Apple: Offer Codes; Google: Promo Codes). Generate them in the respective console and distribute via email, social media or influencer partnerships.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="How do refunds work?">
Apple and Google handle refunds directly. You'll receive a webhook (or RTDN) event when a refund is issued; revoke the user's entitlement in your database at that point.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Can I use Stripe for mobile subscriptions?">
Only for **physical goods or services** (e.g. a marketplace, event tickets). For digital content or features unlocked in the app, you must use native IAP.
</Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

---

## Testing purchases without spending money

<Tabs>
<Tab title="iOS Sandbox">
Create **sandbox test accounts** in App Store Connect → **Users and Access** → **Sandbox Testers**. Sign in with that Apple ID on your device (Settings → App Store → Sandbox Account) to make test purchases that don't charge a real card.
</Tab>

<Tab title="Android License Testing">
Add your Google account email under **Play Console** → **Setup** → **License Testing**. Purchases made by that account will complete instantly without payment.
</Tab>

<Tab title="RevenueCat">
RevenueCat mirrors sandbox/test purchases in its dashboard. You'll see test transactions labelled as **sandbox** so you can verify entitlement logic before going live.
</Tab>
</Tabs>

<Tip title="Accelerated renewals in sandbox">
Apple's sandbox compresses subscription durations: a one-month subscription renews every **5 minutes**. This lets you test renewal, expiry and grace-period logic quickly.
</Tip>

---

## Best practices

1. **Show clear pricing and terms** before the purchase sheet appears—both stores require transparency.
2. **Handle pending transactions**: A purchase can be interrupted (user switches apps, loses connectivity). Resume the transaction flow on next launch.
3. **Log all purchase events**: Store receipts and transaction IDs in your [database](/database-mongodb) for audit trails and customer support.
4. **Offer a restore-purchases button**: Users who reinstall or switch devices need a way to re-validate their entitlements.
5. **Monitor failed renewals**: Set up webhooks (RevenueCat or native RTDN) to catch billing issues and prompt users to update payment info.

<Success title="Ready to monetise">
With native IAP, RevenueCat entitlements and optional Razorpay links, you have flexible monetisation options for any mobile app. Ask your Emergent agent to implement the purchase flow that fits your business model.
</Success>

---

## Related pages

<CardGroup cols={2}>
<Card title="Razorpay" icon="credit-card" href="/razorpay">
Set up direct payment links for India (UPI, cards, wallets).
</Card>

<Card title="Database (MongoDB)" icon="database" href="/database-mongodb">
Store user entitlements, purchase history and subscription state.
</Card>

<Card title="Web ↔ Mobile conversion" icon="arrows-rotate" href="/web-mobile-conversion-canonical">
Understand how Emergent adapts your app for web and mobile platforms.
</Card>

<Card title="App takedown & content moderation" icon="gavel" href="/app-takedown-content-moderation">
Policies and procedures if your app faces a store violation.
</Card>
</CardGroup>
monetisation-in-app-purchases-subscripti.description: Monetise mobile apps via Apple IAP (30%/15% fees), Google Play Billing, cross-platform entitlements through RevenueCat, and Razorpay links for India.

clone-environment.title: Clone environment
clone-environment.content:
## What is Clone Environment?

The **Clone Environment** button creates an exact copy of your current environment—including all code, dependencies, configuration, and database state—into a new, independent environment. This gives you a working snapshot you can modify without affecting the original.

<Note>
Cloning is instantaneous and creates a fully functional copy. The new environment gets its own URL, database instance, and deployment pipeline.
</Note>

## When to Use Clone Environment

Clone Environment is ideal when you need a safe workspace to experiment or iterate without risk:

- **Test major changes** — Try a significant architectural shift, new framework version, or UI overhaul without touching your stable version.
- **Create feature branches** — Work on a new feature in isolation, then merge or discard based on results.
- **Preserve milestones** — Capture a working state before embarking on exploratory work you may want to roll back.
- **A/B testing** — Run two variants side-by-side with identical starting points and compare outcomes.
- **Onboard collaborators** — Give a teammate their own sandbox derived from your current build.

<Tip title="Quick recovery">
If you break something in the clone, simply discard it or clone again. The original environment remains untouched.
</Tip>

## When *Not* to Use Clone Environment

Cloning is powerful but not always the right tool:

- **Minor tweaks** — For small changes or bug fixes, just work directly in your environment. Undo is built into the chat history, and you can always ask Wingman to revert.
- **Production deployments** — Cloning doesn't deploy. If you want to release a stable version, use the deploy flow instead. See [The chat-to-deployment flow](/the-chat-to-deployment-flow).
- **Long-term parallel versions** — If you need ongoing feature branches or staging environments, consider a structured workflow rather than ad-hoc clones.
- **Database migration testing** — While the clone includes a snapshot of your database, changes to the cloned database do *not* sync back. If you're testing data migrations, be mindful that the clone's data is independent.

<Warning>
Cloning duplicates the database at the moment of cloning. Subsequent writes to either environment's database are isolated—they do not affect each other.
</Warning>

## How to Clone an Environment

<Steps>
  <Step title="Open the environment you want to copy">
    Navigate to the environment in your workspace. Make sure it's the one you want to snapshot.
  </Step>
  <Step title="Click Clone Environment">
    Find the **Clone Environment** button in the toolbar or environment settings. Click it.
  </Step>
  <Step title="Name your clone (optional)">
    You'll be prompted to give the new environment a name. Choose something descriptive like "experiment-new-ui" or "feature-checkout."
  </Step>
  <Step title="Work in the clone">
    The cloned environment opens immediately. You can chat with Wingman, modify code, and deploy—all without affecting the original.
  </Step>
</Steps>

<Info>
The clone inherits all environment variables, secrets, and integrations from the original. If you've configured a custom domain or MongoDB connection, those settings carry over.
</Info>

## What Gets Cloned

The following are duplicated into the new environment:

- **Source code** — Every file, folder, and dependency definition.
- **Configuration** — Environment variables, build settings, deployment config.
- **Database snapshot** — A copy of your MongoDB collections at the moment of cloning.
- **Jobs and background tasks** — Definitions and code (but not running state—cloned jobs start fresh).

The following are *not* cloned:

- **Deployment history** — The clone starts with no prior deploys; you can deploy it fresh.
- **Chat history** — The conversation with Wingman resets. The clone is a new workspace.
- **Custom domain bindings** — If the original has a custom domain, the clone gets a new auto-generated URL. You can bind a domain separately if needed. See [Custom domain](/custom-domain).

## Managing Clones

Each cloned environment is independent. You can:

- **Delete** — Remove a clone when you're done experimenting. This does not affect the original.
- **Merge changes** — If the clone proves successful, you can manually copy code back or describe the changes to Wingman in the original environment.
- **Deploy separately** — Each clone can be deployed to its own URL for side-by-side user testing.

<Tip title="Keep clones organized">
Use clear naming conventions (e.g., "clone-experiment-date" or "feature-name") so you can quickly identify which environment is which.
</Tip>

## Related Topics

<CardGroup cols={2}>
  <Card title="A Tour of the Workspace" icon="compass" href="/a-tour-of-the-workspace">
    Learn about environments, the chat interface, and workspace tools.
  </Card>
  <Card title="The Chat-to-Deployment Flow" icon="rocket" href="/the-chat-to-deployment-flow">
    Understand how to take an environment from idea to live deployment.
  </Card>
  <Card title="What is a Job?" icon="calendar" href="/what-is-a-job">
    Background tasks and scheduled jobs are cloned—learn how they work.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Database (MongoDB)" icon="database" href="/database-mongodb">
    Understand how database snapshots work in cloned environments.
  </Card>
</CardGroup>

faqs.title: FAQs
faqs.content:
## Frequently Asked Questions

<AccordionGroup>

<Accordion title="What is Emergent?">
Emergent is an agentic vibe-coding platform where you describe an app in natural language and AI agents build, test, and deploy it for you. You chat with the platform, refine your vision iteratively, and Emergent handles the implementation—front-end, back-end, database, hosting, and deployment.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="How does the chat-to-deployment flow work?">
You describe your app idea in the chat interface. Emergent's AI agents interpret your requirements, generate code, provision infrastructure, and deploy a working application. You can refine and iterate by continuing the conversation. For a detailed walkthrough, see [The chat-to-deployment flow](/the-chat-to-deployment-flow).
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Do I need to know how to code?">
No. Emergent is designed for users of all technical levels. You describe what you want in plain language, and the platform handles the technical implementation. If you *do* know how to code, you can also provide detailed technical guidance or even paste code snippets to steer the agents.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="What types of applications can I build?">
Emergent supports a wide range of applications including web apps, mobile apps (iOS and Android via React Native), dashboards, APIs, SaaS tools, MVPs, prototypes, and internal business tools. The platform handles full-stack development with database integration, authentication, payments, and more.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Can I convert a web app to mobile or vice versa?">
Yes. Emergent can convert web applications to React Native mobile apps and vice versa. The conversion process preserves your data and core functionality while adapting the UI and navigation patterns for the target platform. See [Web ↔ Mobile conversion](/web-mobile-conversion-canonical) for details.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="What technologies does Emergent use under the hood?">
Emergent builds apps using modern, production-ready stacks:

- **Front-end:** React, Next.js, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui components
- **Mobile:** React Native with Expo
- **Back-end:** Node.js, serverless functions, REST and GraphQL APIs
- **Database:** MongoDB Atlas (managed, scalable)
- **Hosting:** Vercel for web, Expo Application Services for mobile
- **Authentication:** Clerk, Auth0, or custom implementations
- **Payments:** Stripe integration

The specific stack may vary based on your app's requirements.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="How is my data stored and secured?">
Data is stored in a dedicated MongoDB Atlas database provisioned for your project. Each app gets its own isolated database with industry-standard encryption at rest and in transit. You own your data and can export it at any time. See [Database (MongoDB)](/database-mongodb) for more.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Can I use my own API keys or bring my own LLM?">
Yes. Emergent provides a [Universal LLM Key](/the-universal-llm-key) for convenience, but you can bring your own API keys for OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, or other providers. You can configure per-project LLM preferences and manage keys in your workspace settings.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="How do I deploy my app to production?">
Deployment happens automatically as part of the chat-to-deployment flow. Emergent provisions hosting (Vercel for web, Expo for mobile), configures environment variables, and pushes your app live. You get a live URL immediately. You can also connect a [custom domain](/custom-domain) to your deployed app.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Can I connect a custom domain to my app?">
Yes. Once your app is deployed, you can connect your own domain name through the workspace settings. Emergent handles DNS configuration and SSL certificate provisioning. See [Custom domain](/custom-domain) for step-by-step instructions.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="What happens if I want to iterate or make changes after deployment?">
Continue the conversation in chat. Describe the changes you want, and Emergent's agents will update the code, re-run tests, and deploy the new version. Your database and user data persist across iterations.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Can I export my code and self-host?">
Yes. You have full access to your application's source code through the workspace. You can export the codebase, clone the repository, and deploy it to any hosting provider you choose. Emergent does not lock you in.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Does Emergent support authentication and user management?">
Yes. You can request user authentication as part of your app requirements. Emergent integrates providers like Clerk, Auth0, or custom auth implementations with email/password, social logins, magic links, and role-based access control.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Can I integrate third-party APIs and services?">
Absolutely. Tell Emergent which APIs or services you want to integrate (Stripe, Twilio, SendGrid, Google Maps, etc.), and the agents will generate the integration code, handle authentication, and configure environment variables.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="How do I manage environment variables and secrets?">
Environment variables and secrets are managed through the workspace settings. You can add, edit, or remove variables, and they are securely injected into your app at build and runtime. Secrets are encrypted and never exposed in the codebase.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="What is the workspace and how do I navigate it?">
The workspace is your project hub where you can view code, logs, database records, deployment history, settings, and more. It provides a visual interface for monitoring and managing your app. See [A tour of the workspace](/a-tour-of-the-workspace) for a complete overview.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Can I collaborate with a team on an Emergent project?">
Team collaboration features vary by plan. You can invite collaborators to view or edit projects, manage permissions, and work together in the same workspace. Check your plan details for collaboration limits.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="What are the pricing plans and limits?">
Emergent offers multiple pricing tiers with different quotas for projects, deployments, compute, storage, and team members. Visit the Emergent pricing page or your account dashboard for the latest plan details and limits.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="How do I upgrade or downgrade my plan?">
You can change your subscription tier at any time from the billing section of your account settings. Upgrades take effect immediately; downgrades apply at the end of the current billing cycle.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="What happens if I hit a usage limit?">
If you reach a plan limit (projects, API calls, storage, etc.), you'll receive a notification. Depending on the limit, the platform may pause certain operations until you upgrade or the next billing cycle begins. Critical functionality like accessing your code and data remains available.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Can I cancel my subscription at any time?">
Yes. You can cancel your subscription from the billing settings. Your access continues until the end of the current billing period, after which your account transitions to a free or read-only tier (depending on plan structure).
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="What support options are available?">
Support options depend on your plan. All users have access to documentation, community forums, and email support. Higher-tier plans may include priority support, dedicated Slack channels, or live onboarding sessions.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="How do I report a bug or request a feature?">
Use the feedback widget in the workspace, or contact support via email. Feature requests are tracked and prioritized based on user demand. You can also join the Emergent community to vote on and discuss upcoming features.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Is there a limit to how many times I can iterate on an app?">
Iteration limits depend on your plan. Most plans allow unlimited iterations within reasonable usage bounds. Compute-intensive operations (like full re-builds) may count toward usage quotas.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Can I build apps in languages other than English?">
Yes. Emergent supports natural-language input in multiple languages. You can describe your app in your preferred language, and the platform will generate code and content accordingly.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Does Emergent support internationalization (i18n) in apps?">
Yes. You can request multi-language support for your app, and Emergent will generate i18n-ready code with locale management, translation keys, and language switchers.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="What testing does Emergent perform on my app?">
Emergent's agents run automated tests during the build process, including unit tests, integration tests, and basic end-to-end smoke tests. You can also request additional test coverage or specific testing scenarios.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Can I access the database directly?">
Yes. You can query and manage your MongoDB database through the workspace interface or by connecting directly using MongoDB clients with the provided connection string.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="How do I back up my database?">
MongoDB Atlas (Emergent's database provider) performs automatic backups. You can also export your data manually from the workspace or configure additional backup policies through Atlas settings.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="What happens to my data if I delete a project?">
<Warning>
Deleting a project permanently removes the codebase, database, and all associated resources. This action cannot be undone. Always export your code and data before deletion.
</Warning>
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Can I import an existing codebase into Emergent?">
Currently, Emergent is optimized for greenfield projects (building from scratch). Importing existing codebases is not directly supported, but you can describe your existing app and Emergent can recreate or extend it.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Does Emergent support mobile app store deployment?">
Yes. For React Native apps, Emergent integrates with Expo Application Services (EAS) to build and submit apps to the Apple App Store and Google Play Store. You'll need developer accounts with Apple and Google.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="How do I handle app updates after publishing to app stores?">
Continue iterating in Emergent as usual. When you're ready to release an update, Emergent can rebuild and submit the new version through EAS. You control the release schedule and versioning.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="What are the system requirements for using Emergent?">
Emergent is a cloud-based platform accessible via any modern web browser (Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge). No local installation or specific hardware is required. For mobile app testing, you can use simulators (included) or physical devices.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Can I use Emergent offline?">
No. Emergent is a cloud platform that requires an internet connection for the AI agents to build, test, and deploy your apps.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Where can I learn more about Emergent-specific terminology?">
See the [Glossary of Emergent terms](/glossary-of-emergent-terms) for definitions of platform-specific concepts like agents, vibes, canonical builds, and more.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="How does Emergent handle versioning and rollbacks?">
Emergent maintains a deployment history in the workspace. You can view past versions and roll back to a previous deployment if needed. Each deployment is tagged with a timestamp and changelog.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Can I schedule deployments or automate workflows?">
Advanced automation features (like scheduled deployments or CI/CD integrations) may be available on higher-tier plans or through API access. Check your plan details or contact support for specifics.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="What happens if an agent makes a mistake or breaks my app?">
Emergent agents are designed to test and validate changes before deployment. If an issue occurs, you can roll back to a previous version, describe the problem in chat, and the agents will attempt to fix it. You can also manually edit code in the workspace.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Is my intellectual property protected?">
Yes. You retain full ownership of the applications and content you create with Emergent. Emergent does not claim ownership of your ideas, code, or data.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Does Emergent comply with data protection regulations (GDPR, etc.)?">
Emergent follows industry best practices for data security and privacy. For specific compliance questions or data processing agreements, contact the Emergent legal or support team.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Can I white-label or resell apps built on Emergent?">
Yes. You own the apps you build and can white-label, resell, or commercialize them as you see fit. Check your plan's terms of service for any restrictions.
</Accordion>

</AccordionGroup>

---

<Callout type="info" title="Still have questions?">
If your question isn't answered here, check the rest of the documentation or reach out to Emergent support. We're here to help you succeed.
</Callout>

cloudinary.title: Cloudinary
cloudinary.content:
## Overview

Cloudinary is a cloud-based media management platform that provides image and video upload, storage, manipulation, optimization, and delivery via a global CDN. Integrating Cloudinary with your Emergent app enables you to offload media hosting, automatically optimize images for different devices, and apply transformations on-the-fly.

This guide walks you through connecting Cloudinary to your Emergent workspace and using it in your application.

---

## Prerequisites

Before you begin, you'll need:

- An Emergent workspace with an active app
- A Cloudinary account ([sign up free](https://cloudinary.com/users/register_free) if you don't have one)
- Your Cloudinary **Cloud Name**, **API Key**, and **API Secret** (found in the Cloudinary dashboard under **Settings → Account**)

---

## Adding Cloudinary credentials to Emergent

<Steps>
<Step title="Open your workspace settings">
Navigate to your workspace in Emergent and open **Settings** from the left sidebar.
</Step>

<Step title="Go to the Integrations tab">
Select the **Integrations** tab, then locate **Cloudinary** in the media & productivity section.
</Step>

<Step title="Enter your Cloudinary credentials">
Paste your **Cloud Name**, **API Key**, and **API Secret** into the respective fields. These values are available in your Cloudinary dashboard under **Settings → Account → API Keys**.

<Tip>
Store these credentials securely. Emergent encrypts integration secrets at rest and in transit.
</Tip>
</Step>

<Step title="Save the integration">
Click **Save**. Emergent will validate the credentials and confirm the connection.
</Step>
</Steps>

---

## Using Cloudinary in your app

Once connected, you can reference Cloudinary in chat to build features like image uploads, galleries, and on-the-fly transformations.

### Example prompts

<AccordionGroup>
<Accordion title="Upload profile pictures to Cloudinary">
"Add a profile picture upload on the user settings page. Store the images in Cloudinary and save the public URL in the user's MongoDB record."

Emergent will generate an upload widget or file input, upload to Cloudinary via its SDK, and persist the returned `secure_url` in your [database](/database-mongodb).
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Optimize and resize images automatically">
"When displaying product images, serve them from Cloudinary with automatic format selection and a max width of 800px."

The agent will construct Cloudinary transformation URLs (e.g., `w_800,f_auto,q_auto`) to deliver optimized images.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Build a photo gallery with lazy loading">
"Create a gallery page that fetches image URLs from MongoDB and displays them using Cloudinary's responsive breakpoints."

The agent will implement lazy-loaded thumbnails and full-size lightbox views, leveraging Cloudinary's transformation API.
</Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

---

## Common transformations

Cloudinary supports URL-based transformations. You can specify these in your prompts or manually in your code:

| Transformation | Parameter | Example |
|----------------|-----------|---------|
| Resize width | `w_<pixels>` | `w_400` |
| Resize height | `h_<pixels>` | `h_300` |
| Crop mode | `c_<mode>` | `c_fill`, `c_thumb` |
| Auto format | `f_auto` | Delivers WebP/AVIF where supported |
| Auto quality | `q_auto` | Optimizes compression |
| Blur | `e_blur:<strength>` | `e_blur:300` |
| Grayscale | `e_grayscale` | Converts to black-and-white |

Combine transformations in a single URL:

```
https://res.cloudinary.com/<cloud_name>/image/upload/w_600,h_400,c_fill,f_auto,q_auto/sample.jpg
```

<Info>
Ask the agent to apply specific transformations by describing the desired effect (e.g., "crop to square and optimize for mobile").
</Info>

---

## File upload patterns

Cloudinary offers several upload methods. Emergent agents can implement any of these based on your requirements:

<Columns cols={2}>
<Card title="Direct upload from browser" icon="upload">
Use Cloudinary's unsigned or signed upload presets to upload files directly from the client, bypassing your backend.
</Card>

<Card title="Server-side upload" icon="server">
Upload files via your backend (e.g., Node.js). Useful when you need to validate, resize, or process images before storing.
</Card>
</Columns>

### Unsigned vs. signed uploads

- **Unsigned**: Faster to set up; requires an upload preset configured in your Cloudinary dashboard. Best for public, low-risk uploads.
- **Signed**: Requires a signature generated server-side using your API secret. Recommended for user-generated content where you want access control.

<Warning>
Never expose your **API Secret** in client-side code. Use signed uploads or server-side proxies for secure workflows.
</Warning>

---

## Managing media assets

Cloudinary organizes assets into folders and supports tagging, metadata, and search:

- **Folders**: Specify a folder in the upload (e.g., `folder: "avatars"`). Assets are accessible at `.../<cloud_name>/image/upload/avatars/<public_id>`.
- **Tags**: Add tags during upload for easier filtering and retrieval.
- **Search & Admin API**: Use Cloudinary's Admin API to list, update, or delete assets programmatically.

You can ask Emergent agents to implement admin panels that list, search, or delete images via the Cloudinary Admin API.

---

## Video uploads and transformations

Cloudinary supports video as well as images. Common video transformations include:

- Transcoding to multiple formats (`f_auto` for adaptive delivery)
- Generating thumbnails at specific timestamps (`so_<seconds>`)
- Applying overlays, watermarks, and effects

Example prompt:

> "Let users upload demo videos to Cloudinary and display them with a play button thumbnail on the landing page."

The agent will handle upload, generate a poster image, and embed the video player.

---

## Troubleshooting

<AccordionGroup>
<Accordion title="Upload fails with 'Invalid signature'">
Check that your **API Secret** is correct and that the signature generation logic (if using signed uploads) matches Cloudinary's specification. Ensure the timestamp is recent (signatures expire after a short window).
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Images not loading or returning 404">
Verify the **Cloud Name** in your URLs. Ensure the `public_id` is correct and that the asset exists in your Cloudinary media library. Check folder paths if you're organizing assets.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Transformations not applying">
Confirm transformation syntax (e.g., `w_400,h_300,c_fill`). Transformations must appear before the `upload` segment in the URL. Clear browser cache if testing changes.
</Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

<Tip>
Use Cloudinary's [URL Inspector](https://cloudinary.com/documentation/image_transformations#url_based_image_transformations) to debug transformation URLs and preview results.
</Tip>

---

## Additional resources

<CardGroup cols={2}>
<Card title="Cloudinary Documentation" icon="book" href="https://cloudinary.com/documentation">
Official Cloudinary docs covering SDKs, transformations, and APIs.
</Card>

<Card title="Database (MongoDB)" icon="database" href="/database-mongodb">
Learn how to store Cloudinary URLs and metadata in your app's database.
</Card>

<Card title="Custom Domain" icon="globe" href="/custom-domain">
Serve Cloudinary assets through your own domain for a branded experience.
</Card>

<Card title="Glossary of Emergent Terms" icon="book-open" href="/glossary-of-emergent-terms">
Understand key Emergent concepts and terminology.
</Card>
</CardGroup>

---

## Next steps

With Cloudinary integrated, you can now:

- Build rich media galleries and portfolios
- Implement profile picture uploads with automatic cropping
- Deliver responsive, optimized images across devices
- Add video hosting and playback features

Describe your media workflow in chat, and the Emergent agents will scaffold the upload, transformation, and display logic for you.

forking.title: Forking
forking.content:
## What is Forking?

**Forking** creates a complete, independent copy of your current app — including its entire codebase, database schema, and chat history up to the fork point. The forked app runs as a separate project with its own build pipeline, database, and deployment.

Use forking when you want to:

- Experiment with a major architectural change without risking your production app
- Create a variant of an app for a different audience or use case
- Preserve a stable snapshot before attempting risky refactors

<Info>
Forking is different from [rollback](/rollback-when-the-agent-goes-wrong). Rollback rewinds your *current* app to an earlier state; forking creates a *new* app that diverges from the original.
</Info>

## How to Fork an App

<Steps>
<Step title="Open the app menu">
In the workspace header, click the app name dropdown or the three-dot menu next to your app title.
</Step>

<Step title="Select Fork">
Choose **Fork App** from the menu. The platform will duplicate the entire app state — code, database, chat history — into a new project.
</Step>

<Step title="Name the fork">
Give your fork a descriptive name (e.g., `MyApp – Experimental Redesign`) so you can distinguish it from the original.
</Step>

<Step title="Continue building">
The forked app appears in your workspace as a standalone project. Chat, build, and deploy independently. Changes to the fork do not affect the original app, and vice versa.
</Step>
</Steps>

<Tip>
Fork *before* starting a risky change. If the experiment succeeds, you can continue with the fork; if it fails, simply delete the fork and return to the original.
</Tip>

## What Gets Copied

When you fork an app, Emergent duplicates:

- **Codebase**: All files, dependencies, and configuration at the moment of the fork.
- **Database schema**: Table structures, indexes, and constraints. *Data rows are not copied* — the forked app starts with an empty database.
- **Chat history**: The entire conversation up to the fork point, so the agent retains context about why the code exists.
- **Build configuration**: Deployment settings, environment variables (non-secret), and integrations.

<Warning>
**Secrets and API keys** are *not* copied for security reasons. You must re-add any required secrets (database URLs, third-party API keys) in the forked app's settings before deploying.
</Warning>

## When to Fork vs. Rollback

| Scenario | Use |
|----------|-----|
| Undo a recent bad change | [Rollback](/rollback-when-the-agent-goes-wrong) |
| Preserve the current app and try a big experiment | **Fork** |
| Create a variant for a different customer or region | **Fork** |
| Recover from multiple bad changes over time | Rollback to a known-good state, *then* fork if you want to try a different approach in parallel |

## Managing Forked Apps

Forked apps consume credits independently. Each fork:

- Runs its own [build jobs](/what-is-a-job) and incurs credit costs for agent work and deployments.
- Maintains a separate database instance (even if empty initially).
- Appears in your workspace alongside the original.

<Note>
Delete forks you no longer need to avoid unnecessary credit usage and workspace clutter. Deleting a fork does not affect the original app.
</Note>

## Context Limits

Every chat — including the history in a forked app — operates within a **context window**: the maximum number of tokens (roughly words and code characters) the AI agent can "see" at once. Emergent uses models with large context windows, but even these have limits.

### How to Work Within Context Limits

- **Scope tasks narrowly**: Instead of "refactor the entire app," ask for one feature or module at a time.
- **Use multiple smaller projects**: If your app grows very large, consider splitting it into microservices or separate Emergent projects that communicate via APIs.
- **Fork strategically**: Forking resets the *future* chat (you start fresh after the fork), but the agent still carries the full pre-fork history in the forked app's context. If context is tight, fork early rather than late.

<Info>
When you approach context limits, Emergent's **Infinite Chat** system (described below) automatically compacts older messages to keep the conversation going.
</Info>

## Infinite Chat (Auto Context Compaction)

Emergent's **Infinite Chat** feature ensures long conversations never hit a hard wall. As your chat history grows, the platform automatically condenses older messages to free up space for new work.

### How It Works

<Steps>
<Step title="Squash at ~70% capacity">
When the chat reaches approximately **70% of the context window**, Emergent **squashes** older messages: it combines consecutive user-assistant exchanges into summary blocks that preserve key decisions and code changes but remove redundant back-and-forth.
</Step>

<Step title="Auto-compact at ~82.5% capacity">
At roughly **82.5% capacity**, the system performs a deeper **compaction**: it condenses multiple squashed blocks into high-level summaries, retaining architectural decisions and major feature descriptions while discarding fine-grained edits.
</Step>

<Step title="Truncation near 275K tokens">
If the chat approaches **~275,000 tokens** (the effective hard limit), Emergent truncates the oldest compacted summaries. Critical information — recent changes, active feature requests, and the current codebase state — always remain.
</Step>
</Steps>

<Tip>
You don't need to do anything to enable Infinite Chat. It runs automatically in the background, and you'll see a brief notification in the chat when compaction occurs.
</Tip>

### What This Means for You

- **Long-lived projects work seamlessly**: You can chat for weeks or months without manually restarting or losing context.
- **Fork preserves pre-fork context**: A forked app inherits the compacted history up to the fork point, so the agent still "remembers" why the original code exists — but the fork's *future* chat starts fresh, giving you more headroom.
- **Older details may fade**: After multiple compaction cycles, very early conversation details (e.g., initial brainstorming) may be summarized heavily. Keep important architectural notes in your codebase comments or README if you need them long-term.

<Note>
If you ever feel the agent has "forgotten" something important, re-state the requirement explicitly in chat. The agent always prioritizes your most recent instructions.
</Note>
forking.description: Forking an app to branch off into a separate app (with its own build/DB). See also Rollback in Build.

firebase.title: Firebase
firebase.content:
## Overview

Firebase is Google's app development platform that provides backend services including real-time databases, authentication, cloud storage, and hosting. You can integrate Firebase into your Emergent app to add features like user authentication, real-time data sync, file storage, and push notifications.

This guide walks you through connecting Firebase to your Emergent app and using common Firebase services.

<Note>
Firebase services are provisioned and billed directly by Google. You'll need a Google Cloud account and Firebase project to use these integrations.
</Note>

## Prerequisites

Before integrating Firebase, ensure you have:

- A Firebase project created in the [Firebase Console](https://console.firebase.google.com)
- Your Firebase project configuration (API keys and project IDs)
- A clear understanding of which Firebase services you need (Authentication, Firestore, Storage, etc.)

## Setting up Firebase

<Steps>
<Step title="Create a Firebase project">
If you haven't already, create a new Firebase project:

1. Go to the [Firebase Console](https://console.firebase.google.com)
2. Click **Add project** and follow the setup wizard
3. Enable Google Analytics if desired (optional but recommended)
</Step>

<Step title="Register your app in Firebase">
In your Firebase project console:

1. Click the **Web** icon (`</>`) to add a web app
2. Register your app with a nickname (e.g., "Emergent App")
3. Copy the Firebase configuration object that appears — you'll need this in the next step

The config object looks like:

```javascript
{
  apiKey: "AIza...",
  authDomain: "your-app.firebaseapp.com",
  projectId: "your-project-id",
  storageBucket: "your-app.appspot.com",
  messagingSenderId: "123456789",
  appId: "1:123456789:web:abcdef"
}
```
</Step>

<Step title="Add Firebase credentials to Emergent">
In your Emergent chat, describe what you need:

> "Add Firebase to this app. Use Firebase Authentication for user login and Firestore for the database. Here's my Firebase config: [paste your config object]"

The AI agents will:
- Install the necessary Firebase SDK packages
- Initialize Firebase with your configuration
- Set up the requested services
- Configure environment variables for sensitive keys

<Warning>
Never commit Firebase API keys directly in your code. The agents will automatically extract sensitive values into environment variables.
</Warning>
</Step>

<Step title="Enable Firebase services">
Back in the Firebase Console, enable the specific services you're using:

- **Authentication**: Go to **Authentication** → **Sign-in method** and enable your desired providers (Email/Password, Google, etc.)
- **Firestore**: Go to **Firestore Database** → **Create database** and choose a security mode (start in test mode for development)
- **Storage**: Go to **Storage** → **Get started** to enable Cloud Storage
- **Hosting**: Go to **Hosting** → **Get started** if you want Firebase to host your app
</Step>

<Step title="Test the integration">
Ask the agents to create a simple test feature:

> "Add a sign-up form that creates a new user with Firebase Authentication"

or

> "Create a button that saves a test document to Firestore"

Run your app and verify the Firebase service is working by checking the Firebase Console for new users, documents, or files.
</Step>
</Steps>

## Common Firebase use cases

<Tabs>
<Tab title="Authentication">
Firebase Authentication handles user sign-up, sign-in, and session management with minimal code.

**Example prompt:**
> "Add Firebase Authentication with email/password sign-up, a login page, and a logout button. Protect the /dashboard route so only authenticated users can access it."

The agents will create:
- Sign-up and login forms with validation
- Authentication state management
- Protected routes that redirect to login
- User session persistence
</Tab>

<Tab title="Firestore Database">
Firestore is a NoSQL document database with real-time sync capabilities.

**Example prompt:**
> "Use Firestore to store user profiles. When a user signs up, create a profile document with their name and email. Show a list of all profiles on the admin page with real-time updates."

The agents will:
- Set up Firestore collections and documents
- Implement real-time listeners for data changes
- Handle create, read, update, delete operations
- Add proper error handling
</Tab>

<Tab title="Cloud Storage">
Firebase Storage lets you upload and serve user-generated files like images, videos, and documents.

**Example prompt:**
> "Add a profile picture upload feature using Firebase Storage. Users should be able to select an image, upload it, and see a preview. Store the image URL in their Firestore profile."

The agents will create:
- File input and upload UI
- Progress tracking for uploads
- Image preview functionality
- Secure storage rules (you'll need to configure these in Firebase Console)
</Tab>

<Tab title="Security Rules">
Firebase services use security rules to control access to data and files.

**Example prompt:**
> "Show me the Firestore security rules needed so users can only read and write their own profile document, but everyone can read all profiles."

The agents will generate rules you can paste into the Firebase Console:

```javascript
rules_version = '2';
service cloud.firestore {
  match /databases/{database}/documents {
    match /profiles/{userId} {
      allow read: if true;
      allow write: if request.auth != null && request.auth.uid == userId;
    }
  }
}
```

<Info>
You must manually apply security rules in the Firebase Console. The agents cannot deploy rules directly but will provide the correct configuration.
</Info>
</Tab>
</Tabs>

## Environment variables

Firebase credentials are stored in environment variables to keep them secure:

| Variable | Purpose |
|----------|---------|
| `VITE_FIREBASE_API_KEY` | Firebase Web API key |
| `VITE_FIREBASE_AUTH_DOMAIN` | Authentication domain |
| `VITE_FIREBASE_PROJECT_ID` | Firebase project identifier |
| `VITE_FIREBASE_STORAGE_BUCKET` | Cloud Storage bucket |
| `VITE_FIREBASE_MESSAGING_SENDER_ID` | Cloud Messaging sender ID |
| `VITE_FIREBASE_APP_ID` | Firebase app identifier |

<Note>
The `VITE_` prefix makes these variables available in your frontend code (Vite convention). For sensitive server-side operations, use Firebase Admin SDK with service account credentials stored without the `VITE_` prefix.
</Note>

## Firebase vs. MongoDB

If you're deciding between Firebase and MongoDB for your Emergent app:

<Columns cols={2}>
<Card title="Choose Firebase if..." icon="flame">
- You need real-time data synchronization
- You want built-in authentication
- You prefer a fully managed solution
- You're building a mobile app (excellent mobile SDKs)
</Card>

<Card title="Choose MongoDB if..." icon="database">
- You need complex queries and aggregations
- You prefer traditional database structures
- You want more control over hosting
- See [Database (MongoDB)](/database-mongodb) for setup
</Card>
</Columns>

## Troubleshooting

<AccordionGroup>
<Accordion title="Firebase not initialized error">
This usually means the Firebase config wasn't loaded correctly. Check that:

- All `VITE_FIREBASE_*` environment variables are set
- You've restarted the dev server after adding env vars
- The Firebase initialization code runs before any Firebase service calls
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Permission denied errors">
Firebase denies access by default. You need to configure security rules:

1. Go to Firebase Console → Firestore/Storage
2. Click **Rules** tab
3. Update rules to allow your operations (start with test mode for development)
4. Publish the rules

<Warning title="Production security">
Never leave Firebase in test mode for production. Always configure proper authentication-based security rules before deploying.
</Warning>
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Authentication not persisting">
Firebase auth state should persist automatically. If users are logged out on refresh:

- Check that you're using `onAuthStateChanged` listener to restore sessions
- Verify no code is explicitly calling `signOut()` on page load
- Check browser console for Firebase errors

Ask the agents: *"Fix the authentication so users stay logged in when they refresh the page"*
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="CORS errors with Firebase Storage">
If you see CORS errors when uploading files:

1. Create a `cors.json` file with your allowed origins
2. Apply it using `gsutil cors set cors.json gs://your-bucket-name`
3. Or ask the agents: *"Show me how to configure CORS for my Firebase Storage bucket"*
</Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

## Next steps

<CardGroup cols={2}>
<Card title="Custom Domain" icon="globe" href="/custom-domain">
Configure a custom domain for your Firebase-hosted app
</Card>

<Card title="Web ↔ Mobile Conversion" icon="mobile" href="/web-mobile-conversion-canonical">
Convert your Firebase web app to mobile using the same backend
</Card>
</CardGroup>

how-the-agent-runs-workflow-stop-reasons.title: How the agent runs (workflow & stop reasons)
how-the-agent-runs-workflow-stop-reasons.content:
## The Temporal workflow loop

Every agent conversation runs as a long-lived Temporal workflow. When you send a message, the workflow spins up (or resumes) and the agent enters an iterative loop:

1. **Reason** — the LLM decides which tool to call next (or whether to reply to you).
2. **Act** — execute the chosen tool (write code, run tests, search the web, etc.).
3. **Observe** — collect the tool result and append it to the conversation context.
4. **Repeat** — loop back to step 1 until a stop condition is met.

This architecture lets the agent chain dozens of actions autonomously—committing files, spinning up preview servers, invoking subagents—without requiring your approval at every step.

<Info title="Temporal resilience">
Because the workflow state persists in Temporal, the agent can survive transient infrastructure failures and resume exactly where it left off.
</Info>

## Stop reasons

The loop terminates when any of these conditions is true:

| Stop reason | Meaning |
|-------------|---------|
| `context_overflow` | The conversation history exceeded the model's context window; the agent cannot fit the next turn. |
| `max_iterations` | The agent hit the per-turn iteration cap (typically 100 steps) to prevent runaway loops. |
| `insufficient_credits` | Your account balance dropped below the cost of the next tool call. |
| `handoff` | The agent explicitly handed control back to you (finished the task or needs clarification). |
| `error` | An unrecoverable workflow error occurred (rare; usually retried automatically). |

When the loop stops, you'll see a status indicator in the chat. A `handoff` stop is normal and means the agent is waiting for your next instruction. `context_overflow` or `max_iterations` usually signals the task grew too large for a single turn; break it into smaller requests or start a fresh conversation.

<Warning title="Context overflow">
If you hit `context_overflow` frequently, try asking the agent to summarize progress before starting a new subtask, or split the work across multiple chat threads.
</Warning>

## Iteration and time caps

To keep costs predictable and prevent infinite loops:

- **Iteration cap**: 100 tool calls per user message (adjustable in the future for enterprise plans).
- **Time cap**: workflows time out after 24 hours of wall-clock time, though most tasks complete in seconds to minutes.

The agent tracks its own loop count and will gracefully hand off to you as it approaches the iteration limit, summarizing what it accomplished and what remains.

## Agent tools & their credit cost

The agent has access to a rich built-in toolset via the **sandbox MCP server**:

- **File operations** — read, write, edit, list, move, delete files in your project.
- **Shell execution** — run `npm`, `pnpm`, framework CLIs, git commands.
- **Preview server** — spin up development servers and capture screenshots.
- **Codex code review** — static analysis and best-practice checks (powered by a dedicated review agent).
- **Testing agent** — writes and executes unit/integration/E2E tests in a separate subagent.
- **Design agent** — generates UI mockups and design assets.

<Info title="Free sandbox tools">
Most MCP sandbox tools (file I/O, shell, Codex) have **no additional credit cost** beyond the base LLM inference. You pay only for the model's input/output tokens.
</Info>

Some **server-side tools** do incur extra charges:

- **Web search** — ~0.5–1 credit per query (varies by provider).
- **Media generation** (images, videos) — cost depends on resolution and model; typically 5–20 credits per asset.

When the agent calls one of these tools, the credit deduction happens immediately. If your balance is too low, the workflow stops with `insufficient_credits` and prompts you to [recharge](/credit-expiry-recharging).

## E-3 autonomous phases

Emergent agents operate in three escalating autonomy levels, inspired by military engagement rules:

1. **E-1 (Supervised)** — the agent proposes each action and waits for your explicit approval before executing.
2. **E-2 (Semi-autonomous)** — the agent executes routine, low-risk actions (file edits, installs) without approval but asks before destructive operations (database migrations, deployments).
3. **E-3 (Fully autonomous)** — the agent runs end-to-end without interruption, only handing off when the task is complete or it needs clarification.

By default, production agents run in **E-3 mode** to maximize speed. You can dial this down in the workspace settings (coming soon) if you prefer tighter control.

<Tip>
E-3 mode is ideal for iterative development (bug fixes, feature additions). For major refactors or schema changes, consider dropping to E-2 to review migrations before they apply.
</Tip>

## Subagents and specialization

Complex tasks often spawn **subagents**—ephemeral worker agents with narrow mandates:

- **Testing subagent** — writes test cases, runs them, reports coverage. Invoked via the `run_tests` tool.
- **Design subagent** — generates wireframes, color palettes, component designs. Invoked via `generate_design`.
- **Review subagent (Codex)** — performs linting, security scans, style checks. Invoked automatically after major code changes.

Subagents run in parallel Temporal workflows and report results back to the parent agent. Their credit usage rolls up into your main conversation's total. This division of labor keeps context focused: the main agent handles orchestration, subagents handle depth.

## Auto-HITL (human-in-the-loop)

Even in E-3 mode, the agent will **automatically pause and ask for input** when:

- It encounters an ambiguous requirement ("Should the button be primary or secondary?").
- A tool fails multiple times and the agent can't auto-recover.
- The task requires a decision outside its training scope (legal compliance, branding choices).

This **Auto-HITL** mechanism ensures you stay in control of critical decisions without micromanaging every step. When the agent pauses, you'll see a highlighted question in the chat; answer it and the workflow resumes immediately.

<Note>
Auto-HITL questions count as `handoff` stops. The iteration and time caps pause while the agent waits for your reply.
</Note>

## Monitoring workflow health

The workspace UI displays:

- **Current step count** — how many iterations the agent has consumed this turn.
- **Estimated credits remaining** — live balance update as tools execute.
- **Subagent activity** — spinner badges when parallel workers are running.

If a workflow stalls or you suspect an infinite loop, you can **cancel** it from the chat overflow menu. The agent will gracefully shut down and hand off with a summary of partial progress.

For a deeper dive into workspace controls, see [A tour of the workspace](/a-tour-of-the-workspace).
