compare-the-4-windows.title: Compare the 4 windows
compare-the-4-windows.content:
## Choose the right window for your project When you start a new project in Emergent, you'll see four distinct windows. Each builds a different kind of application with its own stack, deployment target and capabilities. Read [What is Emergent?](/what-is-emergent) and [A tour of the workspace](/a-tour-of-the-workspace) first to understand how projects and windows work together. --- ## At-a-glance comparison | | **Fullstack Builder** | **Mobile App** | **Landing Page** | **Brainstorm** | |---|---|---|---|---| | **What it's for** | Multi-page web apps with authentication, databases, APIs and complex workflows | Native iOS and Android apps that run on phones and tablets | Single-page marketing sites, portfolios, campaign pages and simple informational sites | Exploring ideas, prototyping concepts and turning rough thoughts into structured specs | | **What it CAN do** | • Build SaaS tools, dashboards, marketplaces, internal tools
• Connect to PostgreSQL, Supabase, Firebase, external APIs
• User sign-up, login, role-based access
• Scheduled tasks, webhooks, payments, email
• Deploy to custom domains | • Build true native apps (Swift/Kotlin under the hood, **not** wrapped web views)
• Publish to Apple App Store and Google Play Store
• Use device features: camera, GPS, push notifications, biometrics
• Offline-first data, local storage
• Custom bundle IDs and app metadata | • Beautiful, responsive single-page sites
• Contact forms, analytics, SEO metadata
• Custom CSS animations and interactive sections
• Deploy to custom domains
• Fast static hosting | • Conversational spec refinement
• Generate project briefs, user stories, data models
• Export structured requirements to other windows
• Iterate on ideas with AI feedback | | **What it CAN'T do** | • Publish to native app stores (use Mobile App for that)
• Access device hardware like camera or GPS natively | • Run at a public web URL (mobile apps require installation)
• Use arbitrary npm packages (curated SDK only)
• Hot-reload local dev (preview via TestFlight/internal tracks) | • Multi-page navigation (everything is on one scrollable page)
• User authentication or databases
• Complex backend logic or scheduled tasks | • Execute or deploy code (it only produces specs and designs)
• Access databases or live APIs
• Persist state between sessions | | **Pick it when** | You need a full-featured web application with backend logic, user accounts or third-party integrations | You want a **real native app** that lives in app stores and uses phone hardware — not a website in a wrapper | You need a fast, focused marketing page or portfolio without the complexity of a full web app | You're not ready to build yet — you want to explore, refine and document your idea before committing to a stack | --- ## Key differences: web vs. native mobile The **Mobile App** window builds using native mobile frameworks (Swift for iOS, Kotlin for Android). This is **not** a web app wrapped in a WebView — it's a fully native application with its own binary, bundle ID and submission flow. **Practical implications:** - **Domain vs. bundle ID**: A Fullstack or Landing Page app deploys to a web domain (`myapp.com`). A Mobile App uses a reverse-domain bundle identifier (`com.mycompany.myapp`) and is distributed through app stores. - **Publication flow**: Web apps go live instantly when you deploy. Mobile apps require [build generation](/build-generation-for-a-pre-existing-play-store-app), app store review and user installation. - **Conversion**: You can port a Fullstack Builder project to Mobile App (or vice versa) using the [web ↔ mobile conversion](/web-mobile-conversion-canonical) flow, but the underlying code is completely rewritten. See [What kind of apps you can build?](/what-kind-of-apps-you-can-build) for real-world examples of each window in action. --- ## Mixing windows in one project A single Emergent project can contain multiple windows. Common patterns: - **Landing Page** (marketing site) + **Fullstack Builder** (web app) on different subdomains (`www.` vs. `app.`) - **Brainstorm** to define requirements → **Mobile App** to build the product - **Fullstack Builder** (admin dashboard) + **Mobile App** (customer-facing app) sharing the same backend Each window maintains its own codebase, deployment pipeline and [job](/what-is-a-job) history, but you can reference shared API endpoints, databases or design tokens across them. --- ## Still unsure? Real examples organized by use case and industry Learn how projects, windows and jobs fit together
compare-the-4-windows.description: 1. SINGLE TABLE PAGE. Columns = Fullstack Builder / Mobile App / Landing Page / Brainstorm; Rows = What it's for / What it CAN do / What it CAN'T do / Pick it when.

pinecone.title: Pinecone
pinecone.content:
## Overview

Pinecone is a vector database designed for storing and querying high-dimensional embeddings at scale. It's commonly used for semantic search, recommendation systems, and RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) applications where you need to find similar content based on meaning rather than exact text matches.

When building applications in Emergent that require vector storage and similarity search, you can integrate Pinecone to power features like intelligent search, content recommendations, or context retrieval for AI assistants.

## Use cases

Common scenarios where Pinecone adds value to your Emergent application:

- **Semantic search** — Find documents or content by meaning, not just keywords
- **RAG pipelines** — Store embeddings of your knowledge base and retrieve relevant context for LLM prompts
- **Recommendation engines** — Match users to similar items based on vector similarity
- **Duplicate detection** — Identify similar or duplicate content across large datasets
- **Question answering** — Retrieve the most relevant passages to answer user queries

## Prerequisites

Before connecting Pinecone to your Emergent application, you'll need:

- A Pinecone account (sign up at [pinecone.io](https://www.pinecone.io))
- A Pinecone API key
- Your Pinecone environment name
- An index created in your Pinecone project

<Note>
Pinecone offers a free tier suitable for development and testing. Check their pricing page for current limits and paid plan options.
</Note>

## Setting up Pinecone

<Steps>

<Step title="Create a Pinecone account and index">
If you haven't already, sign up for Pinecone and create an index in their console. You'll need to specify:

- **Index name** — A unique identifier for your vector collection
- **Dimensions** — Must match the embedding model you're using (e.g., 1536 for OpenAI `text-embedding-ada-002`, 768 for many sentence transformers)
- **Metric** — Distance metric for similarity (`cosine`, `euclidean`, or `dotproduct`)

Note your environment name (visible in the Pinecone console) — you'll need it for the connection.
</Step>

<Step title="Get your API key">
In the Pinecone console, navigate to **API Keys** and copy your API key. Keep this secure — it grants full access to your Pinecone project.
</Step>

<Step title="Add credentials to your Emergent app">
In your Emergent chat, describe that you need to connect to Pinecone:

```
I need to connect to Pinecone. My API key is pk-xxx and my environment is us-west1-gcp.
I want to use the index called "product-embeddings".
```

The AI agents will set up the integration, typically storing credentials as environment variables and installing the necessary client library.
</Step>

<Step title="Verify the connection">
Ask the AI to test the Pinecone connection:

```
Can you verify the Pinecone connection is working and show me the index stats?
```

The agents will write code to connect and query your index metadata, confirming everything is configured correctly.
</Step>

</Steps>

## Common integration patterns

### Storing embeddings

When you generate embeddings (using OpenAI, Cohere, or another provider), you'll typically:

1. Generate a vector embedding from your text content
2. Prepare metadata (e.g., document ID, title, source URL)
3. Upsert the vector and metadata to Pinecone

Describe what you want to store:

```
When a user uploads a document, split it into chunks, generate embeddings 
using OpenAI, and store each chunk's embedding in Pinecone with metadata 
including the document title, chunk index, and upload timestamp.
```

### Querying for similar vectors

To perform similarity search:

1. Generate an embedding for your query text
2. Query Pinecone with the embedding vector
3. Receive the most similar vectors and their metadata
4. Use the metadata to fetch and display the original content

Example request:

```
When a user searches, convert their query to an embedding and find the 
top 5 most similar document chunks from Pinecone. Display the source 
document titles and relevant excerpts.
```

### RAG with context retrieval

For retrieval-augmented generation:

1. User asks a question
2. Convert question to embedding and query Pinecone
3. Retrieve top-k most relevant passages
4. Include those passages in the LLM prompt as context
5. Generate an answer grounded in your knowledge base

Tell the AI:

```
Implement RAG: when the user asks a question, retrieve the 3 most 
relevant chunks from Pinecone and include them in the system prompt 
before calling the LLM. Show which sources were used.
```

## Best practices

<Callout type="tip" title="Match embedding dimensions">
Always ensure your Pinecone index dimensions match your embedding model's output size. Mismatched dimensions will cause upsert errors.
</Callout>

- **Batch operations** — Upsert vectors in batches (e.g., 100–1000 at a time) rather than one-by-one for better performance
- **Metadata filtering** — Use Pinecone's metadata filters to narrow search results before similarity ranking
- **Namespace organization** — Use namespaces to logically separate different datasets or user contexts within a single index
- **Monitor usage** — Track your query volume and vector count to stay within plan limits

<Warning>
Deleting an index in Pinecone is irreversible. Always confirm you're targeting the correct index before issuing delete commands.
</Warning>

## Security considerations

- **Environment variables** — Store your Pinecone API key in environment variables, never hardcode it in your application code
- **Access control** — Pinecone API keys grant full access to all indexes in a project; consider using separate projects for development and production
- **Data sensitivity** — Be mindful of what metadata you store alongside vectors; it's queryable and retrievable

<Info>
Emergent automatically handles secure credential storage when you provide API keys through chat. The agents will configure environment variables appropriately.
</Info>

## Troubleshooting

<AccordionGroup>

<Accordion title="Connection timeout or authentication errors">
Verify your API key and environment name are correct. Check the Pinecone console to ensure your API key is still active and hasn't been rotated.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Dimension mismatch errors">
Confirm your embedding model's output dimensions match the index configuration. You cannot change an index's dimensions after creation — you'll need to create a new index with the correct dimensions.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Slow query performance">
Consider reducing the number of results returned (`top_k`) or using metadata filters to narrow the search space. For very large indexes, check your Pinecone plan's performance tier.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Upsert failures or rate limiting">
Batch your upserts and add retry logic with exponential backoff. Free tier accounts have lower rate limits than paid plans.
</Accordion>

</AccordionGroup>

## Related resources

<CardGroup cols={2}>

<Card title="Database (MongoDB)" icon="database" href="/database-mongodb">
Store structured data and metadata alongside your vector embeddings
</Card>

<Card title="The Universal LLM Key" icon="key" href="/the-universal-llm-key">
Generate embeddings using OpenAI or other providers via Emergent's unified API
</Card>

</CardGroup>

## Next steps

Once Pinecone is connected:

- Describe the embedding workflow you want (which content to vectorize, when, and how)
- Ask the AI to implement search or RAG features using your Pinecone index
- Test with real queries to validate similarity search quality
- Monitor usage and adjust indexing strategies as your dataset grows

Emergent's AI agents will handle the implementation details, from client library setup to query optimization, while you focus on describing the user experience you want to create.

your-data-ownership.title: Your data & ownership
your-data-ownership.content:
## What happens if you stop paying

If your subscription ends or you cancel your paid plan, Emergent does not immediately delete your apps or data.

**Grace period**  
Your workspace enters a read-only state. You can still log in, view your projects, and export code to GitHub, but you cannot run new builds, deploy changes, or edit apps in the chat.

**Data retention**  
We retain your projects, source code, database snapshots and configuration for **30 days** after your subscription lapses. During this window you can:

- Reactivate your subscription to restore full access.
- Export every project's code to a GitHub repository (see [GitHub export & portability](#who-owns-the-code--portability) below).
- Download database backups if you have configured them.

<Warning title="After 30 days">
Projects and databases are permanently deleted. We cannot recover data once the retention window closes.
</Warning>

**Reactivating**  
Simply update your billing details in **Settings → Billing**. Your workspace, projects and databases are restored immediately.

---

## Who owns the code & portability

**You own everything Emergent builds for you.**  
All source code, prompts, configuration files and database schemas generated by the platform belong to you. Emergent claims no intellectual property rights over your apps.

### Exporting to GitHub

Every project includes a **one-click GitHub export**:

<Steps>
<Step title="Open your project">
Navigate to the workspace and select the app you want to export.
</Step>

<Step title="Push to GitHub">
Click **Export to GitHub** in the project menu. Emergent will create a new repository in your GitHub account (or push to an existing one you specify) with the complete source tree, `package.json`, environment variable templates, and a README.
</Step>

<Step title="Run anywhere">
The exported code is standard Node.js (or Python, depending on your stack). Clone the repo, install dependencies, configure environment variables, and deploy to any cloud provider—Vercel, AWS, Render, your own server.
</Step>
</Steps>

<Info>
The exported repository includes a **deployment guide** tailored to your app's stack and dependencies, so you can self-host or migrate without Emergent infrastructure.
</Info>

**Database portability**  
Your MongoDB database is hosted by Emergent, but you can export it at any time as a `.bson` archive or connect directly via the standard MongoDB connection string (available in your project's **Env & Secrets** panel). Restore the dump to MongoDB Atlas, a self-hosted instance, or any compatible service. See [Database (MongoDB)](/database-mongodb) for connection details.

---

## Backups & data safety

Emergent automatically takes **daily snapshots** of every project's MongoDB database. Snapshots are retained for **7 days** on all paid plans.

### Restoring a snapshot

<Steps>
<Step title="Open Database settings">
Go to your project's **Database** tab in the workspace.
</Step>

<Step title="Choose a snapshot">
Select a date from the **Backups** list and click **Restore**. This rolls your database back to that point in time.
</Step>

<Step title="Confirm">
Restoring overwrites the current database. Emergent takes a final snapshot of the live data before proceeding, so you have one last safety net.
</Step>
</Steps>

<Warning title="Manual backups recommended for critical data">
Automated snapshots cover accidental deletions and rollback scenarios, but for mission-critical apps we recommend exporting periodic manual backups. Use the **Export Database** button or `mongodump` via the connection string.
</Warning>

**What if I lose data outside the 7-day window?**  
Snapshots older than 7 days are purged automatically. If you need long-term archival, schedule regular exports to your own storage (S3, Google Drive, etc.) or use a MongoDB Atlas backup policy after exporting your database.

**Hardware and replication**  
Emergent's MongoDB clusters run on replicated infrastructure with automatic failover. Disk failures and transient outages do not cause data loss under normal conditions. However, backups remain your ultimate safety net.

---

## Platform stability & uptime

Emergent aims for **99.9% uptime** for the core platform (workspace, chat, build queue) and deployed production apps.

**Scheduled maintenance**  
We perform infrastructure updates during low-traffic windows (typically late UTC evenings) and announce them at least 24 hours in advance via email and the status page. Maintenance windows rarely exceed 15 minutes.

**Checking platform status**  
Visit **[status.emergent.app](https://status.emergent.app)** for real-time operational status, incident history, and uptime metrics. Subscribe to status notifications to receive alerts if an outage affects your workspace or deployed apps.

<Tip>
If your deployed app is slow or unresponsive, check the [App slow, crashing or cold-starting](/app-slow-crashing-or-cold-starting) troubleshooting guide first—many performance issues stem from cold starts or resource limits rather than platform-wide outages.
</Tip>

**Support during incidents**  
If the status page reports an ongoing incident, our engineering team is already investigating. You can find updates on the status page and in the **#incidents** channel of the Emergent community Discord (link in **Settings → Support**). For urgent production issues not covered by a known incident, email **support@emergent.app** or use the in-app chat.

auth0.title: Auth0
auth0.content:
## Overview

Auth0 is an identity platform that provides authentication and authorization as a service. Integrating Auth0 with your Emergent app enables secure user login, registration, and access control through industry-standard protocols like OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect.

This guide walks you through configuring Auth0 authentication in your Emergent application, from setting up your Auth0 tenant to implementing login flows.

<Note>
Auth0 offers a generous free tier suitable for development and small production apps. Check Auth0's pricing page for current limits.
</Note>

## Before you begin

You'll need:

- An Auth0 account ([sign up free](https://auth0.com/signup))
- An Emergent app where you want to add authentication
- Basic understanding of authentication concepts (optional but helpful)

## Setting up Auth0

<Steps>
<Step title="Create an Auth0 application">
1. Log in to your [Auth0 Dashboard](https://manage.auth0.com)
2. Navigate to **Applications** → **Applications** in the sidebar
3. Click **Create Application**
4. Give your application a name (e.g., "My Emergent App")
5. Select **Single Page Web Applications** as the application type
6. Click **Create**
</Step>

<Step title="Configure application settings">
In your new Auth0 application settings:

1. Note your **Domain** and **Client ID** — you'll need these for your Emergent app
2. Scroll to **Application URIs** section
3. Add your Emergent app URLs to **Allowed Callback URLs**:
   - Development: `http://localhost:3000/callback` (adjust port if different)
   - Production: `https://your-app-domain.com/callback`
4. Add the same URLs to **Allowed Logout URLs**
5. Add your app's base URL to **Allowed Web Origins**
6. Click **Save Changes** at the bottom

<Info>
If you've configured a [custom domain](/custom-domain) for your Emergent app, use that domain in the callback and logout URLs.
</Info>
</Step>

<Step title="Add Auth0 credentials to Emergent">
In your Emergent chat interface, provide your Auth0 configuration:

```
Add Auth0 authentication with these settings:
- Domain: your-tenant.auth0.com
- Client ID: your_client_id_here
```

The AI agents will integrate the Auth0 SDK and configure your application accordingly.
</Step>

<Step title="Describe your authentication flow">
Tell Emergent how you want authentication to work in your app. For example:

```
Users should:
- See a "Log In" button on the home page
- Be redirected to Auth0's hosted login
- Land on a dashboard after successful login
- Have access to their profile information
- Be able to log out from the navigation menu
```

The agents will implement route protection, session management, and UI components based on your requirements.
</Step>
</Steps>

## Common authentication patterns

<Tabs>
<Tab title="Protected routes">
Ask Emergent to restrict access to specific pages:

```
Make the /dashboard and /settings pages require authentication.
Redirect unauthenticated users to the home page.
```

The platform will implement route guards and handle redirects automatically.
</Tab>

<Tab title="User profile">
Access authenticated user information:

```
Show the user's name and email in the navigation bar.
Create a profile page displaying the user's Auth0 profile data.
```

Auth0 provides user metadata that your app can display and use for personalization.
</Tab>

<Tab title="Role-based access">
Implement authorization rules:

```
Add an "admin" role in Auth0.
Only users with the admin role can access the /admin page.
```

You'll need to configure roles in Auth0's dashboard under **User Management** → **Roles**, then reference them in your Emergent app logic.
</Tab>
</Tabs>

## Storing Auth0 configuration securely

<Warning>
Never hard-code your Auth0 credentials directly in your app description or chat messages that might be shared.
</Warning>

Best practices for credentials:

1. **During development**: Provide credentials in the chat — Emergent stores them as environment variables
2. **For production**: Credentials are automatically included in your deployed app's environment
3. **Team collaboration**: Auth0 credentials are scoped to your Emergent project; team members inherit access without seeing the raw values

## Advanced configuration

<AccordionGroup>
<Accordion title="Using Auth0 Rules and Actions">
Auth0 Rules and Actions let you customize the authentication pipeline (add claims, enrich profiles, integrate with external services).

Configure these directly in your Auth0 Dashboard under **Auth Pipeline**. Changes take effect immediately without needing to update your Emergent app.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Social login providers">
To enable Google, GitHub, or other social logins:

1. In Auth0 Dashboard, go to **Authentication** → **Social**
2. Enable and configure the providers you want
3. Auth0's Universal Login automatically shows these options to users

No changes needed in your Emergent app — the login UI updates automatically.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Multi-factor authentication">
Enable MFA in Auth0 Dashboard under **Security** → **Multi-factor Auth**:

1. Choose MFA factors (SMS, authenticator app, email)
2. Set enforcement rules (always, or based on conditions)
3. Configure the user experience

Auth0 handles the MFA flow; your Emergent app receives the final authenticated session.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Custom domains for Auth0">
Auth0 allows using your own domain for the login page (e.g., `auth.yourdomain.com` instead of `yourtenant.auth0.com`).

This is configured in Auth0's **Branding** → **Custom Domains** section and requires DNS verification. Consult Auth0's documentation for detailed steps.
</Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

## Database integration

If your app uses [MongoDB](/database-mongodb), you might want to sync Auth0 user IDs with your database records:

```
When a user logs in for the first time, create a user profile document 
in MongoDB with their Auth0 ID, email, and creation timestamp.
```

This creates a link between Auth0's identity management and your application's data model.

## Troubleshooting

<AccordionGroup>
<Accordion title="Callback URL mismatch error">
**Symptom**: After login, you see "Callback URL mismatch" or similar error.

**Solution**: Verify that the callback URL in your Auth0 application settings exactly matches the URL your app redirects to, including protocol (`http`/`https`) and port number.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="CORS errors during authentication">
**Symptom**: Browser console shows CORS errors when authenticating.

**Solution**: Add your app's origin to **Allowed Web Origins** in Auth0 application settings. Make sure to include the protocol and port (e.g., `http://localhost:3000`).
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Users can't log out">
**Symptom**: Logout doesn't work or users remain authenticated.

**Solution**: Ensure your logout URL is in **Allowed Logout URLs** in Auth0 settings. The app should call Auth0's logout endpoint, not just clear local session.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Lost or rotated credentials">
If you need to rotate your Auth0 Client Secret or have lost your credentials:

1. In Auth0 Dashboard, go to your application's **Settings**
2. Your **Client ID** and **Domain** are always visible
3. To rotate the **Client Secret**, use the rotation feature in the settings (not typically needed for SPAs)

Update your Emergent app by providing the new credentials in chat.
</Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

## Next steps

<CardGroup cols={2}>
<Card title="Database (MongoDB)" icon="database" href="/database-mongodb">
Store user preferences and application data alongside Auth0 identities
</Card>
<Card title="Custom domain" icon="globe" href="/custom-domain">
Use your own domain for a professional authentication experience
</Card>
</CardGroup>

publishing-to-the-stores.title: Publishing to the stores
publishing-to-the-stores.content:
## Overview

Publishing your Emergent-built mobile app to the App Store and Google Play requires coordination across three platforms: Emergent, Expo Application Services (EAS), and the respective app stores. This guide walks you through the one-time setup, the submission process, and the critical safeguards that protect your ability to update the app in the future.

<Note>
Start setting up your developer accounts **early**—Apple Developer approval can take 24–48 hours, and you cannot submit an iOS build without it.
</Note>

---

## Expo & developer accounts

Before you can publish, you need accounts on three services:

<Steps>
<Step title="Create an Expo account">
Sign up at [expo.dev](https://expo.dev) if you don't already have one. Expo Application Services (EAS) orchestrates your cloud builds and store submissions.
</Step>

<Step title="Enroll in the Apple Developer Program">
Visit [developer.apple.com/programs](https://developer.apple.com/programs) and enroll. Apple manually reviews your application, which typically takes **24–48 hours**. You cannot submit an iOS app without an active paid membership ($99/year for individuals).
</Step>

<Step title="Create a Google Play Console account">
Register at [play.google.com/console](https://play.google.com/console). Google charges a one-time $25 registration fee and approves accounts more quickly than Apple—often within hours.
</Step>
</Steps>

<Tip title="Timeline buffer">
Create all three accounts at the start of your project, even if you're weeks away from launch. Apple's approval delay is the most common cause of missed release dates.
</Tip>

---

## Setting up EAS for store builds

Expo Application Services (EAS) produces the final `.ipa` (iOS) and `.aab` (Android) binaries that you upload to the stores.

<Steps>
<Step title="Install the EAS CLI">
Open your terminal and run:

```bash
npm install -g eas-cli
```
</Step>

<Step title="Log in to your Expo account">
```bash
eas login
```
Enter the credentials you created in the previous section.
</Step>

<Step title="Link your Emergent project">
Navigate to your project directory (the one Emergent generated) and run:

```bash
eas build:configure
```

EAS will create an `eas.json` configuration file with default build profiles.
</Step>

<Step title="Configure app credentials">
For **iOS**, EAS will prompt you to generate or upload provisioning profiles and certificates. Choose **"Let EAS manage credentials"** unless you have an existing setup.

For **Android**, EAS will guide you through keystore generation. **Critically important**: this keystore becomes your app's permanent identity—see the [Signing & keystore](#signing--keystore) section below.
</Step>

<Step title="Run your first build">
Test the pipeline with a production build:

```bash
eas build --platform ios --profile production
eas build --platform android --profile production
```

EAS uploads your code to Expo's cloud, compiles the native binary, and returns a download link. This process takes 10–20 minutes per platform.
</Step>
</Steps>

<Info>
EAS builds run in the cloud, so you don't need a Mac to build for iOS. All you need is the Apple Developer enrollment from step 2.
</Info>

---

## iOS vs Android publishing flow

While both platforms require a signed binary and a store listing, the review timelines and compliance requirements differ:

| **Step** | **iOS (App Store Connect)** | **Android (Google Play Console)** |
|----------|-----------------------------|------------------------------------|
| **Build artifact** | `.ipa` file from EAS | `.aab` (Android App Bundle) from EAS |
| **Store listing** | Create app record in App Store Connect; add screenshots, description, support URL, privacy policy | Create app record in Play Console; add screenshots, description, privacy policy, content rating questionnaire |
| **Compliance** | Privacy Nutrition Label (declare data collection); declare third-party SDKs if using analytics, ads, or auth | Data safety form (similar to iOS); declare permissions; must complete content rating questionnaire |
| **Submit for review** | Upload `.ipa` via Transporter or Xcode; submit for review | Upload `.aab` directly in Play Console; submit for review |
| **Review timeline** | **1–3 days** (Apple manually reviews every submission) | Usually **same-day** (often within hours; Google uses automated + spot checks) |
| **Rejection handling** | Apple provides feedback in Resolution Center; fix issues and resubmit (another 1–3 day wait) | Google sends email with policy violation details; fix and resubmit (usually re-reviewed within hours) |

<Warning title="Lock your build before writing the listing">
Do not finalize your store screenshots and description until your build is stable. If you need to change features after submitting metadata, you'll have to update screenshots and potentially re-record demo videos.
</Warning>

### Privacy & compliance

Both stores require you to disclose what data your app collects:

- **iOS Privacy Nutrition Label**: In App Store Connect, declare each data type (location, contacts, analytics identifiers, etc.) and whether it's linked to the user's identity.
- **Android Data safety**: In Play Console, complete the data safety form with similar disclosures.

If you integrate third-party SDKs (analytics, crash reporting, authentication), review their documentation for required disclosures. For example, Firebase Analytics requires you to declare analytics data collection.

<Tip>
Emergent's [data privacy](/data-privacy) page lists the data handling characteristics of common integrations in the [Key integrations catalogue](/key-integrations-catalogue).
</Tip>

---

## Signing & keystore

### Android keystore: the app's permanent identity

When you build an Android app for the first time, EAS generates a **keystore**—a cryptographic file that signs your `.aab`. Google Play uses this signature to verify that updates come from the legitimate developer.

<Danger title="Losing the keystore = losing the app">
Once you publish an app signed with a keystore, **every future update must use the same keystore**. If you lose it, you cannot update the app—you would have to publish a completely new app under a different package name, losing all existing users and reviews.
</Danger>

**Safeguards:**

<Steps>
<Step title="Download and back up the keystore">
After your first `eas build --platform android`, download the keystore from the EAS dashboard (`eas credentials` → select your project → download keystore). Store it in **two secure locations** (e.g., encrypted cloud storage + a password manager vault).
</Step>

<Step title="Enable Google Play App Signing (recommended)">
In Google Play Console, opt in to **Google Play App Signing**. You upload your `.aab` signed with your original keystore, and Google re-signs it with a separate "app signing key" that Google manages. If you lose your upload keystore, Google support can reset it—but the app signing key (which users see) remains intact.
</Step>
</Steps>

### iOS certificates

iOS uses certificates and provisioning profiles managed through your Apple Developer account. If you chose **"Let EAS manage credentials"**, Expo stores these securely and rotates them as needed. You don't need to back them up manually.

---

## App updates after publishing

Releasing a new version follows the same build-and-submit flow:

<Steps>
<Step title="Increment the version number">
In your `app.json` (or `app.config.js`), bump the `version` field (e.g., `"1.0.0"` → `"1.1.0"`) and the platform-specific build numbers (`ios.buildNumber`, `android.versionCode`).
</Step>

<Step title="Build the new version">
```bash
eas build --platform ios --profile production
eas build --platform android --profile production
```
</Step>

<Step title="Submit to the stores">
Upload the new `.ipa` to App Store Connect and the new `.aab` to Google Play Console. Both platforms detect that this is an update to an existing app (matched by bundle ID / package name).
</Step>

<Step title="Wait for review">
iOS updates go through the same 1–3 day review process. Google Play updates are typically approved within hours.
</Step>
</Steps>

<Warning title="Android keystore must match">
For Android, the `.aab` **must** be signed with the original keystore (or the upload keystore if you enabled Google Play App Signing). A mismatched signature will be rejected with an error like `"Upload certificate doesn't match previous upload certificate"`.
</Warning>

<Info title="Over-the-air updates for non-native changes">
If your update only changes JavaScript/TypeScript code (no new native dependencies or permissions), you can use **Expo Updates** to push changes instantly without going through store review. See the Expo documentation for details. Store submissions are required whenever you modify native code, add permissions, or change the app's binary.
</Info>

---

## Next steps

<CardGroup cols={2}>
<Card title="Push notifications" icon="bell" href="/push-notifications">
Set up Firebase Cloud Messaging (Android) and APNs (iOS) to send notifications to your published app.
</Card>

<Card title="Pre-existing Play Store app" icon="rotate" href="/build-generation-for-a-pre-existing-play-store-app">
Migrating an existing app to Emergent? Learn how to preserve your package name and keystore.
</Card>

<Card title="Data privacy" icon="shield-check" href="/data-privacy">
Understand how Emergent-built apps handle user data and what to disclose in store listings.
</Card>

<Card title="App performance troubleshooting" icon="gauge" href="/app-slow-crashing-or-cold-starting">
Diagnose slow launches, crashes, or memory issues before submitting to the stores.
</Card>
</CardGroup>

migrate-to-your-own-database.title: Migrate to your own database
migrate-to-your-own-database.content:
## When & why to migrate

By default, every deployed Emergent app stores its data in a **managed MongoDB database** provided by the platform. This database is included in your subscription at no additional cost and scales automatically to handle typical workloads.

<Info>
Database migration is only available for **deployed** apps. Apps in development always use the Emergent-managed database.
</Info>

You may want to migrate to your own external MongoDB database when:

- **You need advanced control** over backups, retention policies, or access patterns
- **You're approaching production scale** and want dedicated resources or performance SLAs
- **You have compliance requirements** that mandate a specific cloud region or provider
- **You want to consolidate data** across multiple services in your own infrastructure
- **You plan to take your app outside Emergent** and want full ownership of the database layer

<Callout type="tip" title="Data ownership">
Your data is always yours, even on the managed database. See [Your data & ownership](/your-data-ownership) for details on exports and portability.
</Callout>

Most apps run successfully on the Emergent-managed database indefinitely. Migration is optional and typically reserved for apps with specific infrastructure or compliance needs.

## The migration process

Migrating to your own database is designed to be **zero-downtime**. Your app continues to serve traffic while data is copied in the background.

<Steps>
<Step title="Provision your MongoDB database">
Set up a MongoDB instance with your preferred provider (MongoDB Atlas, AWS DocumentDB, self-hosted, etc.). Ensure it's accessible from the internet or configured with the appropriate network rules.

You'll need a **connection string** in the standard MongoDB format:

```
mongodb+srv://username:password@cluster.provider.net/database_name
```
</Step>

<Step title="Add the DATABASE_URL environment variable">
In your app's deployment settings, add a new environment variable:

- **Key**: `DATABASE_URL`
- **Value**: Your MongoDB connection string

The platform automatically detects this variable and triggers the migration process.
</Step>

<Step title="Background migration begins">
Emergent starts copying data from the managed database to your external database. This happens in the background without interrupting your app.

- **Writes continue to the Emergent database** during migration
- **Reads are served from the Emergent database** until migration completes
- Migration time depends on data volume (typically minutes to hours)
</Step>

<Step title="Cutover and synchronization">
Once the initial copy is complete, Emergent synchronizes any writes that occurred during migration, then switches your app to use the new database.

- **The app restarts automatically** to connect to the new database
- **Cold start time may be slightly longer** on first request ([learn more](/app-slow-crashing-or-cold-starting))
- The managed database is retained for 7 days as a rollback option
</Step>
</Steps>

<Warning>
Ensure your external database has sufficient resources and connection limits for your app's workload. The Emergent-managed database automatically scales; your own database does not.
</Warning>

### Rolling back

If you encounter issues after migration, you can roll back by removing the `DATABASE_URL` environment variable. Emergent will restore service using the managed database (available for 7 days post-migration).

<Note>
Any writes to your external database after cutover **will not** be reflected if you roll back. If possible, test the migration on a staging or development copy first.
</Note>

### After migration

Once your app is running on your external database:

- **You are responsible for backups, monitoring, and scaling**
- Emergent continues to deploy, build, and serve your app normally
- The managed database is permanently deleted after the 7-day retention window

For more on how data is handled in Emergent, see [Database (MongoDB)](/database-mongodb) and [Your data & ownership](/your-data-ownership).
